questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Methods of organizing, summarizing and presenting data in an informative way are called
questions.explanation: Descriptive statistics organises, summarises and presents data using tables, charts and measures such as the mean. Option B, inferential statistics, goes further and draws conclusions about a population from a sample. Options C and D describe the kind of statistics (theory versus application), not this task.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: The methods used to determine something about a population on the basis of a sample are called
questions.explanation: Inferential statistics uses information from a sample to make estimates, predictions or decisions about the whole population. Option B, descriptive statistics, only summarises the data actually collected. Options C and D refer to broad branches of the subject rather than this method.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: When the characteristic being studied is nonnumeric, it is called a
questions.explanation: A qualitative variable records a non-numeric characteristic such as hall of residence, gender or colour. Option A, quantitative, is the opposite and is measured with numbers. Options C and D, discrete and continuous, are both types of quantitative variable.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: When the variable studied can be reported numerically, the variable is called a
questions.explanation: A quantitative variable is one whose values are numbers, such as age, income in naira or exam score. Option B, qualitative, describes non-numeric categories. Options C and D describe the role a variable plays in a relationship, not whether it is numeric.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: A set of all units of interest in a study is called a
questions.explanation: A population is the complete set of all units of interest in a study, for example every student at UNILAG. Option A, a sample, is only part of that set. Options C and D are numerical measures describing a population or a sample, not the set of units itself.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: A part of the population selected for study is called a
questions.explanation: A sample is the part of the population that is actually selected and studied. Option D, a parameter, is a numerical summary of the whole population. Option A is the characteristic being measured, and option B, data, is the set of recorded values.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: mu (the population mean) is an example of a
questions.explanation: The population mean mu describes the whole population, so it is a population parameter. Option B, a sample statistic, would be the sample mean x-bar. Option C is a different parameter (sigma^2), and option D is another measure of location.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an example of a non-probability sampling method?
questions.explanation: Random sampling gives every unit a known chance of selection, so it is a probability method, not a non-probability one. Options A, C and D, purposive, judgment and accidental sampling, all depend on the researcher's choice or convenience, so they are non-probability methods.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: The population variance is denoted by
questions.explanation: Population variance is written sigma^2 (sigma squared), since it is the square of the population standard deviation sigma. Option B, sigma alone, is the population standard deviation, option A, mu, is the population mean, and option C, rho, usually denotes a population correlation coefficient.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Statistics published by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the International Labour Organization (ILO), when used by a business, are ____ data.
questions.explanation: These figures come from outside the business (external) and were already collected and published by someone else before the business uses them (secondary). Options A and B are wrong because the data do not come from the firm's own records, and C is wrong because the user did not collect the data first-hand.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: From the point of view of a business, government and non-government publications are ____ data sources.
questions.explanation: Publications are produced outside the business (external) and contain data already collected by someone else (secondary). B would require the business to collect the data itself from outside, while C and D refer to data from the firm's own records.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: A quantity whose value does not change is called a
questions.explanation: A constant keeps the same value throughout, for example the number of days in a week. A variable (B) takes different values, while a parameter (C) and a statistic (D) are summary measures of a population and a sample respectively.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: A parameter is a measure that is computed from
questions.explanation: A parameter is a numerical characteristic of a whole population, such as the population mean mu. A measure computed from sample data (B) is called a statistic, and test statistics (C) are calculated from samples for hypothesis testing.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: The value taken by a constant is
questions.explanation: A constant takes one fixed value that does not change from case to case. Option C describes a variable, whose values change, and a constant can be any fixed number, so it need not be zero (A) or negative (D).

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: A questionnaire survey is a method used to collect
questions.explanation: With a questionnaire the investigator collects fresh, first-hand information directly from respondents, which is primary data. Secondary (A), published (B) and archival (D) data already exist and were collected by someone else.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Which of these represents qualitative data?

options.b: Liking or disliking of a product by 500 persons
options.c: The income of a government worker in a city

questions.explanation: Liking or disliking is an attribute that puts people into categories rather than measuring them with numbers, so it is qualitative data. Height (A), income (C) and crop yield (D) are all measured numerically, so they are quantitative.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Data that have already been collected by someone else are called
questions.explanation: Secondary data are taken from existing records or publications where someone else has already collected and recorded them. Raw data (A) are data not yet organised, which could be primary or secondary, and arrayed data (B) are simply data arranged in order.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: A statistic is a numerical quantity that is calculated from a
questions.explanation: A statistic, such as the sample mean, is computed from sample data and is used to estimate a population parameter. A value calculated from the whole population (A) or a complete census (C) is a parameter, which also rules out D.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Analysis of labour turnover and performance appraisal are examples of the role of statistics in
questions.explanation: Labour turnover and staff performance are about the workforce, so these are uses of statistics in personnel (human resource) management. Finance (B) uses statistics for things like investment and budgeting, marketing (C) for sales and market research, and production (D) for quality control and output planning.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Statistical methods that require data measured on an interval or ratio scale are called ____ statistics.
questions.explanation: Parametric methods work with numerical data on interval or ratio scales, where means and standard deviations are meaningful. Non-parametric methods (B) are used for nominal and ordinal data, while C and D are not names for this branch.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: A set of activities that repeatedly converts inputs into outputs under the same conditions is called a
questions.explanation: A process is a series of activities that turns inputs into outputs, such as a bottling line turning raw materials into filled bottles, again and again under the same conditions. A sample (A) and a population (D) are groups of items being studied, and a parameter (B) is a measure describing a population.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Statistical methods used for data measured on an ordinal or nominal scale are called ____ statistics.
questions.explanation: Nominal and ordinal data are categories or ranks, so means and standard deviations are not meaningful and non-parametric methods are used. Parametric methods (A) need interval or ratio data.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Discrete and continuous variables are the two types of ____ variable.
questions.explanation: Quantitative variables are numerical, and they are either discrete (counted, like the number of students in a hall) or continuous (measured, like height). Qualitative variables (A) are categories or attributes, so they are not split into discrete and continuous.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Sample statistics are usually denoted by
questions.explanation: Sample statistics use Roman (English) letters, such as x-bar for the sample mean and s for the sample standard deviation. Lower case Greek letters (D), such as mu and sigma, are used for population parameters.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: A scale of measurement on which both the differences between values and the ratios of values are meaningful, because it has a true zero, is the ____ scale.
questions.explanation: The ratio scale has a true zero, so both differences and ratios make sense, for example 40 kg is twice 20 kg. The interval scale (D) has meaningful differences but no true zero, so ratios are not meaningful there, as with temperature in Celsius; nominal (A) and ordinal (C) scales do not have meaningful differences.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Questions in a questionnaire that allow respondents to answer in any way they like are called
questions.explanation: Open-ended questions give no fixed answers, so respondents reply freely in their own words. Closed-ended questions (D), including multiple-choice (A) and itemised (B) formats, restrict respondents to a set of given answers.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: In statistics, a sample means
questions.explanation: A sample is a part (subset) of the population selected for study. All the items under investigation (C) make up the population, and A is circular because it defines a sample in terms of itself.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: A characteristic that can take different values is called a
questions.explanation: A variable is a characteristic whose value changes from one individual or item to another, such as age or income. A constant (A) has a fixed value, and a parameter (C) and statistic (D) are summary measures, not characteristics of individual items.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: The symbol mu (the Greek letter) is used to denote the
questions.explanation: mu stands for the population mean. The population variance (A) is sigma^2 and the population standard deviation (C) is sigma, while the sample mean (D) uses the Roman symbol x-bar.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: A qualitative variable is one whose values are ____
questions.explanation: A qualitative (categorical) variable records a quality or category, such as gender, faculty or marital status, so its values are labels rather than numbers. Option B describes a quantitative variable. Options C and D, continuous and discrete, are the two kinds of quantitative variable, so they do not describe qualitative data.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: In descriptive statistics, the main objective is to ____

options.b: Infer something about the population from a sample

questions.explanation: Descriptive statistics organizes, summarizes and presents the data actually collected, using tables, charts, averages and measures of spread. Option B is the aim of inferential statistics, which goes beyond the data to draw conclusions about a population. Option A is too narrow, since an average is only one of many descriptive tools.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: In inferential statistics, the main objective is to ____

options.b: Infer something about the population from a sample

questions.explanation: Inferential statistics uses information from a sample to estimate, test or predict something about the larger population it came from. Option C and Option D describe descriptive statistics, which only summarizes the data in hand. Option A is just one calculation and does not by itself make any inference.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a method of collecting primary data?

options.a: Copying figures from published government reports

questions.explanation: Primary data are collected firsthand by the investigator for a specific purpose, which is exactly what telephone interviews (B), mail questionnaires (C) and door-to-door surveys (D) do. Copying figures from published reports uses data someone else already collected, so it gives secondary data.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: A quantitative variable is one whose values are ____
questions.explanation: A quantitative variable records amounts or counts, so its values are numbers, for example age, income or number of children. Option A describes a qualitative variable. Options C and D are too narrow because a quantitative variable can be either continuous or discrete.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: The science of collecting, organizing, presenting, analysing and interpreting data to assist in making more effective decisions is called:
questions.explanation: Statistics (plural, as a subject) is the science of collecting, organizing, presenting, analysing and interpreting data to help decision making. Option A, a statistic, is a single numerical measure calculated from a sample, such as a sample mean. A parameter (B) is a measure of a population, and a population (C) is the full set of items being studied.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: A numerical characteristic of a population (such as the population mean) is called a:
questions.explanation: A parameter is a numerical measure that describes a population, such as the population mean or population proportion. Option A, a statistic, is the corresponding measure computed from a sample. A variable (C) is the characteristic being measured, and a sample (D) is a subset of the population.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: A numerical characteristic of a sample (such as the sample mean) is called a:
questions.explanation: A statistic is a numerical measure calculated from sample data, such as the sample mean or sample proportion, and it is often used to estimate a parameter. Option C, a parameter, is the matching measure for the whole population. A variable (A) is the characteristic being measured, not a summary measure.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Data collected by an investigator for the first time, for a specific purpose and use, are called:
questions.explanation: Primary data are collected directly, for the first time, by the person or organization that needs them for a specific purpose, for example through a survey or interview. Option C, secondary data, are taken from existing records that someone else collected. Options A and D describe the type of variable, not where the data came from.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: A variable that can take only certain separate (countable) values within a range is called a:
questions.explanation: A discrete variable takes only separate, countable values, such as the number of students in a class (0, 1, 2, ...), with gaps between possible values. Option A, a continuous variable, can take any value within a range, such as height or weight. Option B is too broad, because quantitative variables include both discrete and continuous ones.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: The variable that provides the basis for estimating or predicting another variable is called the:
questions.explanation: The independent (explanatory) variable is the one whose known values are used to estimate or predict another variable, for example advertising spend used to predict sales. Option A, the dependent variable, is the one being predicted. Options C and D describe the type of data, not the role a variable plays in estimation.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: The variable that is being predicted or estimated is called the:
questions.explanation: The dependent (response) variable is the one whose value is predicted or estimated from other variables, for example sales predicted from advertising spend. Option B, the independent variable, is the one used to make the prediction. Options C and D describe the type of data rather than its role.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Monthly rainfall (in mm) in a city over the last ten years is an example of a:
questions.explanation: Rainfall is measured, not counted, and can take any value within a range (for example 112.4 mm or 112.45 mm), so it is a continuous variable. Option A, a discrete variable, only takes separate countable values like the number of rainy days. Options C and D are for categories, while rainfall is numeric.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of descriptive statistics?

options.a: A census shows that 70% of the people in a country live in rural areas
options.b: 50% of people are likely to vote in the next national election
options.c: 20% of the bulbs a factory will produce next month are expected to be defective
options.d: A sample is used to estimate next year's rise in prices

questions.explanation: Option A simply reports what was found in data already collected from everyone counted, so it describes the data and is descriptive statistics. Options B, C and D all go beyond the data to predict or estimate something not yet observed, which is inferential statistics.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of inferential statistics?

options.a: The percentage of smokers among the people interviewed in a survey
options.b: The percentage of skilled workers currently employed in a factory
options.c: An estimate, based on a sample, of the increase in prices next year
options.d: The average age of all staff in a company, from staff records

questions.explanation: Estimating next year's price increase from sample data draws a conclusion about something beyond the data in hand, which is what inferential statistics does. Options A, B and D only summarize data that have already been collected about the group in question, so they are descriptive statistics.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: The branch of statistics that deals with the development of statistical methods and their theory is called:
questions.explanation: Mathematical or theoretical statistics develops and proves statistical methods, often using probability theory. Option C, applied statistics, uses these methods to solve practical problems in fields such as business and economics. Options A and B are areas where statistics is applied, not the branch that develops the methods.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: A variable that can take any numerical value within a given range is called a:
questions.explanation: A continuous variable can take any value in an interval, including fractions and decimals, such as weight or time. Option D, a discrete variable, takes only separate countable values. Options B and C describe categorical data, which are not measured numerically at all.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: A measurement scale that allows data to be ranked but does not allow meaningful arithmetic operations on the values is the:
questions.explanation: The ordinal scale places data in a meaningful order or rank, but the differences between ranks are not fixed, so adding or subtracting the values has no meaning. Option A, the nominal scale, only labels categories with no order. Options B and D, interval and ratio scales, both have fixed units so differences can be calculated.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: A measurement scale in which values are grouped into qualitative categories that can be ranked in a meaningful order is the:
questions.explanation: The ordinal scale has categories with a natural order, for example customer ratings of poor, fair, good and excellent. Option A, the nominal scale, also uses categories but they have no order, such as state of origin. Options C and D are numeric scales with fixed units, not ranked qualitative categories.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: A measure of central tendency computed using data from the whole population is called a:
questions.explanation: A measure calculated from every member of the population, such as the population mean, is a population parameter. Option A, a sample statistic, comes from only part of the population, and Option C, a sample estimate, is a statistic used to estimate a parameter.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: A measure of central tendency computed from sample data drawn from a population is called a
questions.explanation: Any numerical measure computed from a sample, such as the sample mean x-bar, is a sample statistic. Option A, a population parameter, is the corresponding value for the whole population, usually unknown. Option B, sampling error, is the difference between a statistic and the parameter, and option D refers to a value obtained by studying every member of the population.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Which source of data generally helps an investigator to save both time and money?

options.a: Primary data collected by personal interviews
options.b: Primary data collected by direct observation
options.d: A complete census of the population

questions.explanation: Secondary data have already been collected and published by someone else, such as the NBS or CBN, so the investigator avoids the cost and time of fieldwork. Options A and B both involve gathering fresh primary data, which is slower and more expensive. Option D is the most costly method of all because every member of the population is studied.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Misrepresentation and misunderstanding of questions are best reduced when primary data are collected by
questions.explanation: In a personal interview the investigator is face to face with the respondent and can explain any question that is unclear, so misunderstandings are cleared up on the spot. Options A and C rely on the respondent reading the questionnaire alone, with nobody to clarify confusing questions. Option D gives some contact but without seeing the respondent or following up, misunderstandings are harder to catch.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Once a questionnaire has been drafted, it is advisable to first test it on a small group of respondents. This trial is called
questions.explanation: A pilot survey is a small trial run of the questionnaire that reveals confusing or badly worded questions before the main survey starts. Option B, a census, covers the entire population, the opposite of a small group. Option C, the final survey, is what the pilot prepares for, and option D is not a standard type of survey.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: The lottery method of selecting a sample is a method of
questions.explanation: In the lottery method every member of the population is written on a slip, the slips are mixed and the sample is drawn blindly, so every member has an equal chance of being selected, which is simple random sampling. Options B and C are non-random methods where the investigator picks the units. Option D first divides the population into strata, which the plain lottery method does not do.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Which of the following statements about sampling is correct?

options.a: A good sample provides reasonably accurate information about the population
options.b: A good sample provides totally accurate information about the population
options.c: A good sample cannot provide reasonably accurate information about the population

questions.explanation: A well-chosen, representative sample gives estimates that are reasonably close to the true population values at much lower cost than a census. Option B is wrong because every sample carries some sampling error, so it can never be totally accurate. Option C contradicts the whole reason for sampling, and so D is also wrong.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: A researcher conducts a study where they gather data from every single member of the target population. What is this method of data collection called?
questions.explanation: A census collects data from every single member of the target population. Option A, sampling, studies only a part of the population, while experimental design and case study describe research approaches, not complete enumeration.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: A researcher uses data previously collected and published by the National Bureau of Statistics for a new study. This type of data is classified as:
questions.explanation: Data already collected and published by another body, such as the National Bureau of Statistics, are secondary data for the new study. Option A, primary data, would be collected first-hand by the researcher, and option B describes the nature of the data, not its source.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Which of the following variables is an example of quantitative discrete data?

options.a: The number of students in a Statistics class
options.b: The temperature of a classroom in Celsius
options.c: The weight of a newborn baby
options.d: The eye color of participants in a study

questions.explanation: The number of students is counted in whole numbers, so it is quantitative discrete data. Options B and C (temperature and weight) are measured on a continuous scale, and option D (eye colour) is qualitative.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: In the context of data collection methods, which of the following best describes 'Primary Data'?

options.a: Data gathered by the researcher specifically for the current study through direct observation or surveys.
options.b: Data that is purely qualitative and cannot be represented using numerical scales.
options.c: Data that has already been collected by another party and is available in journals or government reports.
options.d: Data that can only be obtained by taking a complete census of the population.

questions.explanation: Primary data are collected first-hand by the researcher for the current study, for example through surveys, interviews or observation. Option C describes secondary data, and option B is wrong because primary data can be quantitative or qualitative.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Statistics is best defined as:

options.a: The collection and presentation of numerical data only
options.b: The science of collecting, organizing, analyzing, and interpreting data for decision-making
options.c: A branch of mathematics dealing only with pure numbers
options.d: A method of counting population size

questions.explanation: Statistics is the science of collecting, organizing, analyzing and interpreting data to support decisions. Option A is too narrow because it stops at collection and presentation, and option D is just one possible use of statistics.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of primary data?

options.c: Direct interviews conducted by a researcher

questions.explanation: Primary data are collected first-hand by the researcher, and direct interviews are a classic primary method. Options A, B and D are published by others, so to the researcher they are secondary data.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Secondary data is data that:

options.a: Is freshly collected from the field
options.b: Was collected by another party for a different purpose
options.c: Is only available through government databases

questions.explanation: Secondary data already exist because another party collected them for a different purpose. Option A describes primary data, and options C and D are too narrow since secondary data come from many sources and can be qualitative too.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: In business research, a 'population' refers to:

options.a: Only the human beings being studied
options.b: The total collection of all elements about which information is sought
options.c: A portion of a larger group selected for study
options.d: Only numerical data in a given study

questions.explanation: A population is the entire collection of all elements (people, firms, items) about which information is sought. Option C defines a sample, and option A is wrong because a population need not be human.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of qualitative data?
questions.explanation: Brand preference is a category or label, so it is qualitative data. Options A, B and D are all numbers obtained by measuring or counting, so they are quantitative.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: A census differs from a sample survey in that it:

options.b: Collects data from every member of the population
options.d: Provides estimates rather than exact values

questions.explanation: A census covers every member of the population, whereas a sample survey covers only part of it. Options A and D actually describe a sample survey, which uses inference to give estimates.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Which sampling method ensures every member of the population has an equal chance of selection?
questions.explanation: In simple random sampling every member of the population has an equal chance of being selected. Option A, stratified sampling, first splits the population into groups, and option D, purposive sampling, relies on the researcher's judgement, so selection chances are not equal.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Structured questionnaires are characterized by:

options.c: Fixed, predetermined questions with defined response options

questions.explanation: A structured questionnaire uses fixed, predetermined questions with set response options, so every respondent answers the same way. Options A, B and D describe unstructured approaches such as open-ended questions or informal interviews.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Does the following question deal with a population or a sample? 'What is the average fuel consumption of cars driven by all UNILAG students?'
questions.explanation: The question covers every car driven by all UNILAG students, the entire group of interest, so it deals with a population. Option B would apply only if a subset of students were chosen, and options C and D are not types of group at all.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Does the following question deal with a population or a sample? 'What percentage of 500 students selected at random support a new hostel policy?'
questions.explanation: The 500 students are a subset chosen at random from the wider student body, so this is a sample. Option A would need every student to be included, and option C (a statistic) is the percentage calculated from the sample, not the group itself.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Does the following question deal with a population or a sample? 'What is the range of income of all residents of Yaba?'
questions.explanation: The question refers to all residents of the area, the whole group of interest, so it deals with a population. Option B would apply only if some residents were selected, and the range itself would then be a statistic, not the group (option C).

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: A firm of chartered accountants in Lagos examines a randomly selected portion of a client's invoices instead of every invoice during an audit. This is an application of statistics in
questions.explanation: Public accounting firms use statistical sampling procedures when conducting audits for their clients, so this is an accounting application. Option C would involve monitoring a production process, and option D would involve studying customers and sales.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: A supermarket chain in Ikeja uses data captured by electronic point-of-sale scanners at its checkout counters to study what customers buy. This is mainly an application of statistics in
questions.explanation: Electronic point-of-sale scanners at retail checkouts collect data for marketing research, such as which products sell together. Option A refers to statistical sampling in audits, and option D refers to forecasting the economy, which is not what the supermarket is doing.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Which of the following is the best example of the use of statistics in production?

options.a: Using quality control charts to monitor a bottling line's output
options.b: Using sampling procedures to audit a client's accounts
options.c: Using economic data to forecast next year's inflation rate
options.d: Using price-earnings ratios to recommend shares to investors

questions.explanation: In production, statistical quality control charts are used to monitor the output of a production process. Option D is a finance application, option B is an accounting application and option C is an economics application.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: An investment adviser in Victoria Island uses price-earnings ratios and dividend yields to guide the shares she recommends to clients. This is an application of statistics in
questions.explanation: Financial advisers use price-earnings ratios and dividend yields to guide investment recommendations, which is a finance application. Option A would involve customer and sales research, and option B would involve audit sampling.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: In statistics, the facts and figures that are collected, summarized, analyzed and interpreted are called
questions.explanation: Data are the facts and figures collected, summarized, analyzed and interpreted. Option A is a characteristic of interest that data are recorded on, option D refers to the entities on which data are collected, and option C is a numerical measure describing a population.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: All the data collected in a particular study are referred to as the
questions.explanation: A data set is the full collection of data gathered in one study. Option A is a list of population elements from which a sample is chosen, option B is the set of measurements for just one element, and option D is the whole group being studied, not the data recorded on it.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: The entities on which data are collected are called
questions.explanation: Elements are the entities (people, firms, items) on which data are collected, for example each student in a university. Option D is a characteristic measured on the elements, and option A is the set of measurements collected for one particular element.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: The set of measurements collected for a particular element is called
questions.explanation: An observation is the set of measurements recorded for one element, such as one row in a data table. Option D is a single characteristic measured across all elements (a column), and option B is a subset of the population.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: A data table lists five quoted companies in rows, with columns for stock exchange, annual sales and earnings per share. In this data set, 'annual sales' is
questions.explanation: Annual sales is a characteristic measured on every company, so it is a variable. Option B would be each company itself, and option D would be one company's full row of measurements (its exchange, sales and earnings per share together).

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: A researcher records 4 variables (age, hall of residence, monthly allowance and CGPA) for each of 25 UNILAG students. How many data values are in the complete data set?
questions.explanation: The total number of data values equals the number of elements multiplied by the number of variables, so 25 x 4 = 100. Option B wrongly adds 25 + 4, option A counts only the elements, and option D multiplies by 5 instead of 4.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Which of the following correctly lists the four scales of measurement from the lowest to the highest level?
questions.explanation: Nominal is the lowest level, followed by ordinal, interval, and finally ratio as the highest level, with each level having all the properties of the one below it plus more. Option D gives the correct scales but from highest to lowest, while options C and B mix up the order.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: In statistics, the scale of measurement of a variable is important mainly because it

options.a: Decides whether the data are cross-sectional or time series
options.b: Indicates which data summarization and statistical analyses are most appropriate
options.c: Determines how large the sample size must be for the study
options.d: Shows whether the data were collected from primary or secondary sources

questions.explanation: The scale determines how much information the data contain and therefore which summaries and analyses are appropriate. Option C is a sampling design issue, option D is about the source of data, and option A is about when the data were collected, none of which is fixed by the scale.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Data that are labels or names used to identify an attribute of an element, with no meaningful order, are measured on the
questions.explanation: The nominal scale uses labels or names only to identify an attribute, and no order or ranking can be imposed. Option A adds a meaningful order or rank, while options C and B are numeric scales with fixed units of measure.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: A Lagos bank codes its customers' state of origin as 1 = Lagos, 2 = Ogun, 3 = Oyo. The variable 'state of origin' is measured on the
questions.explanation: The numbers here are only codes that classify customers; 3 is not 'more' than 1, so the data are nominal. Option B would require the codes to have a meaningful order, and options A and D need equal fixed units between values, which codes for states do not have.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Data that have all the properties of nominal data, and for which the order or rank of the data is meaningful, are measured on the
questions.explanation: Ordinal data are labels that can also be ranked, so the order is meaningful. Option C has no meaningful order at all, while options D and B also need the gaps between values to be in fixed units of measure.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: A firm grades its staff as 1 = Managing Director, 2 = Manager, 3 = Supervisor, 4 = Clerk. The variable 'position in the firm' is measured on the
questions.explanation: The codes show rank within the organization, so the order matters but the gaps between positions are not equal units; this is ordinal data. Option B ignores the meaningful order, and options A and D would require equal, fixed differences between positions.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Which of the following is TRUE of ordinal level data?

options.a: Differences between values are comparable and the zero point is absolute
options.b: Values are only labels and no order can be imposed on them
options.c: Differences between values are comparable but the zero point is arbitrary
options.d: The relative magnitude of values is meaningful but differences between them are not comparable

questions.explanation: With ordinal data we know which value is higher (rank), but we cannot say the gaps between ranks are equal. Option A describes ratio data, option B describes nominal data, and option C describes interval data.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Data that have the properties of ordinal data, where the interval between observations is expressed in a fixed unit of measure but the zero point is arbitrary, are measured on the
questions.explanation: Interval data have order and equal fixed-unit gaps, but zero does not mean 'nothing', so ratios are not meaningful. Option A also has an absolute zero, and option C lacks the fixed unit between observations.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Temperature measured in degrees Celsius is an example of data on the
questions.explanation: Differences in Celsius temperature are in fixed units, but 0 degrees C does not mean 'no temperature', so it is an interval scale; 20 degrees C is not 'twice as hot' as 10 degrees C. Option C would need a true zero, and option B ignores that the differences are equal and comparable.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: The feature that distinguishes the ratio scale from the interval scale is that the ratio scale

options.a: Uses a fixed unit of measure between observations
options.b: Uses numeric codes to identify categories
options.c: Has values that can be arranged in a meaningful order
options.d: Has a true zero indicating that nothing exists for the variable

questions.explanation: A ratio scale must contain a zero value that means nothing exists for the variable at that point, which makes ratios meaningful. Options C and A are properties shared by both interval and ratio data, and option B can apply even to nominal data.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Shop A in Balogun Market made sales of N400,000 last week while Shop B made N100,000, so Shop A sold four times as much as Shop B. Sales revenue is measured on the
questions.explanation: Revenue has a true zero (N0 means no sales), so the statement 'four times as much' is meaningful, which is the mark of ratio data. Option A allows meaningful differences but not meaningful ratios, and options D and C are not based on fixed numeric units.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Which of the following variables is measured on the ratio scale?

options.a: Department in which a student is enrolled
options.b: Weight of a bag of rice in kilograms
options.c: Ranking of five brands of soft drink in a taste test
options.d: Temperature of a cold room in degrees Celsius

questions.explanation: Weight has a true zero and one bag can be twice as heavy as another, so it is ratio data. Option D is interval because 0 degrees Celsius is not an absence of temperature, option C is ordinal, and option A is nominal.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an example of ratio level data?

options.a: Calendar year in which a company was founded
options.b: Inventory turnover ratio of a retailer
options.c: Annual profit of a company in naira

questions.explanation: Calendar time is interval data: the year 0 is an arbitrary starting point, so it makes no sense to say one year is 'twice' another. Options C, D and B are all ratio data, since monetary variables, heights and financial ratios all have a true zero.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Which statement correctly compares interval and ratio data?

options.a: Interval data are qualitative while ratio data are quantitative
options.b: Both have comparable differences, but only ratio data have an absolute zero
options.c: Ratio data have order but interval data have no meaningful order
options.d: Both have an absolute zero, but only interval data have comparable differences

questions.explanation: Interval and ratio data both have order and equal, comparable differences; the difference is that ratio data have an absolute (natural) zero while interval data have an arbitrary zero. Option A is wrong because both are numeric, quantitative scales, and option C is wrong because both have meaningful order.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: At the nominal level of measurement, the only meaningful operations on the data are
questions.explanation: Nominal data can only be classified into categories and counted, for example counting how many customers come from each state. Option D first becomes meaningful at the ordinal level, and options C and A need interval or ratio data.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Which type of statistical methods is generally appropriate for nominal and ordinal data?
questions.explanation: Because nominal and ordinal data only support counting and ranking, nonparametric methods are used for them. Option B, parametric methods, are used for interval and ratio data, where arithmetic operations are meaningful.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: In measurement, the feature that marks the specific beginning of a scale, which in the best scales is an absolute zero, is called the
questions.explanation: The origin marks the specific beginning of a scale, and the best scales start from an absolute zero. Option C is the arranging of objects in their proper positions, and option A specifies the relative gaps between positions on the scale.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: In terms of the three characteristics of a measurement scale (origin, order and distance), the nominal scale has

options.a: Order and distance, but no specific origin
options.c: No origin, no order and no distance
options.d: Order only, but no origin or distance

questions.explanation: The nominal scale only names categories, so it has no origin, no order and no distance. Option D describes the ordinal scale, option A the interval scale, and option B the ratio scale.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Data consisting of labels or names used to identify an attribute of each element, often called categorical data, are
questions.explanation: Qualitative data are labels or names for attributes and are often called categorical data. Option D tells how many or how much, option B is a type of quantitative data obtained by measuring, and option A refers to data collected over several time periods.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Qualitative data use which scales of measurement?
questions.explanation: Qualitative (categorical) data are measured on either the nominal or ordinal scale. Option B lists the scales used by quantitative data, and options A and C each wrongly include a quantitative scale.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Which of the following statements about qualitative data is TRUE?

options.a: They always use the ratio scale
options.b: They can be either numeric or nonnumeric
options.d: They allow all ordinary arithmetic operations

questions.explanation: Qualitative data can be words (e.g. 'Accounting') or numeric codes (e.g. 1 = Accounting), so they may be numeric or nonnumeric. Option C is a property of quantitative data, and options A and D describe quantitative ratio data, for which arithmetic is meaningful.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Data that indicate how many or how much, are always numeric, and for which ordinary arithmetic operations are meaningful, are called
questions.explanation: Quantitative data measure how many or how much, are always numeric and support ordinary arithmetic. Options D, A and B all refer to labels or categories, where arithmetic is not meaningful.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Compared with qualitative data, quantitative data generally

options.a: Can only be summarized by counting categories
options.b: Offer more alternatives for statistical analysis
options.c: Must be measured on the nominal scale
options.d: Offer fewer alternatives for statistical analysis

questions.explanation: In general there are more alternatives for statistical analysis when data are quantitative, because arithmetic is meaningful. Option D reverses this, since analyses of qualitative data are rather limited, and options A and C describe qualitative data.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: For a sample of customers, a bank records the 'method of payment' (cash, card or transfer). This variable is
questions.explanation: Method of payment is a label with no natural order, so it is qualitative and nominal. Option C would require the categories to have a meaningful rank, and options B and A would require numeric measurements of how many or how much.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: A drinks company sells its product in small, medium and large sizes. The variable 'drink size' (small/medium/large) is
questions.explanation: The sizes are category labels that have a natural order, so they are qualitative and ordinal. Option C ignores the meaningful order, and options A and D would apply only if size were recorded as a number such as millilitres or a count.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Quantitative data that measure 'how many', usually obtained by counting, are called
questions.explanation: Discrete data measure how many and are obtained by counting, so they take a finite or countable number of values. Option B measures how much and is obtained by measuring, while options A and C are qualitative scales.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Variables which can assume an infinite number of possible values, usually obtained by measurement, are called
questions.explanation: Continuous variables are measured (e.g. length, weight, time) and can take any value within a range. Option C variables are counted and take countable values, and options B and A are non-numeric categories.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Which of the following is a discrete variable?

options.a: Weight of a bag of cement
options.b: Number of customers served at a bank branch in a day
options.c: Distance from Yaba to the UNILAG main gate
options.d: Time taken to serve a customer at the counter

questions.explanation: The number of customers is counted, so it can only be 0, 1, 2 and so on, which makes it discrete; you cannot serve 2.63 customers. Options D, A and C are all measured quantities (time, weight, distance), so they are continuous.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: The weight of a parcel is recorded to the nearest kilogram as 64 kg. The true weight x lies in the interval
questions.explanation: Continuous data are rounded, so a value recorded as 64 to the nearest whole number is really anything from 63.5 up to (but not including) 64.5. Option C is twice too wide, option B assumes the value was cut off rather than rounded, and option D treats the value as if it were recorded to one decimal place.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: The length of a piece of cable is recorded to two decimal places as 2.47 metres. The true length x lies in the interval
questions.explanation: A value recorded to two decimal places has boundaries with one more decimal place ending in 5, so 2.47 means 2.465 <= x < 2.475. Option D is twice as wide as it should be, and option A assumes the value was cut off rather than rounded.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: A variable whose values are determined by chance is called a
questions.explanation: A random variable takes values that are determined by chance, such as the number of customers arriving in the next hour. Option C is a quantity that does not vary at all, and option B is a variable defined by its non-numeric values, not by chance.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: A researcher records the number of students enrolled in each faculty of UNILAG (Law, Engineering, Management Sciences, and so on) in the 2026 session. These data are
questions.explanation: The figures cover many faculties at the same point in time, so they are cross-sectional. Option C would track one faculty across several years, option D would come from a controlled study, and option B is a scale of measurement, while student numbers are counts.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: An analyst records the monthly sales of a single Lagos supermarket for each of the last 36 months. These data are
questions.explanation: Data on one unit collected over several time periods are time series data. Option C would compare many units at one point in time, and options A and B describe labels, whereas sales are numeric.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Information collected directly for a specific purpose, usually by the person who needs it, is called
questions.explanation: Primary data are gathered first-hand for the specific purpose at hand. Option D is taken from an existing source where it was already recorded, while options A and B describe when data were collected rather than who collected them.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: A marketing student uses inflation figures already published by the National Bureau of Statistics for her project. The data she uses are
questions.explanation: The figures were already recorded and published by another body, so for the student they are secondary data. Option C would apply only if she had collected the figures herself for her project, and option B would require her to control variables in a study.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an existing source of data?

options.a: Records kept by a department within the firm
options.d: A questionnaire the researcher designs and administers for a new study

questions.explanation: A questionnaire designed and administered for a new study produces fresh primary data, not data from an existing source. Options A, C and B are all listed existing sources, along with industry associations, special-interest organizations and the internet.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Which of the following is listed among the existing sources of data?

options.a: Pilot tests of a new product

questions.explanation: Industry associations are existing sources that already hold data, alongside firms' own departments, business database services, government agencies, special-interest organizations and the internet. Options C, A and D are ways of generating new data through statistical studies, not existing sources.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: A course coordinator gives extra tutorials to one group of students and no tutorials to another group, then compares their examination scores. This is
questions.explanation: The coordinator deliberately controls who receives tutorials and then measures the effect, which makes it an experimental study. Option A would only record what students already do without influencing it, and option C would rely on data already recorded elsewhere.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: A researcher records how many hours UNILAG students say they study each week and their examination scores, without trying to influence either. This is
questions.explanation: No attempt is made to control or influence the variables, so it is an observational (nonexperimental) study; a survey is a good example. Options D, B and A all involve the researcher controlling some variable to see its effect.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the data acquisition considerations?
questions.explanation: The three data acquisition considerations are time requirement, cost of acquisition and data errors. Option C 'Sample mean' is a statistic calculated from data, not something to weigh up when acquiring data, while options D, A and B are the genuine considerations.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: A firm spends so long searching for market information that, by the time the information is available, the decision it was needed for has already been made. Which data acquisition consideration does this illustrate?
questions.explanation: Searching for information can be time consuming, and information may no longer be useful by the time it is available; this is the time requirement consideration. Option D is about having to pay for information, and option B is about misleading results from carelessly acquired data.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: A manager uses whatever sales figures happen to be lying around the office, without checking how they were gathered, and reaches a misleading conclusion. Which data acquisition consideration has been ignored?
questions.explanation: Using any data that happen to be available, or that were acquired with little care, can lead to misleading information; this is the data errors consideration. Option C is about how long it takes to get the data, and option A is about the price charged for it.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: The tabular, graphical and numerical methods used to summarize and present data make up
questions.explanation: Descriptive statistics summarize and present data using tables, charts and numerical measures such as the mean. Options B and C use sample data to draw conclusions about a population, which goes beyond simply describing the data.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: A pollster interviews 1,000 randomly selected registered voters in Lagos State and uses the results to predict the outcome of the governorship election. This is an example of
questions.explanation: Using sample results to predict something about all voters is inferential statistics. Option B would only summarize the 1,000 responses themselves, and option C would require interviewing every registered voter.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: A course adviser calculates the average score of the 80 students in her class and reports it only as a summary of that class. This is

options.a: Statistical inference, because a numerical measure has been used
options.b: Inferential statistics, because an average has been calculated
options.c: Descriptive statistics, because conclusions are about the same group only
options.d: Inferential statistics, because the class is a sample of all students

questions.explanation: Descriptive statistics use data gathered on a group to describe that same group only, which is exactly what the adviser does. Options B and A are wrong because calculating an average or any numerical measure does not by itself make it inference, and option D is wrong because she is not generalizing beyond her class.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: A statistical procedure to determine the characteristics of a population by studying a sample is called
questions.explanation: Statistical inference determines population characteristics by studying a sample, such as testing 200 light bulbs to judge the life of all new bulbs. Option B is the arranging of data in rows and columns, and option A is the list from which a sample is drawn.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: A Nigerian bulb manufacturer tests 200 of its newly designed bulbs and uses their average life to conclude whether all bulbs of the new design last longer. In this study, the population is

options.a: The average life of the 200 bulbs
options.c: All bulbs of the new design
options.d: The life of each tested bulb

questions.explanation: The population is the entire group the conclusion is about, which is all bulbs of the new design. Option B is the sample, option A is a sample statistic, and option D is the variable being measured on each element.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: To find out what proportion of UNILAG students support a new hostel fee, the Students' Union randomly selects and interviews 250 students. The 250 students are the
questions.explanation: The 250 students are a subset of the population selected for study, so they form the sample. Option D would be all UNILAG students, option C is a numerical measure of the population, and option B would be the complete list of students from which the 250 were chosen.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: A study finds that the average monthly rent paid by 120 randomly selected traders in Oshodi market is N85,000. The figure N85,000 is
questions.explanation: The average was calculated from a sample of 120 traders, so it is a statistic. Option D would be the average rent of all traders in the market, and option B is 'monthly rent' itself, the characteristic being measured, not the computed average.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Population parameters and sample statistics are usually represented, respectively, by
questions.explanation: Parameters are usually written with Greek letters (mu, sigma), while statistics are written with Roman letters (x-bar, s). Option B reverses the convention, and options A and D do not describe the standard notation.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Before selecting students for a survey, a researcher obtains the official register of all students in a faculty from the Faculty Officer. This register serves as the
questions.explanation: A sampling frame is a complete list of all elements in the population from which the sample is selected, like the official list of all students. Option D is the students actually chosen, and option C is the data later collected from them.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: A researcher uses the formula for the sample mean on a sample of traders and obtains an average age of 34 years, which she uses to estimate the population mean age. In this case,

options.a: The formula is the statistic and 34 years is the parameter
options.b: The formula is the estimator and 34 years is the estimate
options.c: The formula is the estimate and 34 years is the estimator
options.d: The formula is the parameter and 34 years is the estimator

questions.explanation: An estimator is the rule or formula used to estimate a parameter, while the estimate is the numerical value it produces. Option C reverses the two terms, and options D and A misuse 'parameter', since 34 years comes from a sample and not from the whole population.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Which of the following is a reason why researchers often study a sample instead of the whole population?

options.a: Populations are usually large and studying every element is costly
options.b: A sample never requires a sampling frame
options.c: A sample always gives exactly the same results as the population
options.d: Parameters cannot be estimated from sample statistics

questions.explanation: Populations are usually large, data for every element are often impossible to obtain, and the more items surveyed the larger the cost, so samples are used. Option C is false because a sample only estimates the population, and option D is false because statistics are used precisely to estimate parameters.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Sampling in which every possible sample of size n from a finite population has the same probability of being selected is called
questions.explanation: In simple random sampling from a finite population, every possible sample of size n has the same chance of selection, like drawing names from a hat. Option B takes every kth element from a list, option D uses whatever is readily available, and option C selects whole groups.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: A hall warden writes the names of all residents on slips of paper, mixes them in a box and draws 30 names for a survey. This is
questions.explanation: Putting every name in a container and drawing some out gives each resident an equal chance, which is simple random sampling. Option D would pick every kth name on a list, option B would first divide residents into groups by a characteristic, and option A would just use whoever is easy to reach.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Sampling in which data are obtained by selecting every kth element from a list is called
questions.explanation: Systematic sampling 'counts off' a list and takes every kth element. Option C gives every possible sample the same chance without a fixed counting pattern, option A samples within groups formed by a characteristic, and option D takes all elements of randomly chosen groups.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: A researcher wants a systematic sample of 60 students from a list of 1,200 students. What sampling interval k should be used?
questions.explanation: The sampling interval is k = population size / sample size = 1,200 / 60 = 20, so every 20th student on the list is selected. Option C confuses k with the sample size, option B is the result of a wrong division, and option A multiplies the two numbers instead of dividing.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: A reporter standing at the UNILAG main gate interviews the first 40 people who walk past to get views on a new transport policy. This is
questions.explanation: Using readily available people, such as the first persons the surveyor runs into, is convenience sampling; it is easy but probably the worst technique. Option C would require counting off every kth person from a list, and option B would give every person in the population an equal chance.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: A bank divides its customers into salary earners, traders and students, and then randomly selects customers from each of the three groups. This is
questions.explanation: The population is divided into groups (strata) by a characteristic, and a sample is taken from every group, which is stratified sampling. Option C would randomly choose some whole groups and use everyone in them, and option D would simply take every kth customer from a list.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: To survey traders in Lagos, a researcher divides the state into its local government areas, randomly selects 4 of them, and interviews every trader in those 4 areas. This is
questions.explanation: The population is divided into groups (usually geographical), some groups are randomly selected, and all elements in the chosen groups are used, which is cluster sampling. Option A would sample from every group, not just some, and option D would take every kth trader from a list.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes stratified sampling from cluster sampling?

options.a: Stratified sampling requires no groups at all, while cluster sampling divides the population into groups
options.b: In stratified sampling only some groups are chosen, while in cluster sampling every group is sampled
options.c: In stratified sampling every group is sampled, while in cluster sampling only some randomly chosen groups are used in full
options.d: Stratified sampling groups are usually geographical, while cluster groups are based on a characteristic

questions.explanation: Both methods divide the population into groups, but stratified sampling takes a sample from every stratum (formed by a characteristic), while cluster sampling randomly selects some clusters (usually geographical) and uses all their elements. Option B reverses the two, option D swaps how the groups are formed, and option A is wrong because stratified sampling does use groups.

questions.topic: Introduction to Statistics and Data Collection
questions.question: Which of the following sampling methods requires that a complete list of every element in the population be obtained, and is the preferred method even though it is often difficult to do?
questions.explanation: Simple random sampling is the preferred method, but it requires a complete list of every element so that each has an equal chance of selection. Option B uses whoever is readily available and needs no list, and option C only needs a list of the selected clusters.

questions.question: A frequency polygon is

options.a: A rectangle whose side corresponds to frequency
options.c: A line chart of cumulative frequencies
options.d: A series of straight lines joining the midpoints of the tops of the bars of a histogram

questions.explanation: A frequency polygon is drawn by joining the mid-points of the tops of the histogram bars with straight lines. Option B, a histogram, uses bars rather than lines. Option C describes an ogive, which plots cumulative frequencies, and option A describes a single bar.

questions.question: Diagrams such as cubes are classified as ____-dimensional diagrams.
questions.explanation: A cube has length, breadth and depth, so cube diagrams are three-dimensional, with the volume showing the value. One-dimensional diagrams (A) such as bar charts use length only, and two-dimensional diagrams (B) such as squares, rectangles and circles use area.

questions.question: In a stem-and-leaf display, used in exploratory data analysis, the stems are the ____ digits.
questions.explanation: Each value is split into a stem made of its leading (first) digit(s) and a leaf made of the trailing digit, so 47 has stem 4 and leaf 7. Option B, trailing, describes the leaves, not the stems.

questions.question: Three-dimensional diagrams are so named because they take into account
questions.explanation: Three dimensions means all three of length, breadth and depth, which is why cubes, spheres and cylinders are used to show values by volume. Options A, B and D each list only two dimensions, which describes two-dimensional (area) diagrams.

questions.question: The method of classification in which the upper limit of one class interval is the same as the lower limit of the next class interval is called the
questions.explanation: In the exclusive method classes such as 10-20, 20-30, 30-40 share their limits, and a value equal to an upper limit (like 20) is excluded from that class and placed in the next. In the inclusive method (B), classes such as 10-19, 20-29 do not share limits and both limits belong to the class.

questions.question: The largest value in a data set is 60 and the smallest is 40. If 5 classes are desired, the class interval is
questions.explanation: Class interval = (largest - smallest) / number of classes = (60 - 40) / 5 = 20 / 5 = 4. Option A, 20, is the range itself, before dividing by the number of classes.

questions.question: A tabular summary of data showing the number of items in each of several non-overlapping classes is called a ____ distribution.
questions.explanation: A frequency distribution shows how many observations (the frequency) fall into each of several non-overlapping classes. Chronological (C) refers to arranging data by time, and nominal (A) and ordinal (D) are levels of measurement, not types of distribution table.

questions.question: A listing of the data in the form in which they were collected is known as:
questions.explanation: Raw data are the original observations exactly as they were collected, before being sorted, grouped or summarized. Option C, arrayed data, is the same data after arranging it in order of size. Option A refers to where the data came from, not to whether it has been arranged.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about spatial classification of data is true?

options.a: Data are classified on the basis of geographical location
options.b: Data are classified on the basis of time
options.c: Data are classified on the basis of a measurable characteristic such as income
options.d: Data are classified on the basis of attributes such as sex or religion

questions.explanation: Spatial classification groups data by place, such as country, state, LGA or town. Option B describes chronological (temporal) classification. Option C describes quantitative classification and option D describes qualitative classification.

questions.question: The salaries (in naira) of 15 workers are 2500, 2700, 2600, 2800, 2200, 2100, 2000, 2900, 3000, 2800, 2200, 2500, 2700, 2800, 2600. If 10 classes are desired, the width of each class interval is
questions.explanation: Class width = range / number of classes = (largest - smallest) / 10 = (3000 - 2000) / 10 = 100. Option D (200) would give only 5 classes, and options A and B would give even fewer, so none of them matches the 10 classes required.

questions.question: Which of the following is a comprehensive way of classifying (organising) raw data?
questions.explanation: A frequency distribution groups raw data into classes and shows how many observations fall into each, turning a jumble of figures into an organised summary. Option A, a scatter diagram, plots pairs of values to show a relationship. Options C and D are summary measures, not ways of classifying raw data.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about class intervals is true?

options.a: Exclusive class intervals are commonly used for continuous variables
options.b: Inclusive class intervals are commonly used for continuous variables
options.c: Class intervals cannot be used for continuous variables
options.d: Only open-ended class intervals can be used for continuous variables

questions.explanation: In the exclusive method the upper limit of one class is the lower limit of the next (for example 10-20, 20-30), so there are no gaps, which suits continuous variables that can take any value. Option B is wrong because inclusive intervals (10-19, 20-29) leave gaps and are mainly used for discrete data. Options C and D are false because continuous data are routinely grouped into ordinary closed class intervals.

questions.question: Which of the following diagrams is drawn for grouped data on a continuous variable, with bars that touch each other?
questions.explanation: A histogram represents a continuous grouped frequency distribution with adjacent bars, and the area of each bar represents the class frequency. Option B, a bar diagram, has separate bars with gaps and is used mainly for discrete or categorical data. Options A and D show proportions or counts with sectors and pictures, not continuous class intervals.
