questions.question: In a bivariate frequency table, the row and column totals, which give the frequencies of each value of x and of y separately, are called
questions.explanation: Marginal frequencies are the totals in the margins of a two-way table and show the distribution of each variable on its own. Option C, conditional frequencies, are the frequencies of one variable for a fixed value of the other, found inside a single row or column. Option B adds frequencies class by class, and option A simply means the frequency of one class.

questions.question: Squares, circles and rectangles used to present data are classified as
questions.explanation: Squares, circles and rectangles compare magnitudes by their area, which depends on both length and breadth, so they are two-dimensional diagrams. Option A covers bar diagrams, where only length matters. Option B covers cubes and spheres, which use volume, and option C uses pictures or symbols.

questions.question: The type of cumulative frequency distribution in which the frequencies are added from the bottom (the highest class) upwards is called the
questions.explanation: In a more than cumulative frequency distribution, frequencies are accumulated from the highest class upwards, so each figure shows how many observations are greater than or equal to the lower boundary of a class. Option D, the less than type, accumulates from the top (lowest class) downwards using upper boundaries. Options B and C are not cumulative distributions at all.

questions.question: The 'less than type' and 'more than type' distributions are types of
questions.explanation: Both the less than and more than types are cumulative frequency distributions: one accumulates frequencies from the lowest class upward and the other from the highest class downward, and they are graphed as ogives. Option A expresses each class frequency as a proportion of the total, option B cross-classifies two variables, and option D just lists each class frequency without adding them up.

questions.question: The exclusive method and the inclusive method are two ways of forming
questions.explanation: The exclusive method (for example 10-20, 20-30) and the inclusive method (10-19, 20-29) are two ways of writing the class intervals of a frequency distribution. Option C is wrong because class width is a single number obtained after the intervals are set. Options A and B are counts and midpoints, which come after the intervals have been formed.

questions.question: A cumulative distribution that shows the total number of observations lying below the upper limit (upper boundary) of each class is called a
questions.explanation: A less than cumulative frequency distribution counts all observations below the upper boundary of each class, and its graph is the less than ogive. Option B counts observations at or above the lower boundary instead. Options C and D are not cumulative distributions.

questions.question: Classification of data on the basis of measurable variables such as production, cost, height and weight is called
questions.explanation: Quantitative classification groups data by characteristics that can be measured numerically, such as cost, height or weight. Option A, qualitative classification, groups by attributes like sex or religion that cannot be measured. Option C groups by location and option D by time.

questions.question: A table that presents data according to only one characteristic is called a
questions.explanation: A simple (one-way) table shows data classified by a single characteristic, such as the number of students in each faculty. Options B, C and D all classify the data by two or more characteristics at the same time.

questions.question: Area diagrams and surface diagrams are other names for
questions.explanation: Two-dimensional diagrams such as squares, rectangles and circles compare magnitudes by area, so they are also called area or surface diagrams. Option A covers bar diagrams, which use only length. Option C uses volume, as with cubes and spheres, and option D uses pictures.

questions.question: The frequency distribution that results from the cross-classification of two variables is called a
questions.explanation: Cross-classifying two variables, for example age and income, in a two-way table gives a bivariate frequency distribution. Option B involves only one variable. Options C and D are ways of expressing or accumulating the frequencies of a single variable.

questions.question: A set of raw data arranged in ascending or descending order of magnitude is called
questions.explanation: An ordered array is simply the raw data rearranged from smallest to largest (or the reverse), which makes it easy to spot the range and the median. Option B groups the data into classes with frequencies, option C accumulates those frequencies, and option D is the data before any arrangement.

questions.question: The value halfway between the lower class limit and the upper class limit of a class is called the
questions.explanation: The class mid-point (class mark) is (lower limit + upper limit) / 2 and is used as the representative value of the class when computing the mean. Option A is the difference between the boundaries, option C is the point separating one class from the next, and option D is the number of observations in the class.

questions.question: Classification of data on the basis of time is called
questions.explanation: Chronological or temporal classification arranges data by time, such as years, months or days, and gives a time series. Option A classifies by location, option C by attributes, and option D by measurable characteristics.

questions.question: Diagrams that represent statistical data on maps are called
questions.explanation: A cartogram is a map on which regions are shaded, coloured or marked according to the data, for example population density by state. Option C, a pictogram, uses pictures or symbols but not a map. Options B and D are graphs of frequency distributions.

questions.question: Dividing each class frequency by the total number of observations converts a frequency distribution into a
questions.explanation: Relative frequency = class frequency / total frequency, so the resulting table shows the proportion of observations in each class, and these proportions add up to 1. Options A and D come from adding frequencies successively, and option B cross-classifies two variables.

questions.question: Bar diagrams are classified as one-dimensional diagrams because only their
questions.explanation: In a bar diagram the bars have equal, arbitrary widths, so only the length (height) of each bar carries the value; this makes it one-dimensional. Option C describes two-dimensional diagrams such as rectangles and circles that compare areas. Option B is wrong because the width is the same for every bar, and option D describes three-dimensional diagrams.

questions.question: In a stem-and-leaf display, the leaves are the
questions.explanation: Each number is split into a stem (the leading digits) and a leaf (the trailing, last digit), so 47 has stem 4 and leaf 7. Option A describes the stems, not the leaves. Options B and C are features of a grouped frequency table.

questions.question: The process of arranging data into classes or groups on the basis of common characteristics is called
questions.explanation: Classification is the sorting of raw data into classes or groups whose members share a common characteristic, such as age group or faculty. Option B, editing, means checking collected data for errors and omissions, while option C is about selecting part of a population. Option D simply means counting, not grouping.

questions.question: Subtracting the smallest value from the largest value and dividing the result by the desired number of classes gives the
questions.explanation: Class width = (largest value - smallest value) / number of classes, so the calculation described gives the width of each class interval. Option D, the range, is only the first part (largest minus smallest) before dividing. Option C is an input to the formula, not its result, and a class midpoint (A) is the average of a class's limits.

questions.question: The type of chart that allows direct comparison of two or more related data sets (e.g. imports and exports over several years) side by side is the
questions.explanation: A multiple bar chart places bars for two or more variables side by side for each category, so the sets can be compared directly. A simple bar chart (B) shows only one variable. A pie chart (C) shows the parts of a single total, and a histogram (D) shows one frequency distribution of continuous data.

questions.question: A statistical table whose figures (such as totals, ratios or percentages) are obtained from another, original table is called a
questions.explanation: A derived table presents figures worked out from data already given in another table, such as percentages or averages. Option A, an original (primary) table, shows the data in the form in which they were collected. A simple table (B) describes one characteristic only, which says nothing about where its figures came from.

questions.question: If each class frequency in a frequency distribution is divided by the total number of observations, the resulting distribution is called a
questions.explanation: Relative frequency = class frequency / total frequency, so dividing every frequency by the total gives a relative frequency distribution (multiplying by 100 turns it into percentages). Option A is formed by adding frequencies successively, not by dividing. Option D just means the data are arranged in classes.

questions.question: The daily shipments recorded by a Lagos distributor are: 34, 35, 41, 30, 55, 45, 30, 34, 32, 52, 42, 40, 60, 36, 38, 48, 56, 53, 34, 33, 32, 41, 55, 59, 34, 51, 54, 53, 36. What is the range of the data, used to work out the class interval?
questions.explanation: Range = largest value - smallest value = 60 - 30 = 30. Option A adds the two values (60 + 30 = 90) instead of subtracting, and option C divides them (60/30 = 2). Option D multiplies them, which is not a measure of spread.

questions.question: The largest value in a data set is 85, the smallest is 65 and 8 classes are desired. The width of each class interval is
questions.explanation: Class width = (85 - 65)/8 = 20/8 = 2.5. The other options do not come from the range divided by the number of classes; for example 18.75 is 150/8, which would wrongly add the two values (85 + 65) before dividing.

questions.question: In the graphical presentation of data, ideographs are also called
questions.explanation: Ideographs, also called pictographs or pictograms, use pictures or symbols to stand for quantities, such as one car icon for 10,000 cars. Histograms (B) use adjoining bars for frequencies, ogives (C) are cumulative frequency curves, and scatter diagrams (D) plot pairs of values.

questions.question: The stem-and-leaf display is a technique mainly used in
questions.explanation: A stem-and-leaf display is an exploratory data analysis (EDA) tool: it quickly shows the shape and spread of a data set while keeping the actual values. Option A, inferential analysis, draws conclusions about a population from a sample, which a stem-and-leaf plot does not do. It also needs numerical data, so it is not for nominal data (C).

questions.question: The method of forming class intervals that keeps the data continuous (the upper limit of one class is the lower limit of the next) is the
questions.explanation: In the exclusive method, classes are written as 10-20, 20-30, ..., so the upper limit of one class is the lower limit of the next and there are no gaps, which keeps the data continuous. Option D, the inclusive method (10-19, 20-29), leaves gaps between classes, which must be closed by converting to class boundaries.

questions.question: A frequency distribution in which the first class has no lower limit or the last class has no upper limit (e.g. 'below 10' or '60 and above') is called
questions.explanation: When the first or last class has no stated limit, the classes are open-ended, so the distribution is an open-ended distribution. Option C is the opposite, where every class has both limits. Option A describes how class limits are written (as in 10-19), not whether the end classes are open.

questions.question: The graph of a cumulative frequency distribution is also known as
questions.explanation: An ogive is the curve obtained by plotting cumulative frequencies against class boundaries. A histogram (B) and a frequency polygon (C) both show ordinary class frequencies, not running totals. A bar chart (D) is mainly for discrete or categorical data.

questions.question: If the midpoints of the tops of the bars of a histogram are marked and the points are joined by straight lines, the graph obtained is a
questions.explanation: A frequency polygon is drawn by joining the midpoints of the tops of the histogram bars (class marks against frequencies) with straight lines. Option A, the ogive, also joins points, but it plots cumulative frequencies against class boundaries. A bar chart (B) and pie chart (C) do not involve joining points.

questions.question: A 'less than' cumulative frequency distribution is plotted against the
questions.explanation: A 'less than' cumulative frequency counts all observations below each class's upper boundary, so it is plotted against the upper class boundaries. Option B, the lower boundaries, are used for the 'more than' ogive. Options C and D are single values, not a set of points for a curve.

questions.question: The diagram in which the parts of a total are shown as proportions (percentages) of a circle rather than as absolute values is the
questions.explanation: A pie diagram divides a circle into sectors whose angles are (value/total) x 360, so each part is shown as a share of the whole. A histogram (A) and a frequency polygon (C) show actual frequencies of classes, and an ogive (B) shows cumulative frequencies.

questions.question: A 'more than' (greater than) cumulative frequency distribution is plotted against the
questions.explanation: A 'more than' cumulative frequency counts all observations at or above each class's lower boundary, so it is plotted against the lower class boundaries. Option C, the upper boundaries, belong to the 'less than' ogive. Options A and B are single values, not points for a curve.

questions.question: Simple classification and manifold classification are types of
questions.explanation: Classification by attributes is qualitative: in simple classification data are grouped by one attribute only (e.g. literate or illiterate), while in manifold classification they are grouped by two or more attributes at once. Option B groups data by measurable values such as income, and option D groups them by time.

questions.question: The largest value in a data set is 45, the smallest is 25 and 4 classes are desired. The width of each class interval is
questions.explanation: Class width = (45 - 25)/4 = 20/4 = 5. Option D comes from (45 + 25)/4 = 17.5, which wrongly adds the values instead of subtracting. Options A and B are not obtained by dividing the range by the number of classes.

questions.question: In graphical representation, what is the primary difference between a histogram and a bar chart?

options.a: Histograms are used for continuous data, while bar charts are used for categorical data
options.b: Bar charts represent frequencies, while histograms only represent percentages
options.c: Histograms always use vertical bars, whereas bar charts must use horizontal bars
options.d: Histograms need two variables plotted against each other, while bar charts need only one

questions.explanation: A histogram shows the frequency distribution of continuous data with adjacent bars and no gaps, while a bar chart compares separate categories. Option B is wrong because both can show frequencies, and option C is wrong because either chart can be drawn vertically.

questions.question: A frequency distribution table is used to:

options.b: Show how often each value or range of values occurs
options.c: Calculate the mean of a dataset

questions.explanation: A frequency distribution table shows how often each value or class of values occurs. Option A describes a time series, and option C is something you can do with the table, not its purpose.

questions.question: The class width of a frequency distribution is:

options.b: Upper class boundary - Lower class boundary
options.c: Sum of frequencies / Number of classes

questions.explanation: Class width is the upper class boundary minus the lower class boundary of the same class. The other options mix in frequencies or midpoints, which have nothing to do with the size of a class interval.

questions.question: Which graphical tool is MOST appropriate for showing monthly sales trends over a year?
questions.explanation: A line graph joins values over time, so it clearly shows rises and falls in monthly sales. Option A, a pie chart, shows shares of a total, and option D, a histogram, shows a frequency distribution, not a trend.

questions.question: If a category represents 72 out of 360 total observations, its sector angle in a pie chart is:
questions.explanation: Sector angle = (value/total) x 360 = (72/360) x 360 = 72 degrees. Option B, 36 degrees, would be for 36 out of 360, and option C, 90 degrees, would need a quarter of the observations.

questions.question: An ogive (cumulative frequency curve) is primarily used to:

options.b: Estimate medians, quartiles and percentiles graphically

questions.explanation: An ogive plots cumulative frequencies against class boundaries, so medians, quartiles and percentiles can be read off it. Option A, the mode, is estimated from a histogram, and option C describes a pie chart.

questions.question: The class midpoint of the interval 40-50 is:
questions.explanation: The class midpoint is the average of the class limits: (40 + 50)/2 = 45. Option D, 10, is the class width, and options A and B are just the limits.

questions.question: Stem-and-leaf plots are useful because they:

options.b: Retain original data values while showing the distribution shape
options.c: Only work for datasets with fewer than 5 values
options.d: Show cumulative frequencies on a curve

questions.explanation: A stem-and-leaf plot keeps each original data value while also showing the shape of the distribution like a histogram. Option A describes a pie chart, and option D describes an ogive.

questions.question: A box-and-whisker plot displays:

options.b: Minimum, Q1, median, Q3 and maximum
options.c: Only the range of a data set
options.d: The frequency of each class interval

questions.explanation: A box plot is drawn from the five-number summary: the minimum and maximum mark the whisker ends, while Q1, the median and Q3 form the box. Option C is incomplete because the box also shows the quartiles, and option D describes a histogram.

Tallying the heights from 160 to 164 inclusive gives 14 students, the largest class (the full table is 12, 9, 14, 10, 5, totalling 50). Option C is the frequency of 150-154, option A is 165-169 and option B is 155-159.

questions.question: Three coins are tossed 30 times and the number of heads each time is: 0, 1, 2, 2, 1, 2, 3, 1, 3, 0, 1, 3, 1, 1, 2, 2, 0, 1, 2, 1, 3, 0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 2, 2, 0. In a frequency distribution table, the frequency of '1 head' is:
questions.explanation: Tallying the data gives 0 heads: 6, 1 head: 10, 2 heads: 9 and 3 heads: 5, which sum to 30. Option A is the frequency of 2 heads and option B is the frequency of 0 heads, and option C is a miscount, since the frequencies would then total more than 30.

questions.question: In tabulation, classifying data according to attributes such as nationality, physical status or social status is known as
questions.explanation: Qualitative classification groups data by traits or attributes that cannot be measured numerically, such as nationality or social status. Option D is based on measurable numerical features, while B and A use time and location respectively as the basis of grouping.

questions.question: A Lagos State ministry tabulates the number of registered traders in each Local Government Area of the state. This is an example of
questions.explanation: When data are grouped on the basis of location, such as a country, state or local government area, the classification is spatial or geographical. Option D would group the data by time periods like years or months, and A would group by attributes such as gender or religion.

questions.question: A Lekki supermarket arranges its monthly sales figures from January to December 2025 in a table. The basis of classification used is
questions.explanation: Temporal or chronological classification uses time, in years, months, weeks or days, as the categorising variable, so monthly sales fit here. Option C would group by location, and D would group by the size of a measurable characteristic such as income or marks.

questions.question: UNILAG students are grouped into the classes 15-19 years, 20-24 years and 25-29 years according to their ages. This is an example of
questions.explanation: Quantitative classification groups data according to features that can be measured numerically, such as age, income or marks. Option B would use attributes like faculty or state of origin, while D uses time periods and C uses locations.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the four bases of classification used in tabulation?
questions.explanation: The four bases of classification in tabulation are qualitative, quantitative, temporal and spatial. Inferential is a branch of statistics concerned with drawing conclusions about a population from a sample, not a basis for classifying data in a table. Options A, B and C are all genuine bases of classification.

questions.question: In statistics, the three usual methods of presenting data are
questions.explanation: Data are usually presented in words and sentences (textual), in rows and columns (tabular) or with charts and graphs (graphical). Option D lists types of data sources rather than presentation methods, and C and B each mix in a non-presentation term.

questions.question: A systematic and logical arrangement of data in rows and columns with respect to the characteristics of the data is called
questions.explanation: Tabulation is the orderly, compact arrangement of data in rows and columns. Option C is the grouping of data into classes, which usually comes before tabulation, while D uses charts and pictures and B uses words and sentences.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an objective of tabulation?

options.c: To present each individual item of the raw data

questions.explanation: A table presents aggregate data, so showing every individual item is actually one of its limitations, not an objective. Options B, D and A are genuine objectives: tables simplify complex data, make comparison easier and save space.

questions.question: Which of the following is an objective of tabulation?

options.a: To present data that only experts can read
options.b: To bring out the essential features of the data
options.c: To show approximate rather than exact values
options.d: To ignore the qualitative aspects of the facts

questions.explanation: Tabulation aims to bring out the essential features of data, simplify it, aid comparison and analysis and save space. Options D and A describe limitations of a table (it lacks description and needs special knowledge), and C is a disadvantage of diagrams, not of tables.

questions.question: The limitation of a table which states that it represents only figures and ignores the qualitative aspects of the facts is called
questions.explanation: A table lacks description because it shows figures, not attributes, and so ignores qualitative aspects. Option B refers to the table showing only aggregates, D refers to laymen finding tables hard to use, and C is a disadvantage of diagrams rather than tables.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the three limitations of a table?

options.a: It is incapable of presenting individual items
options.c: It needs special knowledge to understand

questions.explanation: Facilitating comparison is an objective of tabulation, so a table certainly can aid comparison. Options D, A and C are the three genuine limitations: tables show only figures, show aggregates rather than individual items, and need special knowledge to read.

questions.question: The part of a table placed just after the title, usually in brackets, which gives the units of the data (for example, 'amount in naira') is the
questions.explanation: The head note sits just below the title and states the units of measurement, usually in brackets. Option A explains special features or exceptions at the bottom of the table, B states where the data came from, and D is a column heading.

questions.question: In a statistical table, the headings given at the top of each column to explain the figures in that column are called
questions.explanation: Column headings are called captions. Option A is the opposite case: stubs are the headings of the horizontal rows. Options C and D give units and explanations of special features, not column headings.

questions.question: The titles of the horizontal rows of a statistical table are known as
questions.explanation: Stubs are the row headings that appear in the first column of a table. Option C refers to column headings, D is the part holding the numerical figures, and A names where the data were obtained.

questions.question: In a statistical table, the source note is

options.a: A brief statement indicating where the data in the table were obtained
options.b: The number placed at the top for easy reference
options.c: The statement of units of the data placed below the title
options.d: An explanation of points of exception not explained elsewhere

questions.explanation: The source note tells the reader where the data came from, for example the National Bureau of Statistics. Option D describes a footnote, C describes a head note and B describes the table number.

questions.question: A table of hostel occupancy in UNILAG halls carries a line at the bottom stating that 'Figures for Moremi Hall exclude 40 rooms under renovation.' This line is the table's
questions.explanation: A footnote explains a specific feature of a table that is not self-explanatory, such as a point of exception. Option B would state where the data came from, D would give units below the title, and C is a row heading.

questions.question: In the layout of a statistical table, which item appears first at the very top for easy identification and reference?
questions.explanation: The table number is the very first item at the top of a table, followed by the title and then the head note. Options A and C come second and third, while D is a column heading inside the table.

questions.question: The body of a statistical table

options.a: Gives the units of measurement in brackets
options.b: Narrates the contents of the table briefly
options.d: Contains the numerical information and is read down the columns and across the rows

questions.explanation: The body holds the actual figures and reveals the whole story of the facts investigated; columns are read from top to bottom and rows from left to right. Option A describes the head note, B the title and C the footnote.

questions.question: In statistics, a table that shows data classified according to only one characteristic, while a table that shows two or more characteristics at the same time, are respectively called

options.a: A simple table and a complex table
options.b: A complex table and a simple table
options.c: A frequency table and a contingency polygon
options.d: A head table and a body table

questions.explanation: A simple (one-way) table classifies data by a single characteristic, while a complex table (two-way or manifold) shows two or more characteristics together, such as students by faculty and by level. Option B reverses the two terms, and C and D are not standard names for these table types.

questions.question: A table shows the number of UNILAG students in each faculty broken down by level (100L, 200L, 300L) and by gender. This kind of table is best described as
questions.explanation: Because the students are classified by three characteristics at once (faculty, level and gender), the table is complex or manifold. Option C would classify by only one characteristic, D lists individual numerical values with their frequencies, and B is a diagram, not a table.

questions.question: Data collected in their original form, before any arrangement or grouping, are called
questions.explanation: Raw data are data in the original form in which they were collected, before being sorted or grouped. Option A has already been placed into classes, and D refers to where data came from (an existing source), not to whether they have been arranged.

questions.question: The organisation of raw data in table form with classes and frequencies is called
questions.explanation: A frequency distribution is a table that shows classes (or values) and how often each occurs. Options B and D are graphs drawn from a frequency distribution, and C is a list of population elements used for sampling.

questions.question: A survey records the blood groups (A, B, AB, O) of 60 students in Jaja Hall and counts how many fall in each group. The resulting table is
questions.explanation: A categorical frequency distribution is used when the data are nominal or ordinal, like blood groups. Option C groups several numerical values into one class, and D lists individual numerical values, but blood groups are not numbers.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes class limits from class boundaries?

options.a: Boundaries leave no gap between consecutive classes, while limits can leave gaps
options.b: Limits leave no gap between consecutive classes, while boundaries can leave gaps
options.c: Limits have one more decimal place than the raw data
options.d: Boundaries always appear in the raw data, while limits never do

questions.explanation: Class boundaries have one extra decimal place, so they never appear in the data and there is no gap between one class's upper boundary and the next class's lower boundary. Class limits, such as 30-39 and 40-49, can actually appear in the data and leave gaps. Option B reverses this, and D and C wrongly give the boundary properties to limits.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a correct way of finding the class width of a frequency distribution with equal classes?

options.a: Difference between the upper limits of two consecutive classes
options.b: Upper boundary minus lower boundary of the same class
options.c: Difference between the lower limits of two consecutive classes
options.d: Upper limit minus lower limit of the same class

questions.explanation: For a class like 30-39, upper limit minus lower limit gives 9, but the true width is 10, so this method is wrong. Options B, C and A all correctly give 10: 39.5 - 29.5, 40 - 30 and 49 - 39.

questions.question: The number in the middle of a class, found by adding the lower and upper class limits and dividing by two, is the
questions.explanation: The class mark (midpoint) is half the sum of the class limits, or equally of the class boundaries. Option D is the size of the class, B is the point separating adjacent classes, and C is a running total of frequencies.

questions.question: In a frequency distribution, relative frequency is

options.a: The frequency divided by the class width
options.b: The number of values less than the lower class boundary
options.c: The running total of the frequencies
options.d: The class frequency divided by the total frequency

questions.explanation: Relative frequency shows the proportion (or percentage) of values in a class: class frequency / total frequency. Option C describes cumulative frequency, and A describes frequency density, which is used for histograms with unequal class widths.

questions.question: In a 'less than' frequency table, the cumulative frequency of a class is

options.a: The frequency of that class divided by the total
options.b: The frequency of that class divided by its width
options.c: The number of values less than the upper class boundary of that class
options.d: The number of values less than the lower class boundary of that class

questions.explanation: A less-than cumulative frequency is a running total, so it counts all values below the upper boundary of the current class. Option D would exclude the class itself, A is relative frequency and B is frequency density.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes inclusive and exclusive class intervals?

options.a: Inclusive classes have no gaps between them, while exclusive classes always leave gaps
options.b: Inclusive classes are used only for qualitative data, exclusive classes only for discrete data
options.c: In exclusive classes both limits belong to the class; in inclusive classes the upper limit belongs to the next class
options.d: In inclusive classes (e.g. 10-19, 20-29) both limits belong to the class; in exclusive classes (e.g. 10-20, 20-30) the upper limit belongs to the next class

questions.explanation: With inclusive classes such as 10-19 and 20-29, a value of 19 or 10 is counted in that class, so the limits leave gaps. With exclusive classes such as 10-20 and 20-30, the upper limit 20 is counted in the next class, so there are no gaps. Option C reverses the definitions, and A wrongly swaps which type leaves gaps.

questions.question: In a frequency distribution, an open-ended class is

options.a: A class whose width differs from the other classes
options.b: A class that is shown in the middle of the table
options.c: A class whose frequency is zero
options.d: A class with no stated lower limit or no stated upper limit, such as 'below 20' or '60 and above'

questions.explanation: An open-ended class is missing either its lower or its upper limit, as in 'below 20' or '60 and above', which makes its midpoint and width uncertain. Option C is simply an empty class, and A describes an unequal class width, which still has both limits stated.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly distinguishes a histogram from a bar chart?

options.a: In a bar chart the bars touch and represent continuous data; in a histogram the bars are separated by gaps
options.b: A histogram is used only for categorical data, a bar chart only for continuous data
options.c: In a histogram the bars touch and represent continuous grouped data; in a bar chart the bars are separated by gaps
options.d: A histogram uses circles while a bar chart uses rectangles

questions.explanation: A histogram represents continuous grouped data, so its bars touch along the class boundaries. A bar chart uses bars of equal width with gaps between them for categorical or discrete data. Option A swaps the two charts, and B reverses the type of data each is used for.

questions.question: In a histogram, the frequency of each class is represented by the
questions.explanation: In a histogram, area represents frequency. When all classes have equal width, height alone is proportional to frequency, but with unequal widths the heights must be adjusted so that area still matches frequency. Options A, D and C carry no frequency information; histograms have no gaps at all.

questions.question: Which graph is most suitable for estimating the median and quartiles of a grouped frequency distribution?
questions.explanation: An ogive (cumulative frequency curve) shows running totals, so the value at half the total frequency gives the median and the values at one quarter and three quarters give the quartiles. Options D, C and A show individual parts or categories and cannot be read for positional measures.

questions.question: A 'less than' cumulative frequency ogive drawn for a distribution with a total frequency of 80

options.a: Starts at the first class frequency at the first midpoint and ends at 80
options.b: Starts at zero at the lowest class boundary and ends at 80
options.d: Starts at 80 at the lowest class boundary and ends at zero

questions.explanation: A less-than ogive begins at a cumulative frequency of zero at the lowest class boundary and rises to the total frequency, here 80, at the highest boundary. Option D describes a 'more than' ogive, which falls from the total to zero, and C describes the shape of a frequency polygon closed at both ends.

questions.question: A bar graph for qualitative data in which the bars are arranged in order of frequency is called a
questions.explanation: A Pareto chart is a bar graph of qualitative categories arranged by frequency, usually from highest to lowest, to show which categories matter most. Option A is for continuous grouped data, C uses pictures or symbols and D uses a map.

questions.question: A Lagos firm wants to show how its total expenses are shared among rent, salaries and materials, as parts of a whole. The most suitable diagram is a
questions.explanation: A pie chart is a circle divided into sectors, each showing a component's share of the total, which is exactly a composition of expenses. Option C shows change over time, D shows a continuous frequency distribution and A shows the relationship between two quantitative variables.

questions.question: A diagram that uses pictures or symbols, each representing a fixed number of items, to present data is a
questions.explanation: A pictogram represents data with pictures or symbols, such as one bag icon standing for 100 bags of rice. Option D uses maps, C splits each value into a stem and a leaf, and B summarises data with a box and whiskers.

questions.question: A bar diagram in which each bar is divided into parts in proportion to the components making up the total (for example, a hall's budget split into food, utilities and maintenance) is a
questions.explanation: A subdivided or component bar diagram splits each bar in the ratio of its components, showing both the total and its parts. Option B places separate bars side by side, A shows positive and negative values on either side of a zero line, and D breaks very long bars to save space.

questions.question: A subdivided bar diagram in which every bar has the same total height of 100 and the components are shown as percentages is called a
questions.explanation: A percentage bar diagram is a subdivided bar diagram drawn on a percentage basis, so each bar totals 100% and the parts show relative shares. Option B has a single undivided bar per category, and D places separate bars side by side without converting to percentages.

questions.question: A company wants to display its profit or loss for each of six years, with profits above and losses below a zero line. The most suitable diagram is a
questions.explanation: A deviation bar diagram represents net positive and negative values, such as profit and loss, with bars extending on either side of a zero line. Option A shows component shares that always total 100%, and C is used for frequency distributions.

questions.question: In a bar chart of branch sales, one Lagos branch's sales are far higher than those of all the other branches. To save space for the smaller bars, the analyst should use a
questions.explanation: A broken-scale bar diagram is used when one value is very large compared with the others; the large bar is broken and its value written at its top. Option A is for positive and negative values, and D converts components to percentages.

questions.question: Bar diagrams, in which only the length (height) of the bars is considered, are classified as
questions.explanation: A one-dimensional diagram varies only in length, which is why simple, multiple and subdivided bar diagrams belong here. Option B varies in both length and breadth (area), such as rectangles, squares and circles, and C uses volume, such as cubes and spheres.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a two-dimensional diagram?
questions.explanation: A cube compares magnitudes by volume (length, breadth and height), so it is three-dimensional. Options A, D and B vary in length and breadth and represent magnitudes by area, which makes them two-dimensional.

questions.question: Three-dimensional diagrams such as cubes and spheres are less commonly used because

options.a: They can only show qualitative data
options.b: They always require a broken scale
options.c: They cannot be given a title
options.d: Volume is harder to judge visually than length or area

questions.explanation: Cubes and spheres compare magnitudes by volume, and readers find volume much harder to judge accurately than length or area. Options A, C and B are not true limitations of three-dimensional diagrams.

questions.question: A graph that plots values of a variable against time on the horizontal axis and joins consecutive points with straight lines is called

options.a: An arithmetic line graph (time series graph)

questions.explanation: An arithmetic line graph, also called a time series graph, shows how a variable such as sales changes over time, with time on the X-axis. Option C also joins points but uses class midpoints and frequencies, not time, and B plots pairs of two quantitative variables without a time order.

questions.question: Monthly rainfall in Lagos and in Abuja for 2025 is plotted as two lines on the same axes for comparison. This is a
questions.explanation: A multiple line graph shows two or more variables on the same graph for comparison, like rainfall in two cities. Option A shows only one variable over time, and D would use side-by-side bars rather than lines.

questions.question: A researcher wants to see whether students' hours of study and their exam scores are related. The most suitable graph is a
questions.explanation: A scatter plot shows the relationship (correlation) between two quantitative variables by plotting each pair as a point. Option D shows parts of a whole, C shows quantities with symbols, and B shows cumulative frequencies of a single variable.

questions.question: In a box plot (box-and-whisker plot), the central box represents the

options.a: Mean plus or minus one standard deviation
options.b: Full range of the data from minimum to maximum
options.d: Interquartile range, the middle 50% of the data, with a line at the median

questions.explanation: The box stretches from the first to the third quartile, covering the middle 50% of the data, and a line inside it marks the median. Option B is shown by the whiskers together with the box, not the box alone, and A and C are not part of a box plot.

questions.question: A data display that splits each value into a leading part and a trailing digit, for example writing 47 as 4 | 7, so that data are sorted quickly while the original values are kept, is a
questions.explanation: In a stem-and-leaf plot each value is split into a stem (here the tens digit 4) and a leaf (the units digit 7), which sorts the data into groups while keeping every original value. Option D is a line graph of frequencies, and C is a bar graph of qualitative categories.

questions.question: For continuous grouped data, such as the heights of students in classes 150-154 cm, 155-159 cm and so on, the most appropriate diagrams are

options.a: A histogram or a frequency polygon
options.b: A pie chart or a pictogram
options.c: A simple bar chart with gaps or a deviation bar diagram
options.d: A cartogram or a Pareto chart

questions.explanation: Continuous grouped data are best shown with a histogram (touching bars) or a frequency polygon. Option C uses gaps between bars, which suits categorical or discrete data, and D is meant for geographical or qualitative data.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an advantage of diagrammatic presentation of data?

options.b: Diagrams show exact values more precisely than tables
options.c: Diagrams save time and simplify data

questions.explanation: Lack of precision is a disadvantage of diagrams: they show approximate values and should be supplemented with a table for exact figures. Options D, C and A are genuine advantages of diagrams.

questions.question: Which statement about the relationship between diagrams and tables is correct?

options.a: Diagrams and tables can never present the same data
options.c: Diagrams are derived from tabulated data and supplement it rather than replace it
options.d: Diagrams are a full substitute for tables and make tables unnecessary

questions.explanation: Diagrams are a supplementary tool: they are drawn from tabulated data and help reveal patterns, but they do not replace the table, which keeps exact figures. Option D contradicts this, and B reverses the order in which they are produced.

questions.question: To avoid distorting the message of a bar chart, the vertical axis should normally

options.a: Start at the smallest data value to exaggerate differences
options.b: Be left unlabelled to reduce clutter
options.c: Start at zero and use a consistent scale
options.d: Use a different scale for each bar

questions.explanation: Using a consistent, honest scale that starts at zero prevents the misleading impression created by truncated axes. Option A is exactly the truncated-axis problem that misrepresents data, and B breaks the rule that axes must be clearly labelled with units.

questions.question: In the design of statistical charts, 'chart junk' refers to

options.a: The legend or key explaining colours and shading
options.b: Decorations, excessive gridlines or 3D effects that do not represent data
options.c: The scale and axis labels of a chart
options.d: The source note placed under a chart

questions.explanation: Chart junk is anything in a chart that does not represent data, such as heavy gridlines, decorations and 3D effects, and it obscures understanding. Options D, A and C are useful elements that good charts should include.

questions.question: When two or more variables are shown on the same diagram with different shading or line patterns, the diagram must include

options.a: A footnote listing every raw value
options.d: An index (legend or key) explaining the patterns

questions.explanation: An index, legend or key tells the reader which shading or line pattern stands for which variable. Options B, A and C do not explain the patterns; a broken scale is used only when one bar is much larger than the rest.

questions.question: A frequency table of ages of traders at Balogun Market uses the classes 25-34, 35-44, 45-54. What is the class width?
questions.explanation: Class width is the upper boundary minus the lower boundary: 34.5 - 24.5 = 10, which also equals the gap between consecutive lower limits (35 - 25). Option A comes from subtracting the limits of the same class (34 - 25), a common mistake.

questions.question: The marks of BUA students are grouped as 40-49, 50-59, 60-69. What are the class boundaries of the class 50-59?
questions.explanation: The lower boundary is the lower limit minus 0.5 (50 - 0.5 = 49.5) and the upper boundary is the upper limit plus 0.5 (59 + 0.5 = 59.5). Option B gives the class limits, not the boundaries, and A wrongly adds 0.5 to the lower limit.

questions.question: What is the class mark (midpoint) of the class 35-44?
questions.explanation: The class mark is (lower limit + upper limit)/2 = (35 + 44)/2 = 39.5; using the boundaries gives the same result, (34.5 + 44.5)/2 = 39.5. Option B rounds up wrongly, and A is half of the class width, not the midpoint.

questions.question: The scores of 8 students in a quiz are 48, 72, 35, 90, 61, 27, 84, 55. What is the range of the scores?
questions.explanation: The range is the highest value minus the lowest value: 90 - 27 = 63. Option B (55) wrongly uses 35 as the lowest score, but 27 is smaller, and D adds the two extremes instead of subtracting them.

questions.question: The weights (kg) of bags of garri in a Mushin depot range from 34 kg to 98 kg. The data are to be grouped into 7 classes, with the class width found by dividing the range by the number of classes and rounding UP to the next whole number. What class width should be used?
questions.explanation: The range is 98 - 34 = 64, and 64 / 7 = 9.14, which rounds up to 10. Option D rounds down, which would leave the largest values outside the last class, and A is the range itself rather than the class width.

questions.question: A UNILAG student's monthly budget totals N48,000, of which N12,000 is spent on feeding. In a pie chart of the budget, what is the sector angle for feeding?
questions.explanation: The sector angle is (value / total) x 360 = (12,000 / 48,000) x 360 = 0.25 x 360 = 90 degrees. Option C is the percentage share (25%) written as if it were degrees, and A and B do not come from multiplying the share by the 360 degrees in a full circle.

questions.question: In a survey of 120 students, 25 said they travel to campus by keke. What sector angle should represent keke users in a pie chart?
questions.explanation: Sector angle = (25 / 120) x 360 = 75 degrees. Option D uses the raw frequency as the angle, and A is the percentage share (about 20.8%) rather than the angle in degrees.

questions.question: In a pie chart of a company's total expenditure of N500,000, the sector for salaries has an angle of 108 degrees. How much was spent on salaries?
questions.explanation: The salary share is 108 / 360 = 0.3 of the total, so salaries = 0.3 x N500,000 = N150,000. Option B simply treats the angle as thousands of naira, and A and D do not come from multiplying the total by 108/360.

questions.question: A sector of a pie chart has an angle of 72 degrees. What percentage of the total does it represent?
questions.explanation: Percentage = (72 / 360) x 100 = 20%, because the full circle of 360 degrees stands for 100% of the total. Option A takes the angle itself as the percentage, and B (36%) comes from dividing by 200 instead of 360.

questions.question: In a frequency table of 80 shop owners in Yaba, the class N20,000-N29,999 (daily sales) has a frequency of 12. What is the relative frequency of this class?
questions.explanation: Relative frequency = class frequency / total frequency = 12 / 80 = 0.15, or 15% of the shop owners. Option D divides by 100 instead of the actual total of 80, A is just the raw frequency, and C is the total divided by the frequency (80 / 12), which is upside down.

questions.question: The classes 10-19, 20-29, 30-39, 40-49, 50-59 have frequencies 5, 9, 14, 8 and 4 respectively. What is the 'less than' cumulative frequency of the class 30-39?
questions.explanation: Cumulative frequency is a running total: 5 + 9 + 14 = 28 values are less than the upper boundary 39.5. Option C is just the class frequency, D adds 9 and 14 but leaves out the first class, and A is the grand total.

questions.question: Using the distribution with classes 10-19, 20-29, 30-39, 40-49, 50-59 and frequencies 5, 9, 14, 8, 4, how many observations are less than 49.5?
questions.explanation: Values less than 49.5 are all those in the first four classes: 5 + 9 + 14 + 8 = 36. Option C is only the frequency of the class 40-49, D stops one class too early at 39.5, and B counts the values above 39.5 instead of below 49.5.

questions.question: Using the distribution with classes 10-19, 20-29, 30-39, 40-49, 50-59 and frequencies 5, 9, 14, 8, 4, what is the 'more than' cumulative frequency at the lower boundary 29.5?
questions.explanation: A 'more than' cumulative frequency counts all observations above the given lower boundary: 14 + 8 + 4 = 26 values exceed 29.5. Option B is only the frequency of the class 30-39, D is the 'less than' cumulative frequency at 39.5, and C counts only the last two classes.

questions.question: Using the distribution with classes 10-19, 20-29, 30-39, 40-49, 50-59 and frequencies 5, 9, 14, 8, 4 (total 40), what is the cumulative relative frequency of the class 30-39?
questions.explanation: Cumulative relative frequency = cumulative frequency / total = 28 / 40 = 0.70, so 70% of the values are below 39.5. Option C is the ordinary relative frequency of that class (14 / 40), A divides the cumulative frequency by 100 instead of 40, and B (36 / 40) belongs to the next class, 40-49.

questions.question:
The ages of 11 traders are shown in a stem-and-leaf plot where 2 | 4 means 24:
2 | 4 7
3 | 1 3 3 8
4 | 0 2 5 9
5 | 6
What is the median age?
questions.explanation: Reading the plot gives the ordered ages 24, 27, 31, 33, 33, 38, 40, 42, 45, 49, 56, and the median is the 6th of the 11 values, 38. Option B is the 7th value, D is the most frequent age (the mode), and C is the number of leaves on the stem 4, not an age.

questions.question:
In the stem-and-leaf plot below (key: 2 | 4 means 24), how many traders are aged 40 years or more?
2 | 4 7
3 | 1 3 3 8
4 | 0 2 5 9
5 | 6
questions.explanation: The values 40, 42, 45, 49 on stem 4 and 56 on stem 5 are all 40 or more, giving 5 traders. Option B counts only stem 4 and forgets stem 5, C wrongly includes 38, and A counts the stems rather than the leaves.

questions.question: The number of children in 20 households in Bariga are: 2, 3, 1, 4, 2, 0, 3, 2, 5, 2, 1, 3, 2, 4, 0, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3. In an ungrouped frequency table, what is the frequency of households with exactly 2 children?
questions.explanation: Tallying the 2s in the list gives 7 households with exactly 2 children, which makes 2 the most common value. Option A is the frequency of 3 children, and B and C come from miscounting the tally marks.

questions.question: For 20 Bariga households with (2, 3, 1, 4, 2, 0, 3, 2, 5, 2, 1, 3, 2, 4, 0, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3 children), how many households have fewer than 2 children?
questions.explanation: Households with fewer than 2 children have 0 or 1 child: there are 2 with none and 3 with one, giving 5. Option C counts only the households with one child, and A counts households with exactly 2 instead of fewer than 2.

questions.question: A histogram is drawn for the exclusive classes 0-10, 10-30 and 30-35 (minutes spent waiting at a BRT stop) with frequencies 20, 40 and 15. Using frequency density = frequency / class width, what is the height of the bar for the class 10-30?
questions.explanation: Because the classes have unequal widths, bar heights must be frequency densities: 40 / 20 = 2 for the class 10-30. Option A uses the raw frequency, which would make the wide class look too big, and D divides by 10 instead of the actual width of 20.

questions.question: For BRT waiting-time data with (classes 0-10, 10-30, 30-35 with frequencies 20, 40, 15), which class has the tallest bar when the histogram is correctly drawn using frequency density?
questions.explanation: The frequency densities are 20/10 = 2, 40/20 = 2 and 15/5 = 3, so the class 30-35 has the tallest bar even though its frequency is the smallest. Option B is the class with the largest frequency, which is tallest only if raw frequencies are wrongly used as heights.

questions.question: In a grouped table most classes have width 10, but the class 50-80 has width 30 and frequency 45. To draw a correct histogram, the adjusted frequency (height) of this class relative to the standard width of 10 is
questions.explanation: The class is three times the standard width (30 / 10 = 3), so its height must be 45 / 3 = 15 to keep the area proportional to frequency. Option B ignores the unequal width, A multiplies instead of dividing, and D divides by 10.

questions.question: In a pictogram of rice sales at Daleko Market, one bag symbol represents 500 bags. How many symbols are needed to represent 2,250 bags?
questions.explanation: Number of symbols = 2,250 / 500 = 4.5, so four full symbols and half a symbol are drawn. Options C and A round off and misstate the quantity, and B divides by 50 instead of 500.

questions.question: A hall's monthly spending of N72,000 consists of food N36,000, utilities N18,000 and maintenance N18,000. In a percentage bar diagram, what percentage of the bar should represent utilities?
questions.explanation: Each component's share is (component / total) x 100, so utilities = (18,000 / 72,000) x 100 = 25%. Option D takes the amount in thousands as a percentage, A is the share of food, and B wrongly assumes the three parts are equal.

questions.question: A table of daily keke fares collected (in N'000) uses the classes 15-19, 20-24, 25-29, 30-34. What is the class width?
questions.explanation: The class width is the difference between consecutive lower limits, 20 - 15 = 5, which equals the boundary difference 19.5 - 14.5. Option B subtracts the limits of the same class (19 - 15), a common error.

questions.question: Monthly incomes (N'000) are grouped in the exclusive classes 'Less than 20', 20-30, 30-40, 40-50. Assuming the open-ended first class has the same width as the next class, what midpoint should be used for it?
questions.explanation: If the first class has the same width of 10 as its neighbour, it becomes 10-20, whose midpoint is (10 + 20)/2 = 15. Option D treats the class as 0-20, A is its upper end, and C is the midpoint of the next class.

questions.question: Weights of parcels (kg), recorded to one decimal place, are grouped as 2.5-2.9, 3.0-3.4, 3.5-3.9. What are the class boundaries of the class 3.0-3.4?
questions.explanation: Boundaries have one more decimal place than the data and end in 5, so they lie halfway between classes: 2.95 (between 2.9 and 3.0) and 3.45 (between 3.4 and 3.5). Option A gives the class limits, and C subtracts and adds 0.5 as if the data were whole numbers.

questions.question: The midpoints of consecutive equal classes in a frequency table are 12, 17 and 22. What are the class boundaries of the class with midpoint 17?
questions.explanation: Consecutive midpoints differ by the class width, 17 - 12 = 5, so the boundaries are 17 - 2.5 = 14.5 and 17 + 2.5 = 19.5. Option D uses the neighbouring midpoints, B gives the class limits (15-19), and A uses a width of 1.

questions.question: In a frequency table, the class 40-49 has frequency 7. When drawing a frequency polygon, this class is plotted at the point
questions.explanation: A frequency polygon plots each class frequency against the class midpoint, (40 + 49)/2 = 44.5, giving the point (44.5, 7). Option B uses the upper boundary, which is used for a 'less than' ogive, and A uses the lower limit.

questions.question: For the exclusive class 20-30 (where 30 is counted in the next class), what are the class width and the midpoint?
questions.explanation: In exclusive classes the stated limits already act as boundaries, so the width is 30 - 20 = 10 and the midpoint is (20 + 30)/2 = 25. Option B treats it like an inclusive class with width 9, and A wrongly applies the inclusive-class midpoint of 24.5.

questions.question: The marks of 12 students are 23, 37, 41, 29, 35, 48, 31, 26, 39, 44, 33, 30. If the marks are grouped into the classes 20-29, 30-39, 40-49, what is the frequency of the class 30-39?
questions.explanation: The marks from 30 to 39 inclusive are 37, 35, 31, 39, 33 and 30, giving a frequency of 6. Option D usually comes from leaving out 30, the lower limit, and B wrongly includes 29 or 41 in the class.

questions.question: Use the data 16, 10, 10, 18, 11, 10, 18, 17, 13, 17. The arithmetic mean of the data is
questions.explanation: The mean is the sum divided by the number of values: 16 + 10 + 10 + 18 + 11 + 10 + 18 + 17 + 13 + 17 = 140, and 140/10 = 14.00. Option C (14.5) is the median, not the mean. Options B (16.70) and D (15.70) do not match the total of 140.

questions.question: Use the data 16, 10, 10, 18, 11, 10, 18, 17, 13, 17. The geometric mean of the data (to 2 d.p.) is
questions.explanation: The geometric mean is the 10th root of the product of the values. Using logs, sum of log x = 11.3309, so log GM = 11.3309/10 = 1.13309 and GM = 10^1.13309 = 13.59. Option A (14.85) and D (15.33) are too large, since the GM must be below the arithmetic mean of 14.

questions.question: Use the data 16, 10, 10, 18, 11, 10, 18, 17, 13, 17. The harmonic mean of the data (to 2 d.p.) is
questions.explanation: The harmonic mean is n divided by the sum of reciprocals. Here sum 1/x = 0.7591, so HM = 10/0.7591 = 13.17. Option A (13.79) is not consistent with AM > GM > HM, because the HM must be below the GM of 13.59, and options B (16.34) and D (14.94) are above the mean of 14.

questions.question: Use the data 16, 10, 10, 18, 11, 10, 18, 17, 13, 17. The median of the data is
questions.explanation: Arranging the data in order gives 10, 10, 10, 11, 13, 16, 17, 17, 18, 18. With 10 values the median is the average of the 5th and 6th values: (13 + 16)/2 = 14.5. Option A (14) is the mean, not the median, and options B and D are not the middle of the ordered data.

questions.question: Use the data 16, 10, 10, 18, 11, 10, 18, 17, 13, 17. The mode of the data is
questions.explanation: The mode is the value that appears most often. In this data 10 appears three times, while 17 and 18 appear only twice each and 13 appears once, so the mode is 10. Options B and D are tempting because they repeat, but less often than 10.

questions.question: Which of the following measures of location may not exist for a data set?
questions.explanation: The mode may not exist when no value repeats, for example in 3, 5, 7, 9. Options B, C and D, the mean, median and first quartile, can always be calculated for any numerical data set, so they always exist.

questions.question: Given the set of numbers 5, 6, 2, 1, 9, 8, 3, the value of sum x^2 is
questions.explanation: Square each number and add: 25 + 36 + 4 + 1 + 81 + 64 + 9 = 220. Option A (34) is sum x, the plain total. Option C (1156) is (sum x)^2 = 34^2, a common mix-up, since sum x^2 is not the same as (sum x)^2.

questions.question: The value that has half of the observations above it and half of the observations below it is called the
questions.explanation: The median is the middle value of ordered data, with half the observations above it and half below it. Option C, the mean, is the arithmetic average and need not split the data in half. Option D is the most frequent value, and option A measures spread.

questions.question: The 2nd quartile, the 5th decile and the 50th percentile of a data set are all equal to the
questions.explanation: Each of these cuts the ordered data at the halfway point: Q2 marks 2/4, D5 marks 5/10 and P50 marks 50/100 of the way through, which is exactly the median. The mean (A) and mode (C) are other averages that only coincide with the median in a symmetrical distribution, and the harmonic mean (D) is a different kind of average altogether.

questions.question: If a distribution has two modes, it is said to be
questions.explanation: 'Bi' means two, so a distribution with two modes (two peaks) is bimodal. Unimodal (D) means one mode and trimodal (B) means three, while 'semi-modal' (A) is not a standard term.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a measure of central tendency?
questions.explanation: Standard deviation measures how spread out the values are, so it is a measure of dispersion, not of central tendency. The mean (A), median (B) and mode (D) are all averages that describe the centre of a data set.

questions.question: The sum of the deviations of a set of values about their mean is always
questions.explanation: The mean is the balancing point of the data, so the positive deviations above it exactly cancel the negative deviations below it and sum(x - mean) = 0. The sum cannot always be positive (D) for that reason, and it is not tied to the range (A) or the standard deviation (C).

questions.question: The middle value of an ordered array of numbers is the
questions.explanation: The median is the value in the middle position once the data are arranged in order. The mode (A) is the most frequent value, the mean (B) is the sum divided by the count, and the mid-range (D) is the average of only the largest and smallest values.

questions.question: Which one of the following does NOT divide a set of ordered observations into equal parts?
questions.explanation: Standard deviation measures spread around the mean and does not split the data into parts. Quartiles (A) divide ordered data into 4 equal parts, deciles (D) into 10 and percentiles (C) into 100, which is why they are called partition values.

questions.question: Which measure of central tendency takes into account the actual magnitude of every score?
questions.explanation: The mean is found by adding all the values and dividing by their number, so every value's size affects it. The median (A) depends only on the middle position, and the mode (B) depends only on which value occurs most often, so changing an extreme value usually leaves them unchanged. Option D, the range, is a measure of dispersion, not of central tendency.

questions.question: A company has two units. Unit one has 650 employees with a mean monthly salary of $2,750, and unit two has 700 employees with a mean monthly salary of $2,500. The combined arithmetic mean salary is approximately:
questions.explanation: The combined mean weights each unit's mean by its number of employees: (650 x 2750 + 700 x 2500)/(650 + 700) = (1,787,500 + 1,750,000)/1,350 = 3,537,500/1,350 = about $2,620. Option B, $2,625, is the simple average of 2,750 and 2,500, which wrongly ignores that unit two has more employees.

questions.question: The number of observations is 30 and the arithmetic mean is 15. The sum of all the values is:
questions.explanation: Since mean = sum of values / n, the sum of values = mean x n = 15 x 30 = 450. Option D, 45, comes from adding 15 and 30 instead of multiplying, and Option A just repeats the mean.

questions.question: Using the assumed mean method with coded deviations u = (x - A)/h, sum fu = 300, the assumed mean A = 35, the number of observations is 15 and the class width h = 5. The arithmetic mean is:
questions.explanation: With coded deviations, mean = A + (sum fu / sum f) x h = 35 + (300/15) x 5 = 35 + 20 x 5 = 35 + 100 = 135. A common slip is to forget to multiply by the class width, which gives 35 + 20 = 55; Options B, C and D do not follow from the formula.

questions.question: The median, quartiles, deciles and percentiles are known as:
questions.explanation: These measures are called positional averages because their values are found from their position in data arranged in order, not by calculation with every value. Option A, mathematical averages, refers to the arithmetic, geometric and harmonic means. Option B refers to measures of dispersion.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the median?

options.a: It is the middle value of the data when arranged in order of size
options.b: It is the value that occurs most often
options.c: It is always less than or equal to the mean
options.d: It is the sum of the values divided by their number

questions.explanation: The median is the middle value once the data are arranged in ascending or descending order, so half the observations lie below it and half above. Option B describes the mode, and Option D describes the arithmetic mean. Option C is false, because in a negatively skewed distribution the median is greater than the mean.

questions.question: In terms of percentiles, the median is the:
questions.explanation: The median divides ordered data into two equal halves, so 50% of the values lie below it, which makes it the 50th percentile. Option B, the 40th percentile, has only 40% of values below it, and the 100th percentile (D) would be at the very top of the data.

questions.question: The arithmetic mean, geometric mean and harmonic mean are all classified as:
questions.explanation: The arithmetic, geometric and harmonic means are mathematical averages because they are calculated from every value using a formula. Option B, positional averages, are the median, quartiles and similar measures found from their position in ordered data. Options C and D measure spread and shape, not the average.

questions.question: Using the assumed mean method with coded deviations d = (x - A)/h, sum fd = 250, A = 25, the number of observations is 12 and the class width h = 6. The arithmetic mean is:
questions.explanation: With coded deviations, mean = A + (sum fd / sum f) x h = 25 + (250/12) x 6 = 25 + 125 = 150. Option D, 275, wrongly adds sum fd straight to A, and Option A just gives the assumed mean without any correction.

questions.question: For two positive numbers, the arithmetic mean is 25 and the harmonic mean is 15. The geometric mean is approximately:
questions.explanation: For two positive numbers, GM^2 = AM x HM, so GM = sqrt(25 x 15) = sqrt(375) = 19.36. This also fits the rule AM > GM > HM, since 25 > 19.36 > 15. Options A, B and C are too far below the true value.

questions.question: Dividing the sum of the values of a data set by the total number of values gives the:
questions.explanation: The arithmetic mean is the sum of the values divided by how many there are. Option B, the weighted mean, multiplies each value by a weight before dividing by the total weight. The geometric mean (C) is the nth root of the product of values, and the harmonic mean (D) is n divided by the sum of reciprocals.

questions.question: A single value that represents the characteristics of a whole data set is called:
questions.explanation: An average, or central value, is a single typical figure that represents the whole data set, such as the mean, median or mode. Options B and C describe the shape of the distribution, and Option D describes how spread out the values are, not a representative value.

questions.question: For a set of positive values that are not all equal, the arithmetic mean (AM), geometric mean (GM) and harmonic mean (HM) are related as:
questions.explanation: For positive values that are not all equal, the arithmetic mean is always the largest and the harmonic mean the smallest, so AM > GM > HM; they are equal only when all the values are equal. Option C reverses the correct order, and Options B and D wrongly place the GM above or below both of the others.

questions.question: In terms of deciles, the median is the:
questions.explanation: Deciles split ordered data into ten equal parts, and the fifth decile has 5/10 = 50% of the values below it, which is exactly the median. Option A, the fourth decile, has only 40% below it, and Option C, the sixth decile, has 60% below it.

questions.question: The positional measures that divide a data set into ten equal parts are called:
questions.explanation: Deciles are the nine values D1 to D9 that divide ordered data into ten equal parts. Option A, percentiles, divide data into 100 parts, Option C, quartiles, into 4 parts, and Option B, quintiles, into 5 parts.

questions.question: The marks (out of 100) of 21 students in a statistics exam are: 90, 95, 95, 94, 90, 85, 84, 83, 85, 81, 92, 93, 82, 78, 79, 81, 80, 82, 85, 76, 85. The mode of the data is:
questions.explanation: The mode is the value that occurs most often. Counting, 85 appears 4 times, while 95, 90, 81 and 82 each appear only twice, so the mode is 85. Options B, C and D each occur just twice, so none of them is the most frequent mark.

questions.question: The measure of central tendency defined as the most frequently occurring value in a data set is the:
questions.explanation: The mode is the value that occurs most often in a data set. Option A, the median, is the middle value of ordered data, Option C, the mean, is the sum divided by the number of values, and Option D, the range, measures spread rather than centre.

questions.question: The number of observations is 11 and the arithmetic mean is 19. The sum of all the values is:
questions.explanation: Since mean = sum of values / n, the sum = mean x n = 19 x 11 = 209. Option B, 30, comes from adding 19 and 11, and Option C, 8, comes from subtracting them, neither of which uses the mean formula.

questions.question: The arithmetic mean is 25 and the sum of the observations is 350. The number of observations is:
questions.explanation: Since mean = sum / n, n = sum / mean = 350 / 25 = 14. Options A, B and D do not satisfy 350/n = 25; for example, 350/70 = 5, not 25.

questions.question: A property of the arithmetic mean is that the sum of the squares of the deviations of the observations from the mean is:

options.a: Less than the sum of the squares of the deviations from any other value
options.b: Greater than the sum of the squares of the deviations from any other value
options.d: Equal to the sum of the deviations from the median

questions.explanation: The sum of squared deviations, sum(x - a)^2, is smallest when a is the arithmetic mean, so it is less than the sum of squared deviations from any other value. Option C confuses this with the plain sum of deviations from the mean, which is zero; the sum of squared deviations is zero only if all values are equal. Option B states the opposite of the true property.

questions.question: In a set of observations, unusually low or unusually high values are called:
questions.explanation: Outliers are values that lie far away from the bulk of the data, either unusually low or unusually high. Options B, C and D are summary measures of the data, not names for extreme observations.

questions.question: In terms of quartiles, the median is the:
questions.explanation: Quartiles split ordered data into four equal parts, and the second quartile Q2 has 50% of the values below it, so it is the median. Option A, Q1, has only 25% below it, and Option C, Q3, has 75% below it.

questions.question: The arithmetic mean is 12 and the number of observations is 20. The sum of all the values is:
questions.explanation: Since mean = sum / n, the sum = mean x n = 12 x 20 = 240. Option B, 32, comes from adding 12 and 20, and Option D, 1.667, comes from dividing 20 by 12 instead of multiplying.

questions.question: Three departments have pass rates of 60%, 75% and 90%, but they have very different numbers of students. To find the overall pass rate for all the students together, which average of the three pass rates should be used?
questions.explanation: The weighted arithmetic mean weights each pass rate by its department's number of students, so a large department counts for more and the result is the true overall pass rate. Option B, the simple arithmetic mean, treats every department as equally important and is misleading when the department sizes differ. Options C and D only pick the middle or most common rate and ignore the sizes altogether.

questions.question: The measure of central tendency best suited to averaging multiplicative changes over time, such as rates of inflation or compound interest, is the
questions.explanation: Growth rates such as inflation and compound interest multiply onto each other from one period to the next, and the geometric mean (the nth root of the product of n values) is the average that respects this multiplication. Option A, the arithmetic mean, adds the rates and overstates the average growth. Option D, the harmonic mean, is suited to averaging rates like speeds over equal distances, not compounding changes.

questions.question: A shop sells four products. Product W has a contribution of N8 per unit with 124 units sold, product X N5 per unit with 105 units sold, product Y N9 per unit with 135 units sold, and product Z N12 per unit with 140 units sold. The weighted average contribution per unit (to 2 d.p.) is
questions.explanation: Weight each contribution by its quantity: sum wx = 8(124) + 5(105) + 9(135) + 12(140) = 992 + 525 + 1215 + 1680 = 4412, and sum w = 124 + 105 + 135 + 140 = 504, so the weighted mean = 4412 / 504 = 8.75 naira. Options A, B and C are 1 to 3 naira too high and come from slips in the products or totals; note also that the simple mean (8+5+9+12)/4 = 8.5 is not the answer because it ignores the quantities sold.

questions.question: In statistics, the population mean is usually denoted by

options.b: x-bar (x with a bar on top)

questions.explanation: Population parameters are normally written with Greek letters, and the population mean is written as mu. Option B, x-bar, is the symbol for the sample mean, which is a statistic rather than a parameter. Options C and D stand for the sample standard deviation and the sample size.

questions.question: The daily wages (in naira) of 15 employees are 620, 640, 750, 850, 650, 720, 730, 785, 630, 740, 900, 880, 780, 690, 850. The mean daily wage (to 2 d.p.) is
questions.explanation: Adding the wages gives sum x = 11215, and dividing by n = 15 gives mean = 11215 / 15 = 747.67 naira. Options A, B and C are exactly 100 or 200 away from this value and come from slips in adding the wages. A quick check: every wage lies between 620 and 900, so a mean near 750 is sensible while 947.67 is impossible.

questions.question: A data set has 24 observations and a mean of 28. The sum of all the observations is
questions.explanation: Since mean = sum x / n, the sum is sum x = n x mean = 24 x 28 = 672. Option C (52) adds the two numbers instead of multiplying, option A subtracts them, and option B divides 28 by 24.

questions.question: The service times (in minutes) at a ticket counter are 4.5, 5.5, 6, 7, 8, 8.5, 4, 3, 3.5, 2.5, 3.8. The median service time is
questions.explanation: Arranged in order the times are 2.5, 3, 3.5, 3.8, 4, 4.5, 5.5, 6, 7, 8, 8.5. With n = 11, the median is the (11+1)/2 = 6th value, which is 4.5 minutes. Option C (4) is the 5th value and option A (3.8) is the 4th, so they come from counting the position wrongly; option D averages two middle values, which is only needed when n is even.

questions.question: The partition values that divide an ordered data set into 100 equal parts are called
questions.explanation: Percentiles are the 99 points that split ordered data into 100 equal parts, so P50 is the median and P25 is the first quartile. Option A, quartiles, divide the data into 4 parts and option B, deciles, into 10 parts. Option D is wrong because there is only one median and it splits the data into just 2 halves.

questions.question: The marks (out of 15) of 20 students in a class test are 10, 11, 12, 12.5, 13.5, 14, 10, 11, 12, 12.5, 13.5, 14, 8, 9, 9, 8, 10, 11, 11.5, 12.5. The mean mark of the class is
questions.explanation: Adding all 20 marks gives sum x = 225, so the mean = 225 / 20 = 11.25. Option A (12.25) is exactly 1 mark too high and comes from an addition slip, while options C and D are larger than almost every mark in the list, so they cannot be the average.

questions.question: The value obtained by dividing sum wx by sum w (where w are weights attached to the values x) is the
questions.explanation: Multiplying each value by its weight, adding the products (sum wx) and dividing by the total weight (sum w) gives the weighted arithmetic mean. Option D, the simple arithmetic mean, is sum x / n and gives every value the same importance. Options B and C use products and reciprocals of the values, not weights.

questions.question: Product A has a contribution of N6 per unit with 120 units sold, product B N8 per unit with 100 units sold, and product C N10 per unit with 130 units sold. The weighted average contribution per unit (to 2 d.p.) is
questions.explanation: Weight each contribution by its quantity: sum wx = 6(120) + 8(100) + 10(130) = 720 + 800 + 1300 = 2820, and sum w = 120 + 100 + 130 = 350, so the weighted mean = 2820 / 350 = 8.06 naira. Options A, C and D differ from this by exactly 1 or 2 naira and come from slips in the products or totals.

questions.question: The partition values that divide an ordered data set into four equal parts are called
