questions.question: The weekly sales (in units) of 40 sales representatives are grouped as follows: 10-19: 4; 20-29: 7; 30-39: 12; 40-49: 10; 50-59: 5; 60-69: 2. Given that the mean is 37.25 units and the (population) standard deviation is 13.04 units, the coefficient of variation is approximately:
questions.explanation: CV = (SD / mean) x 100% = (13.04 / 37.25) x 100% = 35.0%, which shows moderate relative spread around the average. Option C turns the ratio upside down (mean / SD x 100%), and option B simply quotes the SD as a percentage.

questions.question: The marks obtained by 10 students in Mathematics are: 36, 55, 73, 95, 42, 60, 78, 25, 62, 75. The range of the marks is:
questions.explanation: In order the marks run from 25 to 95, so range = highest - lowest = 95 - 25 = 70. Option A subtracts the first listed value from the last (75 - 36), not the extremes, and option C is just the highest mark.

questions.question: The daily sales (in N'000) of a provision kiosk in Yaba over seven days were 45, 62, 38, 71, 55, 49 and 66. The range of the sales is
questions.explanation: The range is the highest value minus the lowest value: 71 - 38 = 33. Option B subtracts the first value from the last one, which ignores the true extremes, and option D adds the extremes instead of subtracting them.

questions.question: For the kiosk sales 45, 62, 38, 71, 55, 49 and 66 (N'000), the coefficient of range, (H - L)/(H + L), is
questions.explanation: The coefficient of range is (H - L)/(H + L) = (71 - 38)/(71 + 38) = 33/109 = 0.3028. Option A divides by the highest value only and option D divides by the lowest value only, so neither uses the correct denominator H + L.

questions.question: In a BUA test, the first quartile of the marks is 24 and the third quartile is 40. The quartile deviation, (Q3 - Q1)/2, is
questions.explanation: The quartile deviation (semi-interquartile range) is half the interquartile range: (40 - 24)/2 = 8. Option C is the interquartile range itself, before halving, and option A is (Q1 + Q3)/2, the midpoint of the quartiles rather than a measure of spread.

questions.question: Given Q1 = 24 and Q3 = 40 for a set of test marks, the coefficient of quartile deviation, (Q3 - Q1)/(Q3 + Q1), is
questions.explanation: The coefficient of quartile deviation is (40 - 24)/(40 + 24) = 16/64 = 0.25. Option D divides the interquartile range by the midpoint 32 instead of the sum 64, while options B and C divide by Q3 or Q1 alone.

questions.question: The first and third quartiles of the daily transport fares paid by a group of UNILAG students are N1,250 and N2,050. The interquartile range is
questions.explanation: The interquartile range is Q3 - Q1 = N2,050 - N1,250 = N800. Option B is the quartile deviation (half of the IQR), and option D is the average of the two quartiles, which is not a measure of spread.

questions.question: Using the (n + 1) position method on ordered data, the interquartile range of the following numbers of customers served per hour at a Surulere bank is: 12, 15, 9, 20, 18, 11, 25, 14, 16, 22, 13
questions.explanation: Ordering gives 9, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 18, 20, 22, 25; with n = 11, Q1 is the 3rd value (12) and Q3 is the 9th value (20), so IQR = 20 - 12 = 8. Option C is the quartile deviation, option D is the range, and option B comes from picking the 3rd and 9th values without first arranging the data in order.

questions.question: The ages of seven traders in a Mushin market association are 30, 42, 35, 50, 28, 46 and 39. Using the (n + 1) position method, the quartile deviation of the ages is
questions.explanation: With n = 7 the ordered data are 28, 30, 35, 39, 42, 46, 50, so Q1 is the 2nd value (30) and Q3 is the 6th value (46). QD = (46 - 30)/2 = 8. Option B forgets to halve the interquartile range, and options D and A use the extreme values instead of the quartiles.

questions.question: The numbers of textbooks sold by a campus bookshop on five days were 4, 7, 9, 10 and 15. The mean deviation about the mean is
questions.explanation: The mean is 45/5 = 9, the absolute deviations are 5, 2, 0, 1 and 6, and their total of 14 divided by 5 gives 2.8. Option C results from adding the signed deviations, which always sum to zero; option B wrongly divides by n - 1, and option A is the total of the absolute deviations before dividing.

questions.question: For the daily textbook sales 4, 7, 9, 10 and 15, the mean deviation about the mean is 2.8. The coefficient of mean deviation (MD/mean) is
questions.explanation: The coefficient of mean deviation is MD divided by the mean: 2.8/9 = 0.3111. Option A inverts the ratio (mean/MD), and option C divides by the largest value instead of the mean.

questions.question: The waiting times (in minutes) of five patients at a Lagos clinic were 3, 5, 8, 12 and 22. The mean deviation about the median is
questions.explanation: The median is 8, so the absolute deviations from it are 5, 3, 0, 4 and 14, totalling 26, and 26/5 = 5.2. Option B is the mean deviation about the mean of 10, which is not what was asked, option D divides by n - 1, and option A is the undivided total.

questions.question: Treating the following as a population, find the variance of the numbers of calls received per hour at a call centre: 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9
questions.explanation: The mean is 40/8 = 5 and the squared deviations total 32, so the population variance is 32/8 = 4. Option A divides by n - 1 = 7, which gives the sample variance, option C is the standard deviation, and option B is the total of the squared deviations.

questions.question: A sample of five POS operators in Ikeja recorded 6, 9, 12, 15 and 18 transactions in an hour. The sample variance (dividing by n - 1) is
questions.explanation: The mean is 12 and the squared deviations are 36, 9, 0, 9 and 36, totalling 90; dividing by n - 1 = 4 gives 22.5. Option C divides by n = 5 (the population formula), option B is the sample standard deviation, and option A is the total of the squared deviations.

questions.question: The weekly wages (N'000) of all five cleaners employed by a small firm are 10, 12, 14, 16 and 18. Treating them as a population, the standard deviation is
questions.explanation: The mean is 14, the squared deviations total 40, and the population variance is 40/5 = 8, so SD = sqrt(8) = 2.8284. Option C uses n - 1 (the sample formula), option A is the variance not its square root, and option B is the mean deviation.

questions.question: A sample of five Lagos households spent 5, 7, 8, 10 and 15 (N'000) on electricity in a month. The sample standard deviation (divisor n - 1) is
questions.explanation: The mean is 9 and the squared deviations are 16, 4, 1, 1 and 36, totalling 58; the sample variance is 58/4 = 14.5 and SD = sqrt(14.5) = 3.8079. Option A divides by n = 5, option D is the sample variance, and option C is the mean deviation about the mean.

questions.question: For a population of 10 values, sum x = 120 and sum x^2 = 1,600. Using variance = (sum x^2)/N - (mean)^2, the variance is
questions.explanation: The mean is 120/10 = 12, so the variance is 1,600/10 - 12^2 = 160 - 144 = 16. Option B is the standard deviation, option C is only the square of the mean, and option D divides the corrected sum of squares by N - 1, which is the sample formula, not the population one.

questions.question: The ages of members of a cooperative society are grouped as 0-10 (5), 10-20 (8), 20-30 (15), 30-40 (8), 40-50 (4), with frequencies in brackets. Using class midpoints and treating the data as a population (divide by sum f), the standard deviation is
questions.explanation: Using midpoints 5, 15, 25, 35, 45, the mean is 24.5 and sum f(x - mean)^2 / sum f = 129.75, so SD = sqrt(129.75) = 11.3908. Option B is the variance, option A divides by sum f - 1, and option C ignores the frequencies and treats the five midpoints as equally likely.

questions.question: The number of children (x) in 20 households is summarised as x: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 with frequencies f: 2, 5, 8, 3, 2. Treating the data as a population, the variance is
questions.explanation: The mean is sum fx / sum f = 58/20 = 2.9, and sum f(x - mean)^2 / sum f = 23.8/20 = 1.19. Option D is the standard deviation, option A divides by 19, and option B is the variance of the x values without weighting by their frequencies.

questions.question: The daily sales (units) of a bakery are x: 10, 20, 30, 40 with frequencies f: 3, 5, 8, 4. The mean deviation about the mean, sum f|x - mean| / sum f, is
questions.explanation: The mean is 530/20 = 26.5; the absolute deviations 16.5, 6.5, 3.5 and 13.5 weighted by 3, 5, 8, 4 total 164, and 164/20 = 8.2. Option D comes from keeping the signs, since weighted deviations from the mean sum to zero; option B ignores the frequencies, and option C divides by 19.

questions.question: The mean monthly rent in a Lagos estate is N80,000 with a standard deviation of N12,000. The coefficient of variation is
questions.explanation: The coefficient of variation is SD/mean x 100% = 12,000/80,000 x 100% = 15%. Option B inverts the ratio (mean/SD), option C forgets to multiply by 100, and option A uses the variance in thousands (144/80) instead of the standard deviation.

questions.question: Bus Route A in Lagos carries a mean of 400 passengers a day with SD 60; Route B carries a mean of 250 with SD 45. Using the coefficient of variation, which route has the more consistent daily passenger numbers?

options.a: Route B, because its CV (18%) is higher than Route A's (15%)
options.b: Neither, because both routes have the same CV
options.c: Route A, because its CV (15%) is lower than Route B's (18%)
options.d: Route B, because its standard deviation is smaller

questions.explanation: CV(A) = 60/400 x 100% = 15% and CV(B) = 45/250 x 100% = 18%; the lower CV shows less variability relative to the mean, so Route A is more consistent. Option D compares raw standard deviations, which is misleading when the means differ, and option A treats a higher CV as more consistent, which is the reverse of the rule.

questions.question: Treating the following as a population, the coefficient of variation of the weekly hours worked by four part-time staff, 20, 24, 26 and 30, is (to 2 d.p.)
questions.explanation: The mean is 25 and the population variance is (25 + 1 + 1 + 25)/4 = 13, so SD = 3.6056 and CV = 3.6056/25 x 100% = 14.42%. Option A uses the sample SD (divisor 3), option C divides the variance rather than the SD by the mean, and option D inverts the ratio.

questions.question: The standard deviation of the monthly salaries of a firm's staff is N12,000. If every salary is increased by N5,000, the new standard deviation is
questions.explanation: Adding the same amount to every value shifts the whole distribution but does not change how spread out it is, so the SD stays N12,000. Options A, B and D all assume that the SD changes in some way, but adding a constant affects only measures of location such as the mean.

questions.question: The standard deviation of the prices of a set of items is N4. If every price is tripled, the new standard deviation is
questions.explanation: Multiplying every value by a constant k multiplies the SD by |k|, so the new SD is 3 x 4 = N12. Option C assumes the SD is unchanged, which only happens when a constant is added; option D multiplies by 3^2, which is what happens to the variance, not the SD.

questions.question: A data set has variance 9. If every observation is multiplied by 2, the variance of the new data is
questions.explanation: When each value is multiplied by k, the variance is multiplied by k^2, so the new variance is 2^2 x 9 = 36. Option C multiplies by k instead of k^2 (that rule applies to the SD), option A assumes no change, and option D adds the constant instead.

questions.question: A variable x has standard deviation 5. If y = -2x + 10, the standard deviation of y is
questions.explanation: For y = a + bx, SD(y) = |b| x SD(x), so SD(y) = |-2| x 5 = 10; the added 10 has no effect on spread. Option B keeps the minus sign, but a standard deviation can never be negative, and option D wrongly adds the constant 10 to the scaled SD.

questions.question: A distribution has mean 50 and standard deviation 10. If 10 is added to every observation, the new coefficient of variation is (to 2 d.p.)
questions.explanation: Adding 10 raises the mean to 60 but leaves the SD at 10, so the CV becomes 10/60 x 100% = 16.67%. Option A assumes the CV is unchanged, which is false because the mean changes; option C also adds 10 to the SD, which does not happen.

questions.question: The coefficient of variation of the daily output of a garment factory is 25% and the mean output is 64 units. The standard deviation is
questions.explanation: Since CV = SD/mean x 100%, SD = CV x mean / 100 = 25 x 64/100 = 16 units. Option D forgets to divide by 100, and option B divides the mean by 25 instead of multiplying by 0.25.

questions.question: A distribution has standard deviation 8 and coefficient of variation 20%. Its mean is
questions.explanation: Rearranging CV = SD/mean x 100% gives mean = SD x 100/CV = 8 x 100/20 = 40. Option C multiplies 8 by 0.2 instead of dividing, and option D multiplies 8 by 20.

questions.question: Treating the five values 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 as a population, their standard deviation is
questions.explanation: The mean is 3 and the squared deviations 4, 1, 0, 1, 4 total 10, so the population variance is 10/5 = 2 and SD = sqrt(2) = 1.4142. Option A uses the sample divisor n - 1, option B is the variance, and option C is the mean deviation.

questions.question: Monthly data-bundle spending (N'00) of 40 students is grouped as 10-20 (5), 20-30 (7), 30-40 (10), 40-50 (12), 50-60 (6), with continuous classes and frequencies in brackets. Using Q = L + ((kN/4 - F)/f) x h, the quartile deviation is (to 2 d.p.)
questions.explanation: Q1 is the 10th value, in class 20-30: 20 + ((10 - 5)/7) x 10 = 27.14; Q3 is the 30th value, in class 40-50: 40 + ((30 - 22)/12) x 10 = 46.67. QD = (46.67 - 27.14)/2 = 9.76. Option C is the interquartile range before halving, and option A is the coefficient of quartile deviation, (Q3 - Q1)/(Q3 + Q1).

questions.question: Five students in a tutorial group each scored exactly 14 out of 20 in a quiz. The standard deviation of their scores is
questions.explanation: When every observation is identical there is no spread at all: each deviation from the mean of 14 is zero, so the SD is 0. Option A confuses the SD with the mean, and option B assumes some minimum spread that does not exist here.

questions.question: The standard deviation of the weekly profits of a small business is N7,000. The variance is
questions.explanation: Variance is the square of the SD: 7,000^2 = 49,000,000, measured in squared units of naira. Option B takes the square root of 7,000 instead of squaring it, and option A doubles the SD instead of squaring it.

questions.question: For a set of five observations, the population variance (divisor n) is 18. The corresponding sample variance (divisor n - 1) is
questions.explanation: The total of squared deviations is 18 x 5 = 90, and dividing by n - 1 = 4 gives 22.5. Option A multiplies by 4/5 instead of 5/4, option C assumes the two divisors give the same result, and option D divides 18 by 4.

questions.question: In statistics, the extent to which the values of a data set are scattered or spread out about a central value is called
questions.explanation: Dispersion (variation) describes how widely observations are spread around an average such as the mean. Option B describes the typical or central value itself, not the spread, and option D describes lack of symmetry, not spread.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an absolute measure of dispersion?
questions.explanation: The coefficient of quartile deviation, (Q3 - Q1)/(Q3 + Q1), is a ratio with no units, so it is a relative measure. Options B, A and C are all absolute measures because they are expressed in the units of the data, such as naira or kilograms.

questions.question: The main difference between absolute and relative measures of dispersion is that relative measures

options.a: are expressed in the same units as the original data
options.b: always give larger values than absolute measures
options.c: are pure numbers free of units, so they can compare distributions measured in different units
options.d: are computed only from the two extreme values of the data

questions.explanation: Relative measures such as the coefficient of variation divide an absolute measure by an average, so the units cancel out and different distributions can be compared. Option A describes absolute measures, and option D describes the range, which is only one particular absolute measure.

questions.question: The interquartile range measures the spread of the

options.d: whole data set from the lowest to the highest value

questions.explanation: The interquartile range is Q3 - Q1, the width of the interval holding the central half of the ordered data. Option D describes the range, and options B and C each describe only one part of the distribution.

questions.question: In computing the mean deviation, absolute values of the deviations from the mean are used because

options.a: absolute values make the result equal to the standard deviation
options.b: negative deviations are always larger than positive ones
options.c: the sum of the deviations from the mean, with signs kept, is always zero
options.d: it makes the mean deviation independent of the mean

questions.explanation: Positive and negative deviations from the arithmetic mean always cancel out exactly, so their sum is zero; ignoring the signs gives a usable average distance. Option A is false because the mean deviation and the standard deviation are generally different numbers.

questions.question: The mean deviation of a set of observations is smallest when the deviations are measured from the
questions.explanation: The sum of absolute deviations is a minimum when taken about the median, so the mean deviation about the median is never larger than about any other value. Option A is tempting, but the mean minimises the sum of squared deviations, not absolute deviations.

questions.question: In statistics, the variance of a set of observations is defined as the

options.a: square root of the mean of the squared deviations
options.b: difference between the largest and smallest observations
options.c: mean of the absolute deviations of the observations from their mean
options.d: mean of the squared deviations of the observations from their mean

questions.explanation: Variance averages the squared distances of the observations from the mean. Option C defines the mean deviation, option A defines the standard deviation, and option B defines the range.

questions.question: The standard deviation of a data set is the

options.b: positive square root of the variance

questions.explanation: Taking the positive square root of the variance returns the measure to the original units of the data, and that is the standard deviation. Option C gives a ratio similar in idea to a relative measure, and option D is the mean deviation.

questions.question: If daily sales are measured in naira, the variance of the daily sales is measured in

options.c: no units, because it is a pure number

questions.explanation: Variance squares each deviation, so its unit is the square of the data unit, here naira squared. Option D is the unit of the standard deviation, while options B and C describe relative measures such as the coefficient of variation.

questions.question: When computing the variance of a sample to estimate the population variance, the sum of squared deviations is divided by n - 1 rather than n because

options.a: it always makes the variance equal to the standard deviation
options.b: it makes the variance a relative measure
options.c: it removes the effect of extreme values
options.d: it gives an unbiased estimate of the population variance

questions.explanation: Deviations measured from the sample mean tend to be slightly smaller than deviations from the true population mean, and dividing by n - 1 corrects this so that the sample variance is unbiased. Options C and B are wrong because the divisor changes neither the effect of outliers nor the units.

questions.question: If the same constant is added to every observation in a data set, then the range, quartile deviation and standard deviation

options.a: are all multiplied by that constant

questions.explanation: Adding a constant shifts every value by the same amount, so the distances between values, and therefore all absolute measures of spread, stay the same. Option B confuses measures of spread with measures of location, such as the mean, which do increase by the constant.

questions.question: A quality controller at a bottling plant in Agbara quickly checks each batch by subtracting the smallest fill volume from the largest. The measure of dispersion being used is the
questions.explanation: Subtracting the smallest value from the largest is exactly the range, which is popular in quality control because it is quick and easy. Option A is a relative measure that needs both a mean and an SD.

questions.question: A researcher wants to compare the variability of the heights (in cm) and the weights (in kg) of UNILAG freshers. The most appropriate measure is the
questions.explanation: Because the two variables are in different units, only a unit-free relative measure such as the CV allows a fair comparison. Options D, C and B are absolute measures in cm or kg (or their squares), so they cannot be compared directly.

questions.question: Two machines fill sachets of pure water. Machine P has a coefficient of variation of 40% and Machine Q has 20%. This means that

options.a: Machine P's output is more variable relative to its mean than Machine Q's
options.b: Machine P is more consistent than Machine Q
options.c: Machine P has twice the mean output of Machine Q
options.d: Machine P must have the larger standard deviation in absolute terms

questions.explanation: A higher CV means more variation relative to the mean, so P is less consistent than Q. Option B reverses the rule, option C confuses the CV with the mean, and option D is not guaranteed because the CV depends on both the SD and the mean.

questions.question: A major demerit of the range as a measure of dispersion is that it

options.b: is based on only the two extreme values and ignores the rest of the data
options.c: cannot be computed for ungrouped data
options.d: is always equal to zero for large samples

questions.explanation: Since the range uses only the largest and smallest values, one unusual observation can change it greatly while the rest of the data say nothing. Option A is wrong because ease of calculation is in fact the main merit of the range.

questions.question: Which of the following is a merit of the standard deviation?

options.a: It is not affected at all by extreme values
options.b: It is based on all the observations and is suitable for further algebraic treatment
options.c: It can be computed easily for open-ended distributions
options.d: It is a unit-free measure for comparing distributions

questions.explanation: The SD uses every observation and fits well into further statistical work such as sampling theory and the normal curve. Option A is false because squaring deviations makes the SD sensitive to outliers, and option D describes the coefficient of variation.

questions.question: A demerit of the mean deviation is that it

options.a: ignores the middle 50% of the observations
options.b: ignores the algebraic signs of the deviations, which makes it unsuitable for further algebraic treatment
options.c: uses only the two extreme values of the data
options.d: can be negative when most values are below the mean

questions.explanation: The mean deviation takes absolute values, and absolute values are awkward to use in further mathematical work. Option C describes the range, and option D is impossible because absolute deviations are never negative.

questions.question: A limitation of the quartile deviation is that it

options.a: requires all observations to be equal
options.b: cannot be computed when the data are grouped
options.c: ignores the lowest 25% and the highest 25% of the observations
options.d: is heavily affected by extreme values

questions.explanation: The quartile deviation is built from Q1 and Q3, so the bottom and top quarters of the data play no part in it. Option D is the opposite of the truth, since ignoring the extremes makes it resistant to outliers.

questions.question: For a frequency distribution with open-ended classes such as "Below 10" and "60 and above", the most suitable measure of dispersion is the
questions.explanation: The quartiles can usually be located without knowing the limits of the end classes, so the quartile deviation can still be computed. Options D, C and A need the extreme values or midpoints of every class, which open-ended classes do not provide.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the standard deviation is NOT true?

options.a: It is zero when all the observations are equal
options.b: It is unchanged when a constant is added to every observation
options.c: It can be negative when most observations are below the mean
options.d: It uses every observation in the data set

questions.explanation: The standard deviation is the positive square root of the variance, so it can never be negative. Options A, B and D are all genuine properties of the SD.

questions.question: Which of the following is a measure of dispersion?
questions.explanation: The mean deviation measures the average distance of observations from a central value, so it describes spread. Options A, C and B are all measures of central tendency (location), which describe a typical value rather than spread.

questions.question: Shop X in Balogun market has mean daily sales of N50,000 with SD N5,000, while Shop Y has mean daily sales of N20,000 with SD N3,000. Which statement is correct?

options.a: Shop Y's sales are relatively more variable, since its CV is 15% against 10% for Shop X
options.b: Shop X's sales are relatively more variable, since its SD is larger
options.c: Shop X's sales are relatively more variable, since its CV is 15% against 10% for Shop Y
options.d: Both shops are equally variable, since each SD is a tenth of the mean

questions.explanation: CV(X) = 5,000/50,000 x 100% = 10% and CV(Y) = 3,000/20,000 x 100% = 15%, so Y varies more relative to its mean. Option B compares absolute SDs, which is misleading when the means are so different, and option C mixes up which shop has which CV.

questions.question: Measures of dispersion are needed alongside averages mainly because

options.a: they show how far the average can be relied on to represent the data
options.b: they always give the same value as the mean
options.c: they replace the need to calculate an average
options.d: they show only the direction of the tail of a distribution

questions.explanation: Two data sets can share the same mean but have very different spreads; a small dispersion means the average represents the data well, while a large one means it does not. Option D describes skewness, not dispersion.

questions.question: A set of data with a coefficient of skewness of -0.8 can be said to be
questions.explanation: A negative coefficient of skewness means the longer tail is on the left side, so the data are skewed to the left (negatively skewed). Option C, skewed to the right, would need a positive coefficient. Option A, symmetrical, would need a coefficient of 0.

questions.question: For a unimodal distribution, if the mode is greater than the median (and the median greater than the mean), the distribution is:
questions.explanation: In a left (negatively) skewed distribution, a long tail of low values pulls the mean down, so mean < median < mode. Option B, right skewness, has the opposite order with the mode smallest. In a symmetrical distribution (A) the mean, median and mode are equal.

questions.question: A frequency distribution in which most of the values are spread more to one side (left or right) of the mode is described as:
questions.explanation: Skewness means lack of symmetry: the values trail off more on one side of the peak than the other, creating a longer tail. Option B, symmetrical, means the two sides are mirror images. Option C, bimodal, refers to having two modes, and Option D describes peakedness (kurtosis), not lopsidedness.

questions.question: For a moderately skewed distribution, the empirical relationship gives (Mean - Mode) approximately equal to:
questions.explanation: The empirical relation Mode = 3 Median - 2 Mean can be rearranged to Mean - Mode = 3(Mean - Median). Option B uses the wrong multiplier, and Option C is also wrong because Median - Mode equals 2(Mean - Median), not Mean - Mode.

questions.question: For a moderately skewed distribution, the mean is 11 and the median is 13. Using the empirical relationship, the mode is:
questions.explanation: Using Mode = 3 Median - 2 Mean, Mode = 3(13) - 2(11) = 39 - 22 = 17. Option A, 15, comes from wrongly assuming the mode is just as far above the median as the mean is below it. Since the mean is less than the median, the distribution is negatively skewed, so the mode must be the largest of the three.

questions.question: In a negatively skewed distribution, the order of the mean, median and mode is:
questions.explanation: In a negatively (left) skewed distribution, the long tail of low values pulls the mean down the most, so Mean < Median < Mode. Option B is the order for a positively skewed distribution, and Option D holds only for a symmetrical distribution.

questions.question: A distribution whose extreme values (outliers) lie on the high side, giving a long tail to the right, is described as:
questions.explanation: When the unusual values are large, they stretch the distribution into a long right tail and pull the mean above the median, which is right (positive) skewness. Option C, left skewness, has its long tail of extreme low values. Option D describes peakedness, not which side has the tail.

questions.question: The degree to which a distribution departs from symmetry about its central value is called
questions.explanation: Skewness measures lack of symmetry: it tells us whether the values trail off more to the right (positive skew) or to the left (negative skew) of the centre. Option A, kurtosis, describes how peaked or flat the curve is, not whether it is lopsided. Option B, dispersion, measures spread, and Option D describes the central value itself.

questions.question: A distribution in which the mean, median and mode are not equal is described as
questions.explanation: When the mean, median and mode pull apart, the distribution is lopsided, that is asymmetrical or skewed, with the mean dragged towards the longer tail. Options A, C and D all describe distributions in which the three averages coincide, which is the opposite of what the question states.

questions.question: If the mean, median and mode of a distribution have the same value, the distribution is
questions.explanation: In a symmetrical distribution the two halves mirror each other about the centre, so the mean, median and mode all fall at the same point. Option A is wrong because in a positively skewed distribution mean > median > mode, and option B because in a negatively skewed one mean < median < mode. Option D is wrong because a bimodal distribution has two modes, so a single mode cannot equal the mean and median.

questions.question: For a moderately skewed distribution, the mode is 14 and the arithmetic mean is 5. Using the empirical relationship, the median is
questions.explanation: From Mode = 3 Median - 2 Mean, 14 = 3 Median - 10, so 3 Median = 24 and the median is 8. Option A, 12, does lie between the mean and the mode, but it does not fit the relation, since 3(12) - 2(5) = 26, not 14. Option D simply repeats the mode, and option B lies outside the range from 5 to 14.

questions.question: A distribution whose few outliers have unusually low values, giving a long tail to the left, is described as
questions.explanation: A few very small values stretch the tail towards the left, which makes the distribution negatively skewed, with mean < median < mode. Option C, positive skew, is caused by unusually high values in a long right tail. Option A is wrong because outliers on only one side destroy symmetry, and option B describes peakedness rather than lopsidedness.

questions.question: If a dataset has a mean of 75 and a median of 60, what can be inferred about the distribution's skewness?
questions.explanation: When the mean (75) is greater than the median (60), a few large values are pulling the mean to the right, so the distribution is positively skewed. Option C would need the mean below the median, and option D describes peakedness (kurtosis), not skewness.

questions.question: In a distribution that is described as being 'Positively Skewed', what is the typical relationship between the mean and the median?

options.a: The mean is greater than the median.
options.b: The mean is less than the median.
options.c: The mean is always double the value of the median.
options.d: The mean and median are exactly equal.

questions.explanation: In a positively skewed distribution the long right tail pulls the mean above the median. Option B describes negative skew, and option D describes a symmetrical distribution; option C has no basis.

questions.question: A probability distribution that is more 'peaked' than a normal distribution and has fatter tails is classified as:
questions.explanation: A leptokurtic distribution is more peaked than the normal curve with heavier tails (beta2 > 3). Option B, platykurtic, is flatter with thinner tails, and option D, mesokurtic, is the normal curve itself.

questions.question: A distribution in which Mean > Median > Mode is:
questions.explanation: In a positively skewed distribution the long tail is on the right, and the extreme high values pull the mean above the median, which sits above the mode. Option B is the reverse pattern (Mean < Median < Mode), and option A would have all three equal. Option D describes peakedness, not skewness.

questions.question: The weekly sales (in units) of 40 sales representatives are grouped as follows: 10-19: 4; 20-29: 7; 30-39: 12; 40-49: 10; 50-59: 5; 60-69: 2. Using interpolation with class boundaries, Q1 = 28.07, median = 37.0 and Q3 = 46.5 units. Based on Bowley's coefficient of skewness, the distribution is:
questions.explanation: Bowley's coefficient = (Q3 + Q1 - 2Q2)/(Q3 - Q1) = (46.5 + 28.07 - 74)/(46.5 - 28.07) = 0.57/18.43 = +0.03. Because Q3 - median (9.5) is slightly larger than median - Q1 (8.93), the upper half is a little more stretched, giving a very slight positive skew. Option B gets the sign the wrong way round, and option A would need the two gaps to be exactly equal.

questions.question: The weekly earnings of okada riders in a Lagos suburb have mean N52,000, mode N46,000 and standard deviation N8,000. Pearson's first coefficient of skewness, (Mean - Mode)/SD, is
questions.explanation: Pearson's first coefficient is (52 - 46)/8 = 6/8 = 0.75, a positive value showing positive skewness. Option D subtracts in the wrong order (Mode - Mean), and option A wrongly applies the factor 3, which belongs only to the second (median-based) coefficient.

questions.question: Scores in a GST test have mean 45, median 48 and standard deviation 6. Pearson's second coefficient of skewness, 3(Mean - Median)/SD, is
questions.explanation: The second coefficient is 3(45 - 48)/6 = -9/6 = -1.5, so the distribution is negatively skewed. Option A leaves out the factor 3, option D drops the minus sign, and option C divides by the median instead of the standard deviation.

questions.question: In a moderately skewed distribution of household sizes in Ajegunle, the mean is 6.0 and the median is 5.6. Using Mode = 3 Median - 2 Mean, the mode is
questions.explanation: Mode = 3(5.6) - 2(6.0) = 16.8 - 12.0 = 4.8, which lies below both the median and the mean, as expected for positive skew. Option D swaps the roles of mean and median (3 x 6.0 - 2 x 5.6), and option C simply averages the mean and median.

questions.question: A moderately skewed distribution has mean 40 and mode 34. Using the empirical relation Mode = 3 Median - 2 Mean, the median is
questions.explanation: Rearranging gives Median = (Mode + 2 Mean)/3 = (34 + 80)/3 = 114/3 = 38. Option C takes the simple average of the mean and mode, and option D lies outside the interval from the mode to the mean, which the median must fall within for a moderately skewed distribution.

questions.question: For a moderately skewed distribution of daily bread sales, the median is 30 loaves and the mode is 27 loaves. Using Mode = 3 Median - 2 Mean, the mean is
questions.explanation: From Mode = 3 Median - 2 Mean, Mean = (3 Median - Mode)/2 = (90 - 27)/2 = 63/2 = 31.5 loaves. Option C is the simple average of median and mode, and option A adds the full median-mode gap of 3 to the median instead of half of it.

questions.question: The quartiles of the monthly rents (N'000) of shops in a Lagos plaza are Q1 = 20, Q2 = 30 and Q3 = 50. Bowley's coefficient of skewness, (Q3 + Q1 - 2Q2)/(Q3 - Q1), is
questions.explanation: Bowley's coefficient is (50 + 20 - 60)/(50 - 20) = 10/30 = 0.3333, a positive value meaning the upper quartile is further from the median than the lower quartile. Option D has the wrong sign, and option C divides by Q3 instead of the interquartile range Q3 - Q1.

questions.question: For a distribution with Q1 = 40, median = 55 and Q3 = 60, Bowley's coefficient of skewness, (Q3 + Q1 - 2Q2)/(Q3 - Q1), is
questions.explanation: Here (60 + 40 - 110)/(60 - 40) = -10/20 = -0.5, so the distribution is negatively skewed: the median is closer to Q3 than to Q1. Option C has the wrong sign, option B divides by Q3 + Q1 instead of Q3 - Q1, and option D divides by Q1.

questions.question: The second and fourth central moments of a distribution are m2 = 4 and m4 = 60. The coefficient of kurtosis beta2 = m4/m2^2 is
questions.explanation: beta2 = m4/m2^2 = 60/4^2 = 60/16 = 3.75. Option D divides by m2 instead of m2 squared, option B is the excess kurtosis (beta2 - 3), not beta2 itself, and option A divides by m2^(3/2) = 8.

questions.question: A distribution has central moments m2 = 5 and m4 = 50. Its excess kurtosis, beta2 - 3, is
questions.explanation: beta2 = 50/5^2 = 2, so the excess kurtosis is 2 - 3 = -1, showing a flatter-than-normal (platykurtic) curve. Option B has the wrong sign, option D is beta2 itself, and option A uses m4/m2 - 3 = 10 - 3 instead of squaring m2.

questions.question: The central moments of the daily returns on a Lagos-listed share are m2 = 3 and m4 = 36. Using beta2 = m4/m2^2, the distribution is
questions.explanation: beta2 = 36/3^2 = 36/9 = 4, which is greater than 3, so the curve is more peaked than the normal curve: leptokurtic. Option D needs beta2 = 3 exactly, and option C needs beta2 below 3.

questions.question: A distribution of exam marks has central moments m2 = 2 and m4 = 8. Using beta2 = m4/m2^2, the distribution is
questions.explanation: beta2 = 8/2^2 = 2, which is less than 3, so the curve is flatter than the normal curve: platykurtic. Option A needs beta2 above 3, and option C is about lack of symmetry, which beta2 does not measure.

questions.question: A distribution has central moments m2 = 4 and m3 = -4. The moment coefficient of skewness beta1 = m3^2/m2^3 is
questions.explanation: beta1 = (-4)^2/4^3 = 16/64 = 0.25; because m3 is squared, beta1 can never be negative. Option D wrongly keeps a negative sign, option C divides by m2^2 instead of m2^3, and option B is m3/m2^(3/2), a different (signed) measure, not beta1.

questions.question: A distribution has central moments m2 = 9, m3 = 0 and m4 = 243. Using beta1 = m3^2/m2^3 and beta2 = m4/m2^2, the distribution is
questions.explanation: beta1 = 0/729 = 0, so the distribution is symmetric, and beta2 = 243/81 = 3, the normal benchmark, so it is mesokurtic. Option A would need beta2 above 3, option B would need beta1 above 0, and option C would need beta2 below 3.

questions.question: A moderately skewed distribution has mean 75, median 72 and standard deviation 12. Using Mode = 3 Median - 2 Mean to find the mode, Pearson's first coefficient of skewness, (Mean - Mode)/SD, is
questions.explanation: Mode = 3(72) - 2(75) = 216 - 150 = 66, so the coefficient is (75 - 66)/12 = 9/12 = 0.75. Option B wrongly uses the median in place of the mode, (75 - 72)/12, and option D reverses the subtraction.

questions.question: Pearson's second coefficient of skewness, 3(Mean - Median)/SD, for a distribution is 0.6. If the mean is 50 and the median is 47, the standard deviation is
questions.explanation: From 0.6 = 3(50 - 47)/SD, we get SD = 9/0.6 = 15. Option C ignores the factor 3 (3/0.6), option D multiplies 9 by 0.6 instead of dividing, and option B multiplies 3 by 0.6.

questions.question: For a distribution, Q1 = 30, Q3 = 50, P10 = 20 and P90 = 70. The percentile coefficient of kurtosis, k = QD/(P90 - P10), where QD = (Q3 - Q1)/2, is
questions.explanation: QD = (50 - 30)/2 = 10 and P90 - P10 = 70 - 20 = 50, so k = 10/50 = 0.2. Option D uses the full interquartile range of 20 instead of the QD, and option B divides by P90 - Q1 = 40 instead of P90 - P10.

questions.question: The prices of second-hand phones at Computer Village have mean N32,000, median N35,000 and mode N37,000. The distribution is
questions.explanation: Here mean < median < mode, which is the pattern of a negatively skewed distribution, with the longer tail to the left pulling the mean down. Option A would need mean > median > mode, option D would need all three equal, and option B describes peakedness, not symmetry.

questions.question: A distribution has beta2 = 4.2. Its excess kurtosis and shape are
questions.explanation: Excess kurtosis is beta2 - 3 = 4.2 - 3 = 1.2; a positive excess means the curve is more peaked than the normal curve, so it is leptokurtic. Option B subtracts in the wrong order, option A gives beta2 itself rather than the excess, and option C pairs a positive excess with the wrong shape.

questions.question: In statistics, the lack of symmetry in a frequency distribution is called
questions.explanation: Skewness measures how far a distribution departs from symmetry, with one tail longer than the other. Option A describes peakedness or flatness, and option D describes spread about the average.

questions.question: In a perfectly symmetric unimodal distribution, the mean, median and mode are

options.a: in the order mean < median < mode
options.d: in the order mean > median > mode

questions.explanation: A symmetric bell-shaped distribution has its centre at a single point, so the mean, median and mode coincide. Option D describes positive skewness and option A describes negative skewness.

questions.question: In a positively skewed distribution, the usual order of the three averages is
questions.explanation: In positive skewness a few very large values in the right tail pull the mean up the most, the median less, and the mode least, giving mean > median > mode. Option C is the order for negative skewness, and option B describes a symmetric distribution.

questions.question: A positively skewed distribution is one in which

options.a: the curve is more peaked than the normal curve
options.b: the longer tail extends to the right
options.c: the longer tail extends to the left
options.d: both tails are of equal length

questions.explanation: Positive (right) skewness means the distribution stretches further towards the high values, giving a longer right tail. Option C describes negative skewness, option D describes symmetry, and option A describes leptokurtosis, which is about peakedness rather than symmetry.

questions.question: In a Lagos firm, most workers earn modest salaries while a few directors earn extremely high salaries. The distribution of salaries is most likely
questions.explanation: A small number of very high values creates a long right tail and pulls the mean above the median, which is positive skewness. Option C would need a few unusually low values instead, and option D is about flatness of the peak, not the direction of the tail.

questions.question: An easy quiz is given to a UNILAG class: most students score near the maximum, but a few score very low. The distribution of scores is most likely
questions.explanation: Scores bunched at the high end with a few very low marks give a long left tail, which is negative skewness, with mean < median < mode. Option C describes a long right tail, and option A refers to kurtosis, not to the direction of the tail.

questions.question: Bowley's coefficient of skewness is based on the

options.d: mean and the standard deviation only

questions.explanation: Bowley's measure, (Q3 + Q1 - 2Q2)/(Q3 - Q1), uses only Q1, the median (Q2) and Q3. Option B is the basis of Pearson's first coefficient, and option C relates to the moment measures of skewness and kurtosis.

questions.question: The value of Bowley's coefficient of skewness always lies between
questions.explanation: Since |Q3 + Q1 - 2Q2| can never exceed Q3 - Q1, Bowley's coefficient is bounded by -1 and +1. Option B ignores negative skewness, which gives negative values, and options C and D borrow the -3 to +3 limits often quoted for Pearson's coefficient.

questions.question: A statistician wants to measure the skewness of a frequency distribution with open-ended classes "Under N10,000" and "N100,000 and above". The most suitable measure is
questions.explanation: Bowley's measure needs only the quartiles, which can be located even when the end classes are open, and it is not affected by extreme values. Options B, A and C all need the mean and standard deviation or moments, which require midpoints for every class.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT used in computing either of Pearson's coefficients of skewness?
questions.explanation: Pearson's coefficients are (Mean - Mode)/SD and 3(Mean - Median)/SD, so they use the mean, mode, median and SD but never the interquartile range. The interquartile range appears instead in the denominator of Bowley's coefficient.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a measure of skewness?
questions.explanation: The coefficient of variation, SD/mean x 100%, is a relative measure of dispersion, not of symmetry. Options A, C and B are all genuine measures of skewness.

questions.question: The degree of peakedness or flatness of a frequency curve compared with the normal curve is called
questions.explanation: Kurtosis describes how peaked or flat-topped a distribution is relative to the normal (mesokurtic) curve. Option D describes lack of symmetry, and option B describes spread about the average.

questions.question: A leptokurtic distribution is one that is

options.a: exactly as peaked as the normal curve, with beta2 equal to 3
options.b: flatter than the normal curve, with beta2 less than 3
options.c: more peaked than the normal curve, with beta2 greater than 3
options.d: skewed to the right, with mean greater than mode

questions.explanation: Lepto means slender: a leptokurtic curve has a higher, sharper peak than the normal curve, so beta2 > 3. Option B describes a platykurtic curve, option A a mesokurtic one, and option D describes positive skewness.

questions.question: A frequency curve that is flatter than the normal curve, with beta2 less than 3, is described as
questions.explanation: Platy means flat or broad, so a platykurtic curve has a lower, flatter peak and beta2 < 3. Option C describes a curve more peaked than normal, option D describes the normal curve itself, and option B is about the direction of the tail.

questions.question: The normal distribution is described as mesokurtic, and its value of beta2 is
questions.explanation: The normal curve is the benchmark for kurtosis, with beta2 = m4/m2^2 = 3. Option A is the normal curve's excess kurtosis (beta2 - 3), not beta2, and option C is the normal value of the percentile coefficient of kurtosis, a different measure.

questions.question: Excess kurtosis is defined as

options.a: m4/m2, which equals 3 for a normal distribution
options.b: beta1 - 3, which equals 0 for a normal distribution
options.c: beta2 - 3, which equals 0 for a normal distribution
options.d: beta2 + 3, which equals 6 for a normal distribution

questions.explanation: Excess kurtosis measures kurtosis relative to the normal curve by subtracting the benchmark 3 from beta2, so a normal curve has excess 0. Option B uses beta1, which measures skewness, and option A omits the square on m2.

questions.question: For any distribution, the second central moment m2 is equal to the
questions.explanation: The second central moment is the mean of the squared deviations from the mean, which is the definition of the (population) variance. Option B is the square root of m2, and option D is beta2 = m4/m2^2.

questions.question: The first central moment (the mean of the deviations from the arithmetic mean) of any distribution is always
questions.explanation: Deviations from the arithmetic mean always add up to zero, so their average, the first central moment, is zero. Option C is the second central moment, and option B is the beta2 value of the normal curve.

questions.question: For a symmetric distribution, the third central moment m3 and beta1 are
questions.explanation: In a symmetric distribution the cubed positive and negative deviations cancel, so m3 = 0 and therefore beta1 = m3^2/m2^3 = 0. Option B confuses this with the beta2 value of the normal curve, and option C is impossible for beta1, which is a square and cannot be negative.

questions.question: The main difference between skewness and kurtosis is that

options.a: skewness concerns peakedness, while kurtosis concerns symmetry
options.b: skewness measures spread, while kurtosis measures the average
options.c: skewness concerns the symmetry of a distribution, while kurtosis concerns its peakedness
options.d: both measure the same feature in different units

questions.explanation: Skewness tells us whether, and in which direction, a distribution leans away from symmetry, while kurtosis tells us how peaked or flat it is compared with the normal curve. Option A reverses the two ideas, and option B describes dispersion and central tendency.

questions.question: In a moderately skewed distribution, the median usually lies

options.b: between the mean and the mode
options.c: above both the mean and the mode
options.d: below both the mean and the mode

questions.explanation: For moderate skewness the empirical relation Mode = 3 Median - 2 Mean places the median between the other two averages, about one-third of the way from the mean to the mode. Options D and C contradict both the positive and negative skewness orderings.

questions.question: A box contains 10 red, 5 white and 11 blue balls. Three balls are drawn at random without replacement. Find the probability that all 3 balls are red.
questions.explanation: There are 26 balls in total, so the number of ways to pick 3 is 26C3 = 2600. All red means 10C3 = 120 ways, giving 120/2600 = 0.0462. Options A, B and D are close but do not equal 120/2600.

questions.question: A box contains 10 red, 5 white and 11 blue balls. Three balls are drawn at random without replacement. Find the probability that all 3 balls are white.
questions.explanation: There are 5 white balls, so the number of ways to pick 3 white ones is 5C3 = 10, out of 26C3 = 2600 possible selections. The probability is 10/2600 = 0.0038. Option A (0.0009) and B (0.0023) are too small and option D (0.0055) too large.

questions.question: A box contains 10 red, 5 white and 11 blue balls. Three balls are drawn at random without replacement. Find the probability that 2 balls are red and 1 ball is white.
questions.explanation: Choose 2 of the 10 red balls and 1 of the 5 white balls: 10C2 x 5C1 = 45 x 5 = 225 ways, out of 26C3 = 2600. The probability is 225/2600 = 0.0865. Options A, B and D are nearby values but do not match 225/2600.

questions.question: A process of obtaining observations whose outcomes depend on chance is called a ____ experiment.
questions.explanation: A random experiment is one whose outcome cannot be predicted with certainty in advance, such as tossing a coin or rolling a die. A deterministic experiment (A) always gives the same, predictable outcome, which is the opposite of chance.

questions.question: The probability that a second event occurs given that a first event has already occurred is called ____ probability.
questions.explanation: Conditional probability, P(B|A) = P(A and B)/P(A), is the probability of B given that A has already happened. Joint probability (C) is the probability that both events happen together, and marginal probability (A) is the probability of a single event on its own.

questions.question: The joint probability of two independent events J and K is equal to
questions.explanation: For independent events the multiplication rule gives P(J and K) = P(J) x P(K). Option B, P(J) + P(K), is the addition rule for mutually exclusive events and gives P(J or K), not the joint probability.

questions.question: The set of all possible outcomes of an experiment is called the
questions.explanation: The sample space lists every possible outcome; for one toss of a coin it is {H, T}. An event (C) is only a subset of the sample space, and a sample (A) is a part of a population in data collection.

questions.question: From a pack of 52 playing cards, one card is drawn at random. What is the probability that it is a jack of spades or queen of hearts?
questions.explanation: There is only one jack of spades and one queen of hearts in the pack, and they cannot both be drawn at once, so the events are mutually exclusive: P = 1/52 + 1/52 = 2/52 = 1/26. Option B is the probability of just one of the two cards. Option D, 1/2704, wrongly multiplies the probabilities, which would be for drawing both cards, not either.

questions.question: 25 lottery tickets are marked with the numbers 1 to 25. A ticket is drawn at random. Find the probability that its number is a multiple of 5 or 7.
questions.explanation: Among 1 to 25 the multiples of 5 are 5, 10, 15, 20, 25 (5 tickets) and the multiples of 7 are 7, 14, 21 (3 tickets). No number up to 25 is a multiple of both (the first is 35), so P = (5 + 3)/25 = 8/25. Option C, 1/25, counts only one ticket, and option A has no link to the counts at all.

questions.question: A fair die is rolled once. Find the probability of getting a number that is either a multiple of 3 or a prime number.
questions.explanation: Multiples of 3 on a die are 3 and 6, and the primes are 2, 3 and 5. The union is {2, 3, 5, 6}, so P = 4/6 = 2/3 (3 is counted once only). Option A, 2/6, gives only the multiples of 3, and option D ignores most of the favourable outcomes.

questions.question: There are 40 pages in a book. A page is opened at random. Find the probability that the number of this opened page is a multiple of 3 or 5.
questions.explanation: Pages 1 to 40 contain 13 multiples of 3 and 8 multiples of 5, but pages 15 and 30 are multiples of both and must not be counted twice. So P = (13 + 8 - 2)/40 = 19/40. Option C, 9/40, and the other small fractions miss most of the favourable pages.

questions.question: A card is drawn from a pack of 52 playing cards. Find the probability that the card drawn is an ace or a red card.
questions.explanation: There are 26 red cards and 4 aces, but 2 aces (hearts and diamonds) are red, so P(ace or red) = 26/52 + 4/52 - 2/52 = 28/52 = 7/13. Option C, 2/13, is double the chance of an ace alone (1/13) and ignores the red cards, and option D also leaves out most of the red cards.

questions.question: A red die and a green die are rolled. What is the probability that the sum rolled is 6, given that the sum is less than 7?
questions.explanation: Sums less than 7 (2, 3, 4, 5, 6) occur in 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 15 of the 36 outcomes, and a sum of 6 occurs in 5 of them, so P(sum = 6 | sum < 7) = 5/15 = 1/3. Option B, 2/3, is the chance that the sum is NOT 6 given it is below 7 (10/15), and 5/36 would be the unconditional probability, which ignores the given condition.

questions.question: A box contains 3 black balls, 2 red balls, and 5 white balls. One ball is drawn, it is not replaced, and a second ball is drawn. Find the probability that the first ball is red and the second is black.
questions.explanation: P(first red) = 2/10, and after removing a red ball P(second black) = 3/9. So P = 2/10 x 3/9 = 6/90 = 1/15. Option A, 1/5, is just the chance of the first red ball, and option D adds outcomes that do not apply.

questions.question: A bag contains 3 red marbles, 4 white marbles, and 3 black marbles. Find the probability of getting a red marble on the first drawn, black marble on the second draw, and a white marble on the third draw if the marbles are drawn without replacement.
questions.explanation: Without replacement the counts and total fall after each draw: P = 3/10 x 3/9 x 4/8 = 36/720 = 1/20. Option D, 3/10, is only the chance of the first red marble, and option B is far too large for three specific draws in a row.

questions.question: A die is rolled. If the outcome is a number greater than 3, what is the probability that it is a prime number?
questions.explanation: Given the outcome is greater than 3, the reduced sample space is {4, 5, 6}, and only 5 is prime, so P = 1/3. Option B, 1/2, is the chance of a prime on an ordinary roll (2, 3, 5 out of 6), which ignores the condition.

questions.question: Two dice are thrown together. Find the probability that the sum of the numbers shown is either 6 or 8.
questions.explanation: A sum of 6 occurs in 5 ways and a sum of 8 in 5 ways out of 36, and the two events cannot happen together. So P = 10/36 = 5/18. Option C, 7/18, overcounts the outcomes, and the other fractions are not out of 36.

questions.question: An urn contains 4 red and 7 blue balls. Two balls are drawn one by one without replacement. Find the probability of getting two red balls
questions.explanation: P(two red) = 4/11 x 3/10 = 12/110 = 6/55, since one red ball has gone before the second draw. Option D, 4/11, is only the chance that the first ball is red, and option C, 3/10, is only the chance of red on the second draw once a red ball has been removed; both stages must be multiplied together.

questions.question: Two cards are drawn from a pack of cards in succession with replacement of first card. Find the probability that both are the cards of heart.
questions.explanation: With replacement the draws are independent, so P(both hearts) = 13/52 x 13/52 = 1/4 x 1/4 = 1/16. Option A, 13/52, is the probability for only one draw.

questions.question: If two events A and B are mutually exclusive, what is the probability of both events occurring simultaneously, P(A n B)?
questions.explanation: Mutually exclusive events cannot occur together, so P(A n B) = 0. Option A, P(A) x P(B), is the rule for independent events, and option C is P(A or B) for mutually exclusive events.

questions.question: The probability of an impossible event is:
questions.explanation: An impossible event can never occur, so its probability is 0. Option B (1) is the probability of a certain event, and option D is not possible because probabilities always lie between 0 and 1.

questions.question: If P(A) = 0.4, P(B) = 0.5 and A and B are mutually exclusive, then P(A u B) is:
questions.explanation: Mutually exclusive events cannot happen together, so P(A n B) = 0 and P(A u B) = P(A) + P(B) = 0.4 + 0.5 = 0.9. Option A (0.2) multiplies the probabilities, which would be P(A n B) for independent events, not the union.

questions.question: Two events A and B are independent if:

options.b: P(A n B) = P(A) x P(B)

questions.explanation: Independence means the occurrence of one event does not change the probability of the other, which gives the multiplication rule P(A n B) = P(A) x P(B). Option A is the condition for mutually exclusive events, which is a different idea. Option C is wrong because independence gives P(A|B) = P(A), not P(B).

questions.question: In a class of 60 students, 35 study Accounting (A), 28 study Finance (F), and 12 study both. A student is selected at random. The probability that the student studies Accounting or Finance, P(A u F), is:
questions.explanation: By the additive rule, P(A u F) = P(A) + P(F) - P(A n F) = 35/60 + 28/60 - 12/60 = 51/60 = 17/20 (0.85). Option C forgets to subtract the 12 students counted twice and gives a probability above 1, while option B is the probability of studying neither.

questions.question: In a class of 60 students, 35 study Accounting (A), 28 study Finance (F), and 12 study both. A student is selected at random. The probability that the student studies neither subject, P(A' n F'), is:
questions.explanation: First P(A u F) = (35 + 28 - 12)/60 = 51/60, so P(neither) = 1 - 51/60 = 9/60 = 3/20 (0.15), meaning 9 students take neither. Option B is P(A u F) itself, and option C is P(A n F) = 12/60, the chance of studying both.

questions.question: In a class of 60 students, 35 study Accounting (A), 28 study Finance (F), and 12 study both. A student is selected at random. The probability that the student studies Accounting, given that the student studies Finance, P(A|F), is:
questions.explanation: P(A|F) = P(A n F) / P(F) = (12/60)/(28/60) = 12/28 = 3/7 (about 0.4286). Option B divides by the Accounting total instead, which is P(F|A), and option C is the joint probability P(A n F) without conditioning.

questions.question: In probability, any process that generates well-defined outcomes, such as tossing a coin or rolling a die, is called
questions.explanation: An experiment is any process that produces well-defined outcomes, like tossing a coin. Option C is the list of all possible outcomes of the experiment, while options D and B are a subset of results and a single result respectively, not the process itself.

questions.question: In probability, an event is best described as

options.a: The set of all possible outcomes of an experiment
options.b: A subset of the sample space (a collection of one or more outcomes)
options.c: A number between 0 and 1 attached to an outcome
options.d: The process that generates the outcomes

questions.explanation: An event is any collection of outcomes, i.e. a subset of the sample space, such as 'getting an even number' on a die. Option D describes an experiment and option A describes the whole sample space, while option C describes a probability rather than an event.

questions.question: An event consisting of exactly one outcome of the sample space is called a
questions.explanation: A simple event contains just one outcome, such as rolling a 4 on a die. A compound event (option A) is made up of two or more outcomes, and a joint event (option D) refers to two events occurring together.

questions.question: A fair die is rolled once. The event 'an even number shows' is an example of a
questions.explanation: The event 'an even number shows' is made up of three outcomes {2, 4, 6}, so it is a compound event. It is not a simple event (option C) because it has more than one outcome, and it is not the sample space (option D) because odd numbers are left out.

questions.question: A statistician reasons that because a fair coin has two equally likely faces, the probability of a head is 1/2, without tossing it at all. This is the
questions.explanation: The classical approach assigns probability by reasoning from equally likely outcomes: P(E) = number of favourable outcomes / total number of outcomes. The relative frequency or empirical approach (options B and C) would need the coin to be tossed many times, and the subjective approach (option D) relies on personal judgement.

questions.question: A Lagos microfinance bank finds that 45 of its last 500 loans defaulted and so estimates the probability of default as 0.09. This is the
questions.explanation: Estimating a probability from the proportion of times an event occurred in past trials (45/500) is the relative frequency, or empirical, approach. The classical approach (option C) needs equally likely outcomes known in advance, and the subjective approach (option A) is based on personal belief rather than recorded data.

questions.question: An entrepreneur in Ikeja says, based on her experience and judgement, that there is a 70% chance her new snack brand will succeed. This probability was assigned by the
questions.explanation: A probability based on a person's judgement, experience or belief is subjective. There are no equally likely outcomes here for the classical approach (option A), and no record of repeated trials for the relative frequency or empirical approach (options B and D).

questions.question: Under the classical approach, the probability of an event E is given by

options.a: Number of outcomes not favourable to E / number favourable to E
options.b: The degree of belief a person holds that E will occur
options.c: Number of times E occurred / number of trials carried out
options.d: Number of outcomes favourable to E / total number of equally likely outcomes

questions.explanation: The classical definition is P(E) = n(E)/n(S), which requires all outcomes to be equally likely. Option C is the relative frequency definition, option B is the subjective view, and option A is a ratio of unfavourable to favourable outcomes, which is not a probability.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an approach to assigning probabilities?
questions.explanation: Least squares is a method for fitting a regression line, not a way of assigning probabilities. The classical, relative frequency and subjective approaches (options A, C and B) are the three standard approaches to probability.

questions.question: Which of the following values can NOT be the probability of an event?
questions.explanation: Every probability must lie between 0 and 1 inclusive, so 1.2 is impossible. A probability of 0 (option C) describes an impossible event, 1 (option A) describes a certain event, and 0.5 (option D) is a perfectly valid value in between.

questions.question: For any experiment, the sum of the probabilities of all the outcomes in the sample space is

options.b: Equal to the number of outcomes

questions.explanation: One of the basic rules of probability is that the probabilities of all outcomes in the sample space add up to exactly 1, because one of them must occur. Option A describes a single probability, not the total, and option B confuses counting outcomes with adding their probabilities.

questions.question: Two events that cannot occur at the same time are said to be
questions.explanation: Mutually exclusive events cannot happen together, so P(A and B) = 0. Independent events (option C) can happen together; independence means one does not change the probability of the other. Collectively exhaustive events (option B) together cover the whole sample space.

questions.question: If the occurrence of event A does not affect the probability that event B occurs, A and B are said to be
questions.explanation: Independence means the occurrence of one event gives no information about the other, so P(B|A) = P(B) and P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B). Mutually exclusive events (option C) are the opposite case in a sense: if one occurs the other cannot, so they strongly affect each other.

questions.question: A set of events is said to be collectively exhaustive when

options.a: The occurrence of one event does not affect the others
options.b: Each event has the same probability of occurring
options.c: At least one of the events must occur when the experiment is performed
options.d: No two of the events can occur together

questions.explanation: Collectively exhaustive events together make up the entire sample space, so at least one of them must occur. Option D describes mutually exclusive events, option A describes independent events, and option B describes equally likely events.

questions.question: If A and B are mutually exclusive events with P(A) > 0 and P(B) > 0, then A and B are
questions.explanation: If A occurs, B cannot occur, so P(B|A) = 0, which is not equal to P(B); the events therefore depend on each other. They cannot be independent (option B) because P(A and B) = 0 while P(A) x P(B) > 0. They are complementary or exhaustive (options D and C) only if together they cover the whole sample space, which is not always so.

questions.question: Two events that are both mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive are called
questions.explanation: Complementary events, such as A and not-A, cannot occur together and between them cover the whole sample space, so P(A) + P(A') = 1. Independent events (option B) can occur together, and joint events (option A) refer to the intersection of two events.

questions.question: The probability that event A does NOT occur is given by
questions.explanation: Since A and its complement A' together cover the sample space and cannot occur together, P(A) + P(A') = 1, giving P(A') = 1 - P(A). Option B would give a negative value, and options C and A can give values greater than 1, which are not valid probabilities.

questions.question: The general addition rule of probability for any two events A and B states that

options.a: P(A or B) = P(A) x P(B)
options.c: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) + P(A and B)
options.d: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B)

questions.explanation: The general addition rule subtracts P(A and B) so that the overlap is not counted twice. Option B is the special rule that holds only for mutually exclusive events, option A is the multiplication rule for independent events (giving P(A and B)), and option C counts the overlap three times.

questions.question: The conditional probability of A given B, where P(B) > 0, is
questions.explanation: Conditioning on B shrinks the sample space to B, so we divide the joint probability by P(B). Option B gives P(B|A) instead, option C gives P(A and B) only when the events are independent, and option D is the inverted ratio, which can exceed 1.

questions.question: In a contingency table, the probability obtained by dividing a row total or a column total by the grand total is called a
questions.explanation: A marginal probability is the probability of a single event, found in the margins of the table (row or column totals) divided by the grand total. A joint probability (option A) uses a single cell, and a conditional probability (option C) divides a cell by a row or column total rather than the grand total.

questions.question: The probability that two events occur together, read from a single cell of a contingency table divided by the grand total, is a
questions.explanation: A joint probability, P(A and B), measures two events happening together; in a contingency table it is the cell count divided by the grand total. A marginal probability (option D) uses a row or column total, and a conditional probability (option C) divides the cell by a row or column total instead of the grand total.

questions.question: Bayes' theorem is used to

options.a: Assign probabilities from personal judgement alone
options.b: Revise prior probabilities in the light of new information to obtain posterior probabilities
options.c: Count the number of arrangements of objects when order matters
options.d: Add the probabilities of mutually exclusive events

questions.explanation: Bayes' theorem combines prior probabilities with the likelihood of new evidence to produce revised (posterior) probabilities. Option C describes permutations, option D is the special addition rule, and option A describes subjective probability.

questions.question: In Bayes' theorem, the revised probabilities obtained after new information has been taken into account are called
questions.explanation: Posterior probabilities are the updated probabilities after the new evidence has been used. Prior probabilities (option B) are the initial estimates before the new information, and marginal probabilities (option D) are single-event probabilities from table totals.

questions.question: Counting arrangements of objects in which the ORDER of selection matters is done using
questions.explanation: A permutation counts ordered arrangements, so choosing A then B is different from B then A. Combinations (option C) count selections in which order does not matter, and options B and A are probability rules, not counting methods.

questions.question: A class rep must choose 3 students out of 10 to form a welfare committee in which all members have equal status. The number of possible committees is found using

options.a: The multiplication rule for independent events

questions.explanation: Because the members have equal status, the order in which they are picked does not matter, so we count combinations (10C3). Permutations (option D) would be right only if positions such as chairman and secretary were assigned.

questions.question: When two balls are drawn one after the other from a bag WITH replacement, the outcomes of the two draws are

options.a: Collectively exhaustive, because one ball is drawn each time
options.b: Independent, because the bag is the same for the second draw
options.c: Mutually exclusive, because both cannot be red
options.d: Dependent, because the first ball changes the bag

questions.explanation: Replacing the first ball restores the bag to its original state, so the second draw has the same probabilities whatever happened first; the draws are independent. Option D describes drawing WITHOUT replacement, and option C is wrong because both balls can certainly be red.

questions.question: An event that is certain to occur has a probability of
questions.explanation: A certain (sure) event always occurs, so its probability is 1, the maximum value. A probability of 0 (option D) describes an impossible event, and 100 (option A) confuses a percentage of 100% with the probability scale of 0 to 1.

questions.question: A fair die is rolled once. What is the probability that the number shown is greater than 4?
questions.explanation: Only 5 and 6 are greater than 4, so P = 2/6 = 1/3. Option B (1/2) would include 4, option C (2/3) is the probability of 4 or less, and option D (1/6) counts only one of the two outcomes.

questions.question: Two fair dice are rolled together. What is the probability that the sum of the scores is 7?
questions.explanation: There are 36 equally likely outcomes and six give a sum of 7: (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1). So P = 6/36 = 1/6. Option B (7/36) wrongly uses the target sum as the count, and option A (5/36) is the probability of a sum of 6 (or of a sum of 8).

questions.question: Two fair dice are rolled together. What is the probability that the sum of the scores is 9?
questions.explanation: A sum of 9 comes from (3,6), (4,5), (5,4) and (6,3), which is 4 of the 36 equally likely outcomes, so P = 4/36 = 1/9. Option B (3/36) misses one ordering, and option A (1/6) is the probability of a sum of 7.

questions.question: A fair coin is tossed three times. How many outcomes are in the sample space?
questions.explanation: Each toss has 2 outcomes, so three tosses give 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 outcomes (HHH, HHT, ..., TTT). Option D (6) adds or doubles instead of multiplying, and option C counts tosses rather than outcomes.

questions.question: A fair coin is tossed three times. What is the probability of getting exactly two heads?
questions.explanation: Exactly two heads occur in HHT, HTH and THH, which is 3 of the 8 equally likely outcomes, so P = 3/8. Option B (1/4) counts only 2 of the arrangements, and option A (1/2) is the probability of at least two heads.

questions.question: A fair coin is tossed three times. What is the probability of getting at least one head?
questions.explanation: The complement of 'at least one head' is 'no heads' (TTT), with probability 1/8, so P = 1 - 1/8 = 7/8. Option C (1/8) is the probability of the complement itself, and option B (3/8) is the probability of exactly one head.

questions.question: A card is drawn at random from a well-shuffled standard pack of 52 playing cards. What is the probability that it is a king?
questions.explanation: There are 4 kings in 52 cards, so P = 4/52 = 1/13. Option B (1/52) is the probability of one particular king, such as the king of hearts, and option C (1/4) is the probability of a particular suit.

questions.question: A card is drawn at random from a standard pack of 52 playing cards. What is the probability that it is a heart or a king?
questions.explanation: Using the general addition rule, P(heart or king) = 13/52 + 4/52 - 1/52 = 16/52 = 4/13; the king of hearts is subtracted once because it was counted twice. Option C (17/52) forgets to subtract the overlap, and option D (1/52) is only the king of hearts.

questions.question: A card is drawn at random from a standard pack of 52 playing cards. Taking face cards to be jacks, queens and kings, what is the probability of drawing a face card?
questions.explanation: There are 3 face cards in each of 4 suits, giving 12 face cards, so P = 12/52 = 3/13. Option C (3/52) counts the face cards of only one suit, and option B (4/13) would wrongly add aces as a fourth face value.

questions.question: Two cards are drawn one after the other WITHOUT replacement from a standard pack of 52 cards. What is the probability that both are aces?
questions.explanation: Without replacement, P(both aces) = 4/52 x 3/51 = 12/2652 = 1/221, because one ace has gone before the second draw. Option C (1/169) is the answer WITH replacement, and option A (2/13) wrongly adds the probabilities instead of multiplying.

questions.question: A bag contains 5 red, 3 blue and 2 green balls. One ball is picked at random. What is the probability that it is blue?
questions.explanation: There are 10 balls in total and 3 are blue, so P(blue) = 3/10. Option B (3/7) wrongly divides by the number of non-blue balls, and option A (1/3) treats the three colours as equally likely.

questions.question: A bag contains 5 red, 3 blue and 2 green balls. Two balls are drawn one after the other WITH replacement. What is the probability that both are red?
questions.explanation: With replacement the draws are independent, so P(both red) = 5/10 x 5/10 = 1/4. Option D (2/9) is the answer WITHOUT replacement, and option B (1/2) is the probability that a single ball is red.

questions.question: A bag contains 5 red, 3 blue and 2 green balls. Two balls are drawn one after the other WITHOUT replacement. What is the probability that both are red?
questions.explanation: Without replacement, P(both red) = 5/10 x 4/9 = 20/90 = 2/9, since only 4 red balls remain out of 9 for the second draw. Option B (1/4) is the with-replacement answer, and option A (4/9) is only the second-draw conditional probability.

questions.question: A bag contains 5 red, 3 blue and 2 green balls. Two balls are drawn WITHOUT replacement. What is the probability of getting one red and one blue ball (in any order)?
questions.explanation: The ball pair can come as red then blue or blue then red: 5/10 x 3/9 + 3/10 x 5/9 = 30/90 = 1/3. Option B (1/6) counts only one order, and option A (3/20) also ignores the second order while treating the draws as with replacement.

questions.question: The probability that it will rain in Lagos tomorrow is 0.35. What is the probability that it will NOT rain tomorrow?
