questions.explanation: By the complement rule, P(no rain) = 1 - 0.35 = 0.65. Option B repeats the probability of rain, option D adds 1 instead of subtracting, giving an impossible value above 1.

questions.question: For two events A and B, P(A) = 0.4, P(B) = 0.5 and P(A and B) = 0.2. Find P(A or B).
questions.explanation: By the general addition rule, P(A or B) = 0.4 + 0.5 - 0.2 = 0.7, because the overlap is counted in both P(A) and P(B) and must be removed once. Option A (0.9) forgets to subtract the overlap, and option C (0.5) subtracts the overlap twice.

questions.question: A and B are mutually exclusive events with P(A) = 0.25 and P(B) = 0.4. Find P(A or B).
questions.explanation: For mutually exclusive events P(A and B) = 0, so P(A or B) = 0.25 + 0.4 = 0.65. Option D (0.1) multiplies the probabilities, which would be P(A and B) for independent events, and option B (0.55) wrongly subtracts that product.

questions.question: A and B are independent events with P(A) = 0.6 and P(B) = 0.3. Find P(A and B).
questions.explanation: For independent events, P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B) = 0.6 x 0.3 = 0.18. Option B (0.9) adds the probabilities, and option C (0.72) is P(A or B), not P(A and B).

questions.question: A and B are independent events with P(A) = 0.6 and P(B) = 0.3. Find P(A or B).
questions.explanation: Using the addition rule with P(A and B) = 0.6 x 0.3 = 0.18, P(A or B) = 0.6 + 0.3 - 0.18 = 0.72. Option C (0.9) ignores the overlap, and option D (0.18) is P(A and B).

questions.question: For two events, P(A and B) = 0.12 and P(B) = 0.4. Find P(A|B).
questions.explanation: P(A|B) = P(A and B)/P(B) = 0.12/0.4 = 0.3. Option C (0.048) multiplies instead of dividing, and options B and D add or subtract the two values, which has no meaning here.

questions.question: For two events, P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4 and P(A|B) = 0.5. Which statement is correct?

options.a: A and B are mutually exclusive, because P(A|B) = P(A)
options.b: A and B are independent, because P(A|B) = P(A)
options.c: A and B are collectively exhaustive, because P(A) + P(A|B) = 1
options.d: A and B are dependent, because P(A|B) is not equal to P(B)

questions.explanation: Events are independent when knowing B occurred does not change the probability of A, i.e. P(A|B) = P(A); here both equal 0.5. They are not mutually exclusive (option A), since that would need P(A|B) = 0, and option D compares P(A|B) with the wrong probability.

questions.question: Given P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.6 and P(A or B) = 0.8, find P(A and B).
questions.explanation: Rearranging the addition rule, P(A and B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A or B) = 0.5 + 0.6 - 0.8 = 0.3. Option A (1.1) is just P(A) + P(B), and option C (0.1) subtracts the wrong pair of values.

questions.question: A and B are mutually exclusive, P(A) = 0.45 and P(A or B) = 0.7. Find P(B).
questions.explanation: For mutually exclusive events P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B), so P(B) = 0.7 - 0.45 = 0.25. Option A (0.315) multiplies the given values, and option D (1.15) adds them, which is not a valid probability.

questions.question: For two events, P(A) = 0.3, P(B) = 0.45 and P(A and B) = 0.15. What is the probability that NEITHER A nor B occurs?
questions.explanation: First P(A or B) = 0.3 + 0.45 - 0.15 = 0.6, and 'neither' is its complement, so P = 1 - 0.6 = 0.4. Option C (0.6) is P(A or B) itself, and option B (0.25) is 1 - 0.3 - 0.45, which forgets to add back the overlap.

questions.question: A survey of 200 UNILAG students gave the following: Business students: 48 live in a hall of residence, 72 do not; Science students: 42 live in a hall, 38 do not. If one student is chosen at random, what is the probability that the student is a Business student?
questions.explanation: There are 48 + 72 = 120 Business students out of 200, so the marginal probability is 120/200 = 3/5. Option B (6/25) is the joint probability of Business AND resident, and option A (9/20) is the marginal probability of living in a hall.

questions.question: A survey of 200 UNILAG students gave the following: Business students: 48 live in a hall of residence, 72 do not; Science students: 42 live in a hall, 38 do not. What is the probability that a randomly chosen student is a Business student who lives in a hall?
questions.explanation: This is a joint probability: the cell count divided by the grand total, 48/200 = 6/25. Option C (2/5) divides by the Business total and so gives a conditional probability, and option D (8/15) divides by the hall total.

questions.question: A survey of 200 UNILAG students gave the following: Business students: 48 live in a hall of residence, 72 do not; Science students: 42 live in a hall, 38 do not. Given that a randomly chosen student is a Business student, what is the probability that the student lives in a hall?
questions.explanation: Conditioning on Business restricts us to the 120 Business students, of whom 48 live in a hall, so P = 48/120 = 2/5. Option B (8/15) is the reverse conditional P(Business | hall), and option A (6/25) is the joint probability.

questions.question: A survey of 200 UNILAG students gave the following: Business students: 48 live in a hall of residence, 72 do not; Science students: 42 live in a hall, 38 do not. Given that a randomly chosen student lives in a hall, what is the probability that the student is a Business student?
questions.explanation: There are 48 + 42 = 90 hall residents, and 48 of them are Business students, so P = 48/90 = 8/15. Option D (2/5) is the reverse conditional P(hall | Business), and option C (3/5) ignores the condition entirely.

questions.question: A survey of 200 UNILAG students gave the following: Business students: 48 live in a hall of residence, 72 do not; Science students: 42 live in a hall, 38 do not. What is the probability that a randomly chosen student is a Business student OR lives in a hall?
questions.explanation: Using the addition rule, P = 120/200 + 90/200 - 48/200 = 162/200 = 81/100. Option A (21/20) forgets to subtract the 48 students counted twice and exceeds 1, and option B (6/25) is only the overlap.

questions.question: A survey of 200 UNILAG students gave the following: Business students: 48 live in a hall of residence, 72 do not; Science students: 42 live in a hall, 38 do not. Are the events 'Business student' and 'lives in a hall' independent?

options.a: No, because P(Business and hall) = 0.24 is not equal to P(Business) x P(hall) = 0.27
options.b: No, because the two events are mutually exclusive
options.c: Yes, because every student is either a Business or a Science student
options.d: Yes, because P(Business and hall) = 0.24 is equal to P(Business) x P(hall)

questions.explanation: For independence we need P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B). Here P(Business and hall) = 48/200 = 0.24, while 0.6 x 0.45 = 0.27, so they are not independent. Option D gets the check wrong, option B is false because 48 students are in both groups, and option C describes exhaustive categories, which says nothing about independence.

questions.question: A Lagos factory has two machines. Machine A makes 60% of the output and machine B makes 40%. 2% of A's items and 5% of B's items are defective. What is the probability that a randomly chosen item is defective?
questions.explanation: By the total probability rule, P(defective) = 0.6 x 0.02 + 0.4 x 0.05 = 0.012 + 0.020 = 0.032. Option B (0.07) simply adds the two defect rates, and option A (0.035) averages them without weighting by each machine's share of output.

questions.question: A Lagos factory has two machines. Machine A makes 60% of the output and machine B makes 40%. 2% of A's items and 5% of B's items are defective. An item is found to be defective. Using Bayes' theorem, what is the probability that it came from machine A?
questions.explanation: Bayes' theorem gives P(A | defective) = (0.6 x 0.02)/(0.6 x 0.02 + 0.4 x 0.05) = 0.012/0.032 = 0.375. Option B (0.625) is the posterior probability for machine B, option A (0.6) is the prior for A before the defect was observed, and option C (0.012) is the joint probability, not yet divided by P(defective).

questions.question: 1% of a population has a certain disease. A screening test is positive for 90% of people who have the disease and for 5% of people who do not. A person tests positive. What is the probability that the person has the disease? (4 d.p.)
questions.explanation: By Bayes' theorem, P(disease | positive) = (0.01 x 0.9)/(0.01 x 0.9 + 0.99 x 0.05) = 0.009/0.0585 = 0.1538. Option D (0.9) confuses P(positive | disease) with P(disease | positive), option B (0.0585) is the overall probability of a positive test, and option A (0.009) is the joint probability before dividing.

questions.question: A student has probability 0.8 of passing a first test. If she passes it, the probability she passes a second test is 0.7; if she fails it, the probability she passes the second is 0.4. Using a tree diagram, what is the probability that she passes the second test?
questions.explanation: Adding the two branches that end in a pass: 0.8 x 0.7 + 0.2 x 0.4 = 0.56 + 0.08 = 0.64. Option A (0.56) uses only the 'pass first' branch, option C (1.1) adds the two conditional probabilities, and option D (0.55) is their simple average.

questions.question: A student has probability 0.8 of passing a first test and, if she passes it, probability 0.7 of passing a second test. What is the probability that she passes BOTH tests?
questions.explanation: By the multiplication rule, P(first and second) = P(first) x P(second | first) = 0.8 x 0.7 = 0.56. Option D adds the probabilities, option B is only the conditional probability, and option A (0.14) is 0.2 x 0.7, which uses the probability of failing the first test.

questions.question: In how many ways can a chairman and a secretary be chosen from 8 members of a cooperative society?
questions.explanation: The two posts are different, so order matters and we use permutations: 8P2 = 8 x 7 = 56. Option B (28) is 8C2, which ignores who gets which post, and option A (64) allows the same person to hold both posts.

questions.question: In how many ways can a committee of 3 be chosen from 7 people?
questions.explanation: Committee members have no order, so we use combinations: 7C3 = 7!/(3! x 4!) = 35. Option D (210) is 7P3, which counts ordered selections, and option A (343) is 7^3, which allows repeats.

questions.question: In how many different ways can 5 different textbooks be arranged in a row on a shelf?
questions.explanation: Arranging 5 distinct items in a row gives 5! = 5 x 4 x 3 x 2 x 1 = 120 arrangements. Option C (25) is 5^2, and option B (60) is 5P3, which arranges only 3 of the books.

questions.question: Two people are chosen at random from a group of 4 men and 3 women. What is the probability that both are women?
questions.explanation: The number of ways to choose 2 women is 3C2 = 3, and the number of ways to choose any 2 people is 7C2 = 21, so P = 3/21 = 1/7. Option C (9/49) treats the selection as with replacement, and option A (3/7) is the probability for just one person.

questions.question: Of 400 customers at a Yaba supermarket last month, 92 paid by bank transfer. Using the relative frequency approach, estimate the probability that the next customer pays by bank transfer.
questions.explanation: The relative frequency estimate is the number of times the event occurred divided by the number of trials: 92/400 = 0.23. Option B (0.2987) divides by the customers who did not use transfer, option D (0.77) is the probability of not paying by transfer, and option C wrongly assumes two equally likely outcomes.

questions.question: A fair die is rolled twice. What is the probability of getting a six on both rolls?
questions.explanation: The rolls are independent, so P(six and six) = 1/6 x 1/6 = 1/36. Option D (1/6) is for one roll only, and option C (1/3) adds the two probabilities instead of multiplying.

questions.question: A fair coin is tossed and a fair die is rolled. What is the probability of getting a head and an even number?
questions.explanation: The coin and die are independent, so P(head and even) = 1/2 x 3/6 = 1/4; equivalently 3 of the 12 outcomes. Option B (1/12) counts only one even number, and option D (3/4) is P(head or even).

questions.question: The expected value, E(X), of a discrete random variable is calculated by summing the products of each possible value and its corresponding probability. This value is also known as the:
questions.explanation: E(X) = sum x P(x) is the mean of the probability distribution, so it is the population mean mu of X. Option A and option D are measures of spread and relative spread, and option B is the standard deviation of a sampling distribution.

questions.question: In statistics, a random variable is

options.a: A variable whose value is chosen by the researcher
options.b: A numerical description of the outcome of an experiment
options.c: The set of all possible outcomes of an experiment
options.d: A probability attached to a particular event

questions.explanation: A random variable assigns a number to each outcome of an experiment, for example the number of heads in three tosses. Option C describes the sample space, option D describes a probability, and option A is wrong because the value of a random variable is determined by chance, not chosen.

questions.question: A random variable that can take only a finite or countable number of distinct values is called a
questions.explanation: A discrete random variable takes separate, countable values such as 0, 1, 2, 3. A continuous random variable (option C) can take any value in an interval, and a qualitative variable (option D) records categories rather than numbers.

questions.question: A random variable that can take any value within an interval, such as any value between 2 and 5, is called a
questions.explanation: A continuous random variable can assume any value in a range, so its values are measured rather than counted. A discrete random variable (option B) takes only separate, countable values.

questions.question: The number of customers who arrive at a bank branch in Lekki in one hour is an example of a
questions.explanation: The number of customers is counted (0, 1, 2, ...), so it is a discrete random variable. It is not continuous (option B) because it cannot take values like 3.7 customers, and it is not a constant (option D) because it varies from hour to hour by chance.

questions.question: The time taken to serve a customer at a fast-food outlet in Surulere is an example of a
questions.explanation: Time is measured and can take any value within an interval, such as 3.25 minutes, so it is a continuous random variable. A discrete random variable (option B) would only take countable values, and a qualitative variable (option C) is non-numerical.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a discrete random variable?

options.a: The number of defective bulbs in a carton
options.b: The number of goals scored in a football match
options.c: The weight of a bag of rice sold in Mile 12 market
options.d: The number of children in a household

questions.explanation: Weight is measured on a continuous scale and can take any value in a range, so it is a continuous random variable. Options A, B and D are all counts that take whole-number values, which makes them discrete.

questions.question: For a table to be a valid discrete probability distribution, it is necessary that

options.a: Each P(x) is greater than 1 and the values add up to the number of outcomes
options.b: Each P(x) lies between 0 and 1 inclusive and all the P(x) values add up to 1
options.c: The values of x add up to 1
options.d: The P(x) values are all equal

questions.explanation: The two conditions are 0 <= P(x) <= 1 for every x and sum P(x) = 1. Option C wrongly applies the condition to the x values instead of the probabilities, and option D describes only a uniform distribution, which is a special case.

questions.question: The expected value (mean) of a discrete random variable X is given by
questions.explanation: The expected value weights each value of X by its probability: E(X) = sum x P(x). Option D is the simple mean of the x values, which ignores the probabilities, option B always equals 1, and option A is E(X^2).

questions.question: The variance of a discrete random variable X can be computed as
questions.explanation: The variance is the mean of the squares minus the square of the mean: Var(X) = E(X^2) - [E(X)]^2. Option C reverses the order and would give a negative value, and option D forgets to square E(X).

questions.question: If a and b are constants and X is a random variable, then E(aX + b) equals
questions.explanation: Expectation is linear, so multiplying X by a multiplies the mean by a, and adding b shifts the mean by b: E(aX + b) = aE(X) + b. Option C forgets the constant b, and option A uses a^2, which belongs to the variance rule.

questions.question: If a and b are constants and X is a random variable, then Var(aX + b) equals
questions.explanation: Adding a constant b shifts every value equally and does not change the spread, while multiplying by a multiplies the variance by a^2. So Var(aX + b) = a^2 Var(X). Options A and B wrongly add b, and option D forgets to square a.

questions.question: If a constant of 500 is added to every value of a random variable X, the variance of the new variable is
questions.explanation: Adding a constant moves the whole distribution along without changing how spread out it is, so Var(X + 500) = Var(X). Option A confuses this with the mean, which does increase by 500, and option D squares the constant as if it were a multiplier.

questions.question: The expected value of a random variable is best interpreted as

options.a: The long-run average value of X over many repetitions of the experiment
options.b: The value of X that is most likely to occur
options.c: The value that X must take on the next trial
options.d: The middle value of X when the values are ordered

questions.explanation: E(X) is the average value we would get if the experiment were repeated a very large number of times. The most likely value (option B) is the mode, the middle value (option D) is the median, and E(X) need not be a value X can actually take, so option C is wrong.

questions.question: For a discrete random variable X, the cumulative distribution function F(x) is defined as
questions.explanation: The cumulative distribution function gives the probability that X takes a value less than or equal to x, F(x) = P(X <= x). Option D is the probability function itself, and option B is 1 - F(x).

questions.question: Which of the following can NOT be the variance of a random variable?
questions.explanation: A variance is an average of squared deviations, so it can never be negative. Zero (option B) occurs when X is a constant, and positive values such as 0.25 and 16 are perfectly possible.

questions.question: A discrete random variable X has the distribution: x = 0, 1, 2, 3 with P(x) = 0.1, 0.3, 0.4, 0.2 respectively. Find E(X).
questions.explanation: E(X) = sum x P(x) = 0(0.1) + 1(0.3) + 2(0.4) + 3(0.2) = 0 + 0.3 + 0.8 + 0.6 = 1.7. Option A (1.5) is the simple average of 0, 1, 2 and 3, which ignores the probabilities, and option C (3.7) is E(X^2).

questions.question: A discrete random variable X has the distribution: x = 0, 1, 2, 3 with P(x) = 0.1, 0.3, 0.4, 0.2 respectively. Find E(X^2).
questions.explanation: E(X^2) = sum x^2 P(x) = 0(0.1) + 1(0.3) + 4(0.4) + 9(0.2) = 0.3 + 1.6 + 1.8 = 3.7. Option C (2.89) is [E(X)]^2, which is a different quantity, and option A (14) just adds the squared values without probabilities.

questions.question: A discrete random variable X has the distribution: x = 0, 1, 2, 3 with P(x) = 0.1, 0.3, 0.4, 0.2 respectively. Find Var(X).
questions.explanation: Var(X) = E(X^2) - [E(X)]^2 = 3.7 - 1.7^2 = 3.7 - 2.89 = 0.81. Option A (0.9) is the standard deviation, option D (3.7) is E(X^2) without subtracting the squared mean, and option C (2) subtracts E(X) instead of its square.

questions.question: A discrete random variable X has the distribution: x = 0, 1, 2, 3 with P(x) = 0.1, 0.3, 0.4, 0.2 respectively. Find the standard deviation of X.
questions.explanation: Var(X) = 3.7 - 1.7^2 = 0.81, so SD = sqrt(0.81) = 0.9. Option B (0.81) is the variance itself, and option C (1.9235) is the square root of E(X^2) rather than of the variance.

questions.question: A discrete random variable X has the distribution: x = 0, 1, 2, 3 with P(x) = 0.1, 0.3, 0.4, 0.2 respectively. Find P(X >= 2).
questions.explanation: P(X >= 2) = P(X = 2) + P(X = 3) = 0.4 + 0.2 = 0.6. Option C (0.4) includes only X = 2, option D (0.2) includes only X = 3, and option A (0.9) is P(X >= 1).

questions.question: A discrete random variable X has the distribution: x = 0, 1, 2, 3 with P(x) = 0.1, 0.3, 0.4, 0.2 respectively. Find the cumulative probability F(1).
questions.explanation: F(1) = P(X <= 1) = P(0) + P(1) = 0.1 + 0.3 = 0.4. Option A (0.3) is P(X = 1) alone, and option C (0.6) is P(X > 1).

questions.question: A discrete random variable X has the distribution: x = 0, 1, 2, 3 with P(x) = 0.1, 0.3, 0.4, 0.2 respectively. Find E(2X + 3).
questions.explanation: E(2X + 3) = 2E(X) + 3 = 2(1.7) + 3 = 6.4. Option B (3.4) forgets to add 3, option A (4.7) forgets to multiply by 2, and option C (9.4) multiplies the constant 3 by 2 as well.

questions.question: A discrete random variable X has the distribution: x = 0, 1, 2, 3 with P(x) = 0.1, 0.3, 0.4, 0.2 respectively. Given Var(X) = 0.81, find Var(2X + 3).
questions.explanation: Var(2X + 3) = 2^2 Var(X) = 4 x 0.81 = 3.24; the constant 3 does not affect the spread. Option B (1.62) multiplies by 2 instead of 4, and options D and C wrongly add the constant 3.

questions.question: The probability distribution of X is: x = 1, 2, 3, 4 with P(x) = 0.15, 0.25, p, 0.3 respectively. Find the value of p.
questions.explanation: The probabilities must add up to 1, so p = 1 - (0.15 + 0.25 + 0.3) = 1 - 0.7 = 0.3. Option C (0.7) is the sum of the known probabilities, not what remains, and option A (0.35) uses the wrong total.

questions.question: A discrete random variable X has P(X = x) = kx for x = 1, 2, 3, 4. Find the value of k.
questions.explanation: The probabilities must sum to 1: k(1 + 2 + 3 + 4) = 10k = 1, so k = 1/10. Option A (1/4) treats all four values as equally likely, option D (1/24) uses the product 1 x 2 x 3 x 4 instead of the sum, and option B (1/16) uses 4^2.

questions.question: A discrete random variable X has P(X = x) = x/10 for x = 1, 2, 3, 4. Find E(X).
questions.explanation: E(X) = sum x P(x) = (1x1 + 2x2 + 3x3 + 4x4)/10 = 30/10 = 3. Option D (2.5) is the simple average of 1, 2, 3 and 4, and option B (1) is the sum of the probabilities.

questions.question: A discrete random variable X has P(X = x) = x/10 for x = 1, 2, 3, 4, so that E(X) = 3. Find Var(X).
questions.explanation: E(X^2) = (1 + 8 + 27 + 64)/10 = 10, so Var(X) = 10 - 3^2 = 1. Option A (10) is E(X^2), option D (9) is [E(X)]^2, and option C (7) subtracts E(X) instead of its square.

questions.question: Which of the following is a valid probability distribution for a discrete random variable X taking the values 1, 2 and 3?
questions.explanation: Only 0.2, 0.5, 0.3 has every value between 0 and 1 and a total of exactly 1. Option B adds up to 1.1, option D contains a negative probability even though it sums to 1, and option C adds up to only 0.6.

questions.question: A trader in Balogun market estimates that a consignment will make a profit of N50,000 with probability 0.6 or a loss of N20,000 with probability 0.4. Find the expected profit.
questions.explanation: Expected profit = 50,000(0.6) + (-20,000)(0.4) = 30,000 - 8,000 = N22,000. Option A (N30,000) leaves out the possible loss, option D (N38,000) treats the loss as a gain, and option B (N15,000) is a simple average that ignores the probabilities.

questions.question: Project A gives a profit of N50,000 with probability 0.6 or a loss of N20,000 with probability 0.4. Project B gives a profit of N40,000 with probability 0.5 or a loss of N30,000 with probability 0.5. Using expected value as the decision rule, which project should be chosen?

options.a: Either project, since both have the same expected profit
options.b: Project A, with expected profit N22,000 against N5,000 for B
options.c: Project A, with expected profit N30,000 against N20,000 for B
options.d: Project B, with expected profit N35,000 against N22,000 for A

questions.explanation: E(A) = 50,000(0.6) - 20,000(0.4) = N22,000 and E(B) = 40,000(0.5) - 30,000(0.5) = N5,000, so A has the higher expected profit. Option D adds the loss for B instead of subtracting it, and option C ignores the losses for both projects.

questions.question: An insurance company charges a premium of N10,000 for a one-year policy. It pays out N200,000 if a claim is made, and the probability of a claim is 0.02. Ignoring other costs, find the company's expected profit per policy.
questions.explanation: Expected payout = 200,000 x 0.02 = N4,000, so expected profit = 10,000 - 4,000 = N6,000. Option A (N4,000) is the expected payout rather than the profit, option D ignores claims altogether, and option B adds the expected payout to the premium.

questions.question: X is the score obtained when a fair die is rolled once. Find E(X).
questions.explanation: Each score 1 to 6 has probability 1/6, so E(X) = (1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6)/6 = 21/6 = 3.5. Option D (7) is the sum of the smallest and largest scores without dividing by 2, option C is the largest score, and option B (21) is the sum of the scores without the probabilities.

questions.question: X is the score obtained when a fair die is rolled once, so E(X) = 3.5. Find Var(X), correct to 4 decimal places.
questions.explanation: E(X^2) = (1 + 4 + 9 + 16 + 25 + 36)/6 = 91/6, so Var(X) = 91/6 - 3.5^2 = 35/12 = 2.9167. Option C (15.1667) is E(X^2), option B (12.25) is [E(X)]^2, and option D (1.7078) is the standard deviation.

questions.question: A fair coin is tossed twice and X is the number of heads obtained. Find E(X).
questions.explanation: The distribution is P(0) = 1/4, P(1) = 1/2, P(2) = 1/4, so E(X) = 0(1/4) + 1(1/2) + 2(1/4) = 1. Option B (0.5) is P(X = 1), and option D (2) is the maximum number of heads, not the average.

questions.question: A game at a UNILAG fun fair costs N100 to play. A fair die is rolled and the player receives N300 if a six shows, otherwise nothing. Find the player's expected gain per game.
questions.explanation: The expected receipt is 300 x 1/6 = N50, and the player pays N100, so expected gain = 50 - 100 = -N50, an average loss of N50 per game. Option C (N50) forgets the cost of playing, option D (N200) treats a win as certain, and option B (-N100) ignores the chance of winning.

questions.question: For a discrete random variable X, the cumulative distribution function has F(1) = 0.35 and F(2) = 0.75. Find P(X = 2).
questions.explanation: Since F(2) = P(X <= 2) and F(1) = P(X <= 1), P(X = 2) = F(2) - F(1) = 0.75 - 0.35 = 0.4. Option B (0.75) is F(2), which includes all values up to 2, option D adds the cumulative values, and option C (0.25) is 1 - F(2).

questions.question: X takes the values 0, 1, 2, 3 and its cumulative distribution function is F(0) = 0.2, F(1) = 0.5, F(2) = 0.9, F(3) = 1. Find P(1 < X <= 3).
questions.explanation: P(1 < X <= 3) = F(3) - F(1) = 1 - 0.5 = 0.5, which is P(2) + P(3) = 0.4 + 0.1. Option C (0.8) is F(3) - F(0), which wrongly includes X = 1, option D (0.1) is P(X = 3) only, and option B (0.4) is P(X = 2) only.

questions.question: A random variable X has Var(X) = 4. Find Var(5 - 3X).
questions.explanation: Var(a + bX) = b^2 Var(X), so Var(5 - 3X) = (-3)^2 x 4 = 9 x 4 = 36; the constant 5 does not change the spread. Option B (-12) forgets to square -3 and gives an impossible negative variance, option D (12) also fails to square, and option A (41) wrongly adds the constant 5.

questions.question: A random variable X has E(X) = 3. Find E(5 - 2X).
questions.explanation: E(5 - 2X) = 5 - 2E(X) = 5 - 2(3) = -1. Option B (2) forgets to multiply E(X) by 2, option D (11) adds 6 instead of subtracting it, and option A (-6) forgets the constant 5.

questions.question: Daily demand X for loaves of bread at a kiosk in Akoka is 10, 20 or 30 with probabilities 0.2, 0.5 and 0.3 respectively. Find the expected daily demand.
questions.explanation: E(X) = 10(0.2) + 20(0.5) + 30(0.3) = 2 + 10 + 9 = 21 loaves. Option C (20) is the simple average of 10, 20 and 30 or simply the most likely value, and option A (60) is the sum of the possible demands.

questions.question: Daily demand X for loaves of bread at a kiosk in Akoka is 10, 20 or 30 with probabilities 0.2, 0.5 and 0.3 respectively. Given E(X) = 21, find Var(X).
For a continuous random variable X, the probability that X takes any one exact value c, P(X = c), is

options.c: Equal to the height of the curve at c

questions.explanation: For a continuous random variable, probabilities are areas under the curve over intervals, and a single point has zero width, so P(X = c) = 0. Option C confuses the height of the density curve with a probability, and option B is true only for intervals, not single values.

questions.question: Which of the following is a continuous random variable?

options.a: The number of students in a tutorial class
options.b: The number of defective phones in a carton of 12
options.c: The time a student waits for a shuttle at the UNILAG main gate
options.d: The number of goals scored in a Faculty football match

questions.explanation: Waiting time is measured, not counted, and can take any value within an interval, so it is continuous. Options A, B and D are all counts that take only whole-number values, so they are discrete random variables.

questions.question: A discrete random variable has P(X = 0) = 0.2, P(X = 1) = 0.35, P(X = 2) = k and P(X = 3) = 0.15. For this to be a valid probability distribution, k must be
questions.explanation: The probabilities of a discrete distribution must add up to 1, so k = 1 - (0.2 + 0.35 + 0.15) = 1 - 0.7 = 0.3. Option A is the sum of the known probabilities, not the missing one. Options C and D would make the total 0.95 and 1.05.

questions.question: The probability that a salesperson will sell a magazine subscription to someone randomly selected and called on the telephone is 0.2. The salesperson calls 6 individuals this evening (binomial). What is the probability that there will be no subscriptions?
questions.explanation: With n = 6 and p = 0.2, the chance of no sale is P(X = 0) = q^6 = 0.8^6 = 0.262. Option A (0.531) is 0.9^6, which would use the wrong p, and option B (0.118) does not come from these figures.

questions.question: The probability that a salesperson will sell a magazine subscription to someone randomly selected and called on the telephone is 0.2. The salesperson calls 6 individuals this evening (binomial). What is the probability that exactly 3 subscriptions will be sold?
questions.explanation: P(X = 3) = 6C3 x 0.2^3 x 0.8^3 = 20 x 0.008 x 0.512 = 0.08192, which is about 0.082. Option B (0.185) and D (0.276) are far too large for three sales when only one in five calls succeeds. Option A (0.015) is close to P(X = 4), not P(X = 3).

questions.question: The probability that a salesperson will sell a magazine subscription to someone randomly selected and called on the telephone is 0.2. The salesperson calls 6 individuals this evening (binomial). What is the probability that at least 3 subscriptions will be sold?
questions.explanation: At least 3 means P(X = 3) + P(X = 4) + P(X = 5) + P(X = 6) = 0.08192 + 0.01536 + 0.00154 + 0.00006 = 0.09888, about 0.099. Option A (0.016) is roughly P(X = 4) alone, and option B (0.256) is far too large.

questions.question: The probability that a salesperson will sell a magazine subscription to someone randomly selected and called on the telephone is 0.2. The salesperson calls 6 individuals this evening (binomial). What is the probability that at most 3 subscriptions will be sold?
questions.explanation: At most 3 means P(X = 0) + P(X = 1) + P(X = 2) + P(X = 3) = 0.26214 + 0.39322 + 0.24576 + 0.08192 = 0.98304, about 0.983. A quicker check is 1 - P(X >= 4) = 1 - 0.01696 = 0.983. Option A (0.999) and B (0.930) do not match this total.

questions.question: The average number of claims per day made to an insurance company for damages or losses is 5.1, and the number of claims follows a Poisson distribution. What is the probability that fewer than 2 claims will be made on a given day?
questions.explanation: Fewer than 2 claims means P(X = 0) + P(X = 1) = e^-5.1 (1 + 5.1) = 0.00610 x 6.1 = 0.0372, about 0.037. Option D (0.016) is too small, and options A (0.189) and B (0.085) are too large for such a high average of 5.1 claims per day.

questions.question: The average number of claims per day made to an insurance company for damages or losses is 5.1, and the number of claims follows a Poisson distribution. What is the probability that exactly 2 claims will be made on a given day?
questions.explanation: P(X = 2) = e^-5.1 x 5.1^2 / 2! = 0.00610 x 26.01 / 2 = 0.0793, about 0.079. Option C is the only value matching this formula; options A (0.216) and B (0.139) are much higher than the chance of so few claims when the average is 5.1.

questions.question: The average number of claims per day made to an insurance company for damages or losses is 5.1, and the number of claims follows a Poisson distribution. What is the probability that 2 or more claims will be made on a given day?
questions.explanation: 2 or more claims is the complement of fewer than 2, so P(X >= 2) = 1 - [P(X = 0) + P(X = 1)] = 1 - 0.0372 = 0.963. Option D (0.984) and B (0.915) do not equal 1 minus 0.0372.

questions.question: The average number of claims per day made to an insurance company for damages or losses is 5.1, and the number of claims follows a Poisson distribution. What is the probability that more than 2 claims will be made on a given day?
questions.explanation: More than 2 means 3 or more, so P(X > 2) = 1 - [P(0) + P(1) + P(2)] = 1 - (0.0061 + 0.0311 + 0.0793) = 1 - 0.1165 = 0.884. Option D (0.942) and B (0.776) do not match, and remember that more than 2 excludes exactly 2 claims, unlike 2 or more.

questions.question: A courier service company has found that the delivery time of parcels to clients is normally distributed with mean 47 minutes and standard deviation 10 minutes. Given P(Z < 0.4) = 0.6554 and P(Z < -0.2) = 0.4207, what is the probability that a randomly selected parcel takes between 45 and 51 minutes to deliver?
questions.explanation: Standardise: z = (45 - 47)/10 = -0.2 and z = (51 - 47)/10 = 0.4. Then P(45 < X < 51) = P(Z < 0.4) - P(Z < -0.2) = 0.6554 - 0.4207 = 0.2347. Options A, B and D do not come from this subtraction.

questions.question: A courier service company has found that the delivery time of parcels to clients is normally distributed with mean 47 minutes and standard deviation 10 minutes. Given P(Z < 0.1) = 0.5398, what is the probability that a randomly selected parcel takes less than 48 minutes to deliver?
questions.explanation: Standardise: z = (48 - 47)/10 = 0.1, so P(X < 48) = P(Z < 0.1) = 0.5398. Option D (0.5000) would be the probability of less than the mean, 47 minutes, not 48. Options A and B are too large for a point only 1 minute above the mean.

questions.question: A courier service company has found that the delivery time of parcels to clients is normally distributed with mean 47 minutes and standard deviation 10 minutes. What is the probability that a randomly selected parcel takes more than 47 minutes to deliver?
questions.explanation: The normal distribution is symmetric about its mean, so exactly half the area lies above the mean. Since 47 minutes is the mean, z = (47 - 47)/10 = 0 and P(X > 47) = 0.5000. Options A, B and D would only fit values away from the mean.

questions.question: Which of the following are characteristics of the normal distribution?
questions.explanation: The normal distribution is symmetric about its mean, bell-shaped, and asymptotic, meaning its tails get closer to the horizontal axis without ever touching it. Options A, B and C are each true on their own, so D, all of the above, is the complete answer.

questions.question: Which probability distribution is most appropriate for modeling the number of successes in n independent trials, where each trial has the same probability of success?
questions.explanation: The binomial distribution counts the number of successes in n independent trials with the same probability of success p. Option B, Poisson, counts events in a fixed interval of time or space, while the normal and exponential distributions are for continuous variables.

questions.question: In a standard normal distribution, what are the values of the mean (mu) and the standard deviation (sigma)?
questions.explanation: The standard normal distribution has mean 0 and standard deviation 1, which is why Z = (X - mu)/sigma converts any normal variable into it. A standard deviation of 0 (options A and D) would mean no spread at all.

questions.question: In a Binomial distribution where n is the number of trials and p is the probability of success, what is the formula for the variance?
questions.explanation: For a binomial distribution the variance is npq = np(1 - p). Option D, np, is the mean, and option B, sqrt[np(1 - p)], is the standard deviation rather than the variance.

questions.question: Which of the following is a fundamental property of a Continuous Probability Distribution's probability density function (pdf), f(x)?

options.a: The total area under the curve is equal to 1
options.b: P(X = x) > 0 for every specific value x
options.c: The graph must be perfectly symmetrical
options.d: The function f(x) can take negative values

questions.explanation: A probability density function must never be negative and the total area under its curve equals 1. Option B is wrong because for a continuous variable P(X = x) = 0 at any single point, and option C is wrong because many pdfs (like the exponential) are skewed.

questions.question: Which of the following is a key characteristic that distinguishes a 'Continuous' probability distribution from a 'Discrete' one?

options.a: Probabilities are assigned to individual exact points, such as P(X = 5).
options.b: The random variable can take on any value within a specified interval.
options.c: The sum of all probabilities is greater than one.
options.d: The outcomes must always be positive integers.

questions.explanation: A continuous random variable can take any value within an interval, such as weight or time. Option A describes a discrete distribution, since for a continuous one P(X = 5) = 0, and option C is impossible because probabilities always total 1.

questions.question: The binomial distribution applies when:

options.a: There are more than two outcomes per trial
options.b: There is a fixed number of independent trials, each with exactly two outcomes
options.d: The data follow a normal distribution

questions.explanation: A binomial experiment has a fixed number n of independent trials, each ending in success or failure with the same probability p. Option A breaks the two-outcome requirement, and option C is not a condition at all, since binomial problems often use small n.

questions.question: For a binomial distribution with n = 10 and p = 0.3, the mean is:
questions.explanation: The binomial mean is np = 10 x 0.3 = 3. Option D (2.1) is the variance npq = 10 x 0.3 x 0.7, and option A (7) is nq, the expected number of failures.

questions.question: The Poisson distribution BEST models:

options.a: The result of a single coin toss
options.b: The number of events occurring in a fixed interval of time or space

questions.explanation: The Poisson distribution counts how many times a random event occurs in a fixed interval, such as calls per hour or defects per metre. Option C needs a continuous distribution such as the normal, and options A and D describe a single two-outcome (Bernoulli) trial.

questions.question: The normal distribution is characterised by:

options.b: A bell-shaped curve that is symmetric about its mean
options.d: A curve that is skewed to the right

questions.explanation: The normal curve is bell-shaped and perfectly symmetric about its mean, so its mean, median and mode coincide. Option C is wrong because the normal is a continuous distribution, and option D describes a positively skewed curve.

questions.question: Which statement about the normal distribution is TRUE?

options.a: About 68% of values lie within 1 standard deviation of the mean
options.b: About 99.7% of values lie within 1 standard deviation of the mean
options.d: The mean and mode always differ

questions.explanation: By the empirical rule, about 68% of values fall within 1 SD of the mean, about 95% within 2 SD and about 99.7% within 3 SD. Option B attaches the 3-SD figure to 1 SD, and options C and D contradict the symmetry of the normal curve, where mean = median = mode.

questions.question: A machine produces items of which 8% are defective. An inspector randomly selects 10 items, and the number of defectives follows a binomial distribution. The probability that exactly 2 items are defective is (to 4 d.p.):
questions.explanation: With n = 10, p = 0.08 and q = 0.92, P(X = 2) = C(10,2) x 0.08^2 x 0.92^8 = 45 x 0.0064 x 0.5132 = 0.1478. Option B is just 0.08^2, forgetting the 45 arrangements and the q^8 term, and option D omits the C(10,2) factor. Option A is roughly P(X <= 1), a different event.

questions.question: A machine produces items of which 8% are defective. An inspector randomly selects 10 items, and the number of defectives follows a binomial distribution. The probability that at most 1 item is defective is (to 4 d.p.):
questions.explanation: P(X <= 1) = P(X = 0) + P(X = 1) = 0.92^10 + 10 x 0.08 x 0.92^9 = 0.4344 + 0.3777 = 0.8121. Options D and C are only one of the two terms each, and option B is 1 - 0.8121, the probability of 2 or more defectives.

questions.question: A machine produces items of which 8% are defective. An inspector randomly selects 10 items, and the number of defectives follows a binomial distribution. The mean and standard deviation of the number of defective items are:
questions.explanation: For a binomial distribution the mean is np = 10 x 0.08 = 0.8 and the SD is sqrt(npq) = sqrt(10 x 0.08 x 0.92) = sqrt(0.736) = 0.858. Option D quotes the variance npq as the SD, and option C uses sqrt(np), forgetting q. Option A uses nq, the expected number of good items.

questions.question: The monthly revenue of a Lagos supermarket is normally distributed with a mean of N5.2 million and a standard deviation of N0.6 million. Given P(Z < 1.3333) = 0.9088, the probability that revenue in a given month exceeds N6.0 million is:
questions.explanation: Standardise: Z = (6.0 - 5.2)/0.6 = 0.8/0.6 = 1.3333, so P(X > 6.0) = P(Z > 1.3333) = 1 - 0.9088 = 0.0912. Option C is P(Z < 1.3333), the probability of revenue below N6.0 million, and option A is only the area between the mean and Z = 1.3333.

questions.question: The monthly revenue of a Lagos supermarket is normally distributed with a mean of N5.2 million and a standard deviation of N0.6 million. Given P(Z < 1.1667) = 0.8783 and P(Z < 1.00) = 0.8413, the probability that revenue in a given month is between N4.5 million and N5.8 million is:
questions.explanation: Z1 = (4.5 - 5.2)/0.6 = -1.1667 and Z2 = (5.8 - 5.2)/0.6 = 1.00. P(Z < -1.1667) = 1 - 0.8783 = 0.1217, so P(4.5 < X < 5.8) = 0.8413 - 0.1217 = 0.7196. Option B subtracts the two table values directly, ignoring that Z1 is negative, and option A is the probability of falling outside the interval.

questions.question: A single random experiment that has exactly two possible outcomes, usually called success and failure, is called a
questions.explanation: A Bernoulli trial is one experiment with only two outcomes, success with probability p and failure with probability q = 1 - p. Option D describes events occurring randomly over an interval of time or space, not a single two-outcome trial. Options C and A are not names used for a two-outcome experiment.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a condition for a binomial experiment?

options.a: The number of occurrences is counted over a continuous interval of time
options.b: The trials are independent of one another
options.c: The number of trials n is fixed in advance
options.d: The probability of success p is the same on every trial

questions.explanation: Counting occurrences over a continuous interval of time is the setting for the Poisson distribution, not the binomial. A binomial experiment needs a fixed number of trials (option C), a constant probability of success (option D) and independent trials (option B), each with two outcomes.

questions.question: A quality inspector at a Lagos bottling plant picks 20 bottles from a large batch and counts how many are underfilled, where each bottle independently has a 5% chance of being underfilled. The number of underfilled bottles follows a
questions.explanation: There is a fixed number of trials (20 bottles), each with two outcomes (underfilled or not), a constant probability 0.05 and independence, so the count is binomial. Option C would fit a count of events in an interval with no fixed number of trials. Options D and A are continuous distributions and cannot model a whole-number count out of 20.

questions.question: The number of customer calls received by a bank call centre in Ikeja per 10-minute interval, with calls arriving randomly and independently at a constant average rate, is best modelled by the
questions.explanation: A count of random, independent events in a fixed interval of time at a constant average rate is the classic Poisson setting. Option A needs a fixed number of trials, which a call count does not have. Option D models the time between such calls, not the number of calls, and option C would make every count equally likely.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an assumption of the Poisson distribution?

options.a: The average rate of occurrence is constant over the interval
options.b: The probability of an occurrence is proportional to the length of the interval
options.c: There is a fixed number of trials n, each with probability of success p
options.d: Occurrences are independent of one another

questions.explanation: A fixed number of trials with success probability p is a binomial condition; the Poisson distribution counts occurrences in an interval and has no fixed n. Options D, A and B are genuine Poisson assumptions: independent occurrences, a constant rate, and probability proportional to interval length.

questions.question: A distinctive property of the Poisson distribution with parameter lambda is that

options.a: its mean and its variance are both equal to lambda
options.b: its mean is lambda and its variance is lambda squared
options.c: its mean is np and its variance is npq
options.d: its mean is lambda and its variance is sqrt(lambda)

questions.explanation: For a Poisson variable, E(X) = lambda and Var(X) = lambda, so the mean equals the variance. Options B and D give the wrong variance (sqrt(lambda) is actually the standard deviation). Option C gives the binomial mean and variance.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes the binomial distribution from the Poisson distribution?

options.a: The binomial distribution always has mean equal to variance, while the Poisson does not
options.b: A binomial variable can take values only from 0 to n, while a Poisson variable has no fixed upper limit
options.c: A binomial variable is continuous, while a Poisson variable is discrete
options.d: The Poisson distribution requires a fixed number of trials, while the binomial does not

questions.explanation: A binomial count is out of a fixed n trials, so it runs from 0 to n, whereas a Poisson count (0, 1, 2, ...) has no upper limit. Option C is wrong because both are discrete. Option A reverses the facts, since it is the Poisson whose mean equals its variance, and option D reverses which distribution has a fixed number of trials.

questions.question: For any probability density function f(x) of a continuous random variable, the total area under the curve is

options.c: equal to the mean of X

questions.explanation: The total area under a pdf represents the probability of all possible values together, which must be 1. Option A would mean no value is possible, option C confuses area with the centre of the distribution, and option B mixes up probability with percentage.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a property of the normal distribution?

options.a: It is positively skewed with a long right tail
options.b: It is symmetric about its mean
options.c: Its mean, median and mode are equal

questions.explanation: The normal curve is symmetric, so it has no skew at all. Options D, B and C are genuine properties: the curve is bell-shaped, symmetric about the mean, and that symmetry makes the mean, median and mode coincide.

questions.question: The tails of the normal curve get closer and closer to the horizontal axis but never touch it. This property is described as
questions.explanation: Asymptotic means the curve approaches the horizontal axis without ever meeting it, so the normal curve extends from minus infinity to plus infinity. Option B describes the peakedness (kurtosis) of the normal curve, not its tails. Option C means two peaks, and option A means the curve is cut off, both of which are wrong for the normal curve.

questions.question: A particular normal distribution is completely determined by its
questions.explanation: Once you know the mean (centre) and the standard deviation (spread), the whole normal curve is fixed. Options B and A are wrong because in a normal curve the mean, median and mode are all equal, so they give only the centre and say nothing about spread. Option C does not define a normal curve.

questions.question: The standard normal distribution has
questions.explanation: The standard normal variable Z is a normal variable with mean 0 and standard deviation 1, obtained by converting x to z = (x - mean)/SD. Options C and A are impossible because a standard deviation of 0 means no spread at all. Option D has the wrong mean.

questions.question: In statistics, the z-score of an observation tells us

options.a: the difference between the observation and the median, in original units
options.b: the probability that the observation occurs
options.c: the percentage of observations below it
options.d: how many standard deviations the observation lies above or below the mean

questions.explanation: A z-score, z = (x - mean)/SD, measures distance from the mean in units of standard deviation. Option B confuses z with a probability, which must be read from the table. Option C describes a percentile rank, and option A uses original units instead of standard deviations.

questions.question: A student's score in an ACS examination has a z-score of -0.75. This means the score is

options.c: in the bottom 75% of the class

questions.explanation: A negative z-score means the value lies below the mean, and its size is measured in standard deviations, so -0.75 is three-quarters of a standard deviation below the mean. Option A gets the direction wrong. Option D treats the z-score as marks rather than standard deviations, and option C treats it as a percentage.

questions.question: The normal distribution gives a good approximation to the binomial distribution when

options.a: n is large and p is very close to 0
options.b: n is small and p is close to 0
options.c: n is large and p is not too close to 0 or 1

questions.explanation: When n is large and p is not extreme, the binomial histogram becomes nearly bell-shaped, so a normal curve with mean np and variance npq fits it well. Option A (large n, very small p) is the setting where the Poisson approximation is used instead. Options B and D give a skewed or degenerate binomial that a normal curve fits badly.

questions.question: When a binomial probability P(X <= 10) is approximated by a normal distribution using the continuity correction, it becomes
questions.explanation: The continuity correction treats the whole number 10 as the interval from 9.5 to 10.5, so 'at most 10' must include everything up to 10.5. Option C would cut off the value 10 itself. Option A ignores the correction, and option B adds a whole unit instead of half a unit.

questions.question: The exponential distribution has the 'memoryless' property. This means that

options.a: it is symmetric about its mean
options.b: its mean is equal to its variance
options.c: every value in its range is equally likely
options.d: the probability of waiting a further t minutes does not depend on how long you have already waited

questions.explanation: Memoryless means that, for example, the chance a machine survives another 5 hours is the same whether it has run 1 hour or 100 hours already. Option B describes the Poisson distribution. Option A is false since the exponential is skewed to the right, and option C describes the uniform distribution.

questions.question: If the number of arrivals per hour at a Lekki toll gate follows a Poisson distribution, then the time between successive arrivals follows the
questions.explanation: The exponential distribution models the continuous waiting time between events in a Poisson process. Option B counts successes in a fixed number of trials, option C is a symmetric bell curve, and option D is for a finite set of equally likely values; none of these describes the gap between Poisson arrivals.

questions.question: Which of the following random variables follows a discrete uniform distribution?

options.a: The number of heads when a fair coin is tossed 10 times
options.b: The height of a randomly chosen UNILAG student
options.c: The number of accidents on Third Mainland Bridge in a day
options.d: The number shown when a fair six-sided die is rolled once

questions.explanation: A fair die gives the values 1 to 6, each with the same probability 1/6, which is exactly a discrete uniform distribution. Option A is binomial, where middle values like 5 heads are more likely than 0 or 10. Option C is a Poisson-type count, and option B is a continuous variable.

questions.question: The graph of the probability density function of a continuous uniform distribution on the interval a to b is

options.a: a triangle with its peak at (a + b)/2
options.c: a curve that decreases steadily from a to b
options.d: a bell-shaped curve centred at (a + b)/2

questions.explanation: In a continuous uniform distribution every value between a and b is equally likely, so the pdf is a flat line at height 1/(b - a), giving a rectangle with area 1. Option D describes the normal curve, option C resembles the exponential shape, and option A is a triangular distribution.

questions.question: A binomial distribution is symmetric when
questions.explanation: When p = 0.5 success and failure are equally likely, so P(X = k) = P(X = n - k) and the distribution is symmetric for any n. Option D gives a distribution skewed to the right and option C gives one skewed to the left. Option A with n = 1 is just a single Bernoulli trial, which is symmetric only if p = 0.5.

questions.question: The Poisson distribution is commonly used to approximate the binomial distribution when

options.a: n is large and p is small
options.b: n is small and p is large

questions.explanation: When there are many trials and success is rare, binomial probabilities are well approximated by a Poisson with lambda = np. Option C (large n, p = 0.5) is better handled by the normal approximation. Options B and D have small n, where the binomial is easy to compute directly and the Poisson does not fit well.

questions.question: In a normal distribution, the proportion of the total area that lies to the left of the mean is
questions.explanation: Because the normal curve is symmetric about its mean and the total area is 1, exactly half of the area, 0.5, lies on each side of the mean. Options D and C are the approximate areas within 1 and 2 standard deviations of the mean, and option B is the area between the mean and one standard deviation on one side.

questions.question: Two normal distributions have the same mean, but distribution P has a larger standard deviation than distribution Q. Compared with Q, the curve of P is
questions.explanation: A larger standard deviation spreads the same total area of 1 over a wider range, so the curve must be flatter and wider. Option B describes a smaller standard deviation. Option D would need a larger mean, and option A is wrong because the standard deviations differ.

questions.question: Which of the following is a continuous probability distribution?
questions.explanation: The normal distribution describes a measured variable that can take any value on the real line, so it is continuous. Options D, A and B all assign probabilities to countable values such as 0, 1, 2, ..., so they are discrete distributions.

questions.question: A customer entering a Yaba electronics shop makes a purchase with probability 0.3. If X = 1 for a purchase and X = 0 otherwise (a Bernoulli variable), the variance of X is
questions.explanation: For a Bernoulli variable the variance is pq = 0.3 x 0.7 = 0.21. Option D is the mean p, option B is q, the probability of no purchase, and option A is sqrt(0.21), the standard deviation rather than the variance.

questions.question: Each loan application at a microfinance bank in Ibadan is rejected with probability 0.15, independently. For 20 applications, the mean number rejected is
questions.explanation: The binomial mean is np = 20 x 0.15 = 3. Option A is the variance npq, option C is the standard deviation sqrt(npq), and option D is nq, the expected number accepted.

questions.question: For a binomial distribution with n = 50 and p = 0.4, the variance is
questions.explanation: The binomial variance is npq = 50 x 0.4 x 0.6 = 12. Option B is the mean np, option A is the standard deviation sqrt(12), and option D is nq.

questions.question: For a binomial distribution with n = 100 and p = 0.2, the standard deviation is
questions.explanation: The standard deviation is sqrt(npq) = sqrt(100 x 0.2 x 0.8) = sqrt(16) = 4. Option C is the variance, option A is the mean np, and option B is sqrt(pq) without multiplying by n.

questions.question: A binomial distribution has mean 6 and variance 4.2. The values of n and p are
questions.explanation: Dividing variance by mean gives q = 4.2/6 = 0.7, so p = 0.3 and n = 6/0.3 = 20. Option D swaps p and q, which would make the mean 14. Options C and A give a mean of 6 but variances of 4.8 and 3.6, not 4.2.

questions.question: A sales agent in Surulere closes a sale on any visit with probability 0.4, independently. Out of 6 visits, the probability of exactly 2 sales is
questions.explanation: P(X = 2) = 6C2 x 0.4^2 x 0.6^4 = 15 x 0.16 x 0.1296 = 0.3110. Option B leaves out the coefficient 6C2 = 15. Option A swaps p and q, and option C is P(X <= 2), not exactly 2.

questions.question: Ten percent of eggs supplied to a Mushin bakery are cracked. In a random sample of 8 eggs (binomial), the probability that none is cracked is
questions.explanation: P(X = 0) = 0.9^8 = 0.4305, since all 8 eggs must be uncracked. Option B is the probability of at least one cracked egg, option A is P(X = 1), and option D is the probability for just one egg.

questions.question: The probability that a POS transaction at a Balogun market stall fails is 0.2, independently. In 5 transactions, the probability of at least one failure is
questions.explanation: P(at least one) = 1 - P(X = 0) = 1 - 0.8^5 = 1 - 0.3277 = 0.6723. Option D is P(X = 0) itself, option B is P(X = 1), and option C is P(X <= 1), none of which is 'at least one'.

questions.question: Five percent of bulbs from a supplier are defective. In a binomial sample of 10 bulbs, P(X <= 1), the probability of at most one defective, is
questions.explanation: P(X <= 1) = P(0) + P(1) = 0.95^10 + 10 x 0.05 x 0.95^9 = 0.5987 + 0.3151 = 0.9139. Options D and A are only one of the two terms, and option B is P(X >= 2).

questions.question: A UNILAG student answers each of 5 multiple-choice items correctly with probability 0.6, independently. The probability of at least 4 correct answers is
questions.explanation: P(X >= 4) = P(4) + P(5) = 5 x 0.6^4 x 0.4 + 0.6^5 = 0.2592 + 0.0778 = 0.3370. Option C is only P(X = 4), option B is only P(X = 5), and option A is P(X <= 3), the complement.

questions.question: Each of 4 independent generators in an estate starts on the first attempt with probability 0.9. The probability that all 4 start on the first attempt is
questions.explanation: All four must succeed, so P(X = 4) = 0.9^4 = 0.6561. Option C is the probability for a single generator, option A is the probability that all four fail, and option D is P(X = 3).

questions.question: Thirty percent of shoppers at a Lagos mall use a loyalty card. For a binomial sample of 40 shoppers, the mean and standard deviation of the number using a card are
questions.explanation: Mean = np = 40 x 0.3 = 12 and SD = sqrt(npq) = sqrt(40 x 0.3 x 0.7) = sqrt(8.4) = 2.8983. Option B gives the variance instead of the SD, option A uses nq for the mean, and option D takes the square root of the mean instead of npq.

questions.question: Breakdowns of BRT buses on a route follow a Poisson distribution with a mean of 2 per day. The probability of no breakdown on a given day is
questions.explanation: P(X = 0) = e^-2 x 2^0 / 0! = e^-2 = 0.1353. Option D is P(X = 1), option C is the probability of at least one breakdown, and option B uses e^-1 instead of e^-2.

questions.question: Typing errors on a page follow a Poisson distribution with mean 2 errors per page. The probability that a page has exactly 3 errors is
questions.explanation: P(X = 3) = e^-2 x 2^3 / 3! = 0.1353 x 8 / 6 = 0.1804. Option C is P(X = 2), option A is P(X <= 3), and option B divides by 2 instead of 3! = 6.

questions.question: Walk-in customers at a Ketu pharmacy arrive at an average of 1.5 per 15 minutes, following a Poisson distribution. The probability of at most 2 arrivals in a 15-minute period is
questions.explanation: P(X <= 2) = e^-1.5 (1 + 1.5 + 1.5^2/2) = 0.2231 x 3.625 = 0.8088. Option B is only P(X = 2), option A is P(X < 2), which leaves out X = 2, and option D is P(X > 2).

questions.question: The number of complaints received daily by a hostel porter follows a Poisson distribution with mean 0.8. The probability of at least one complaint on a given day is
questions.explanation: P(X >= 1) = 1 - P(X = 0) = 1 - e^-0.8 = 1 - 0.4493 = 0.5507. Option D is P(X = 0), option B is only P(X = 1), and option C is the mean, which is not a probability here.

questions.question: Cars arrive at a filling station in Ojota at an average rate of 6 per hour, following a Poisson distribution. The probability that exactly 1 car arrives in a 20-minute period is
questions.explanation: First rescale the rate: 20 minutes is 1/3 of an hour, so lambda = 6 x 1/3 = 2. Then P(X = 1) = 2e^-2 = 0.2707. Option A uses the hourly rate lambda = 6 without rescaling, option B uses lambda = 3 (a 30-minute period), and option C is P(X = 0) with lambda = 2.

questions.question: A small business in Oshodi receives an average of 3 customer complaints per day, following a Poisson distribution. The Poisson mean to use for the number of complaints in a 5-day working week is
questions.explanation: The Poisson mean is proportional to the length of the interval, so lambda for 5 days = 3 x 5 = 15. Option C keeps the daily rate unchanged, option D divides instead of multiplying, and option A adds the numbers instead of scaling.

questions.question: A Poisson random variable has variance 4. Its mean and standard deviation are
questions.explanation: For a Poisson distribution the mean equals the variance, so the mean is 4, and the standard deviation is sqrt(4) = 2. Option D swaps the two values, option B squares the variance instead of taking its root, and option C wrongly takes the mean as sqrt(4).

questions.question: Each of 200 parcels handled by a courier in Lagos has probability 0.01 of being damaged, independently. Using the Poisson approximation to the binomial, the probability that exactly 1 parcel is damaged is
questions.explanation: The Poisson approximation uses lambda = np = 200 x 0.01 = 2, so P(X = 1) = 2e^-2 = 0.2707. Option D is P(X = 0), option B is P(X <= 1), and option C is P(X >= 2).

questions.question: Power outages in a Surulere street follow a Poisson distribution with mean 3 per week. The probability of exactly 2 outages in a week is
questions.explanation: P(X = 2) = e^-3 x 3^2 / 2! = 0.0498 x 9 / 2 = 0.2240. Option C is P(X <= 2), option A is P(X = 1), and option D forgets to divide by 2!.

questions.question: A raffle at a UNILAG hall draws one ticket at random from tickets numbered 1 to 10, each equally likely (discrete uniform). The probability that the number drawn is at most 4 is
questions.explanation: There are 4 favourable values (1, 2, 3, 4) out of 10 equally likely values, so P(X <= 4) = 4/10 = 0.4. Option C counts only 3 values (X < 4), option A is the probability of one particular number, and option D is the probability of the lower half.

questions.question: For a fair die with values 1 to 6 (discrete uniform), the variance is given by (n^2 - 1)/12. The variance of the number shown is
questions.explanation: With n = 6, variance = (36 - 1)/12 = 35/12 = 2.9167. Option A is the standard deviation, option D is the mean, and option B uses 36/12 without subtracting 1.

questions.question: The time to process a document at a registry is uniformly distributed between 10 and 30 minutes. The height of its probability density function is
questions.explanation: For a uniform distribution on a to b, f(x) = 1/(b - a) = 1/(30 - 10) = 1/20 = 0.05. Option D is the width b - a itself, option B uses 1/b, and option A uses 1/a.

questions.question: The daily sales of a kiosk (in thousands of naira) are uniformly distributed between 20 and 50. The mean daily sales, in thousands of naira, is
questions.explanation: The mean of a uniform distribution is (a + b)/2 = (20 + 50)/2 = 35. Option C is (b - a)/2, half the width, option A is the width b - a, and option B is a + b without dividing by 2.

questions.question: A random variable is uniformly distributed between 0 and 12. Its variance is
questions.explanation: The variance of a uniform distribution is (b - a)^2/12 = 12^2/12 = 144/12 = 12. Option D is the mean (a + b)/2, option B is the standard deviation sqrt(12), and option C forgets to square (b - a).

questions.question: The travel time from Akoka to Yaba is uniformly distributed between 10 and 40 minutes. The probability that a trip takes between 15 and 25 minutes is
questions.explanation: For a uniform distribution, P(c < X < d) = (d - c)/(b - a) = (25 - 15)/(40 - 10) = 10/30 = 0.3333. Option C divides by 40 instead of the width 30, option D is 25/40, and option B has no basis in the formula.

questions.question: A random variable is uniformly distributed between 2 and 8. Its standard deviation is
questions.explanation: Variance = (b - a)^2/12 = 6^2/12 = 3, so SD = sqrt(3) = 1.7321. Option B is the variance, option D is the mean (2 + 8)/2, and option A is (b - a)/12 without squaring.

questions.question: The waiting time for a keke at a junction is uniformly distributed between 0 and 20 minutes. The probability of waiting more than 15 minutes is
questions.explanation: P(X > 15) = (20 - 15)/(20 - 0) = 5/20 = 0.25. Option B is P(X < 15), option C is the pdf height 1/20, and option D has no basis in the formula.

questions.question: Marks in a test are normally distributed with mean 60 and standard deviation 8. The z-score of a mark of 72 is
questions.explanation: z = (x - mean)/SD = (72 - 60)/8 = 12/8 = 1.5. Option B has the wrong sign, since 72 is above the mean. Option C inverts the fraction, and option A is the raw difference without dividing by the SD.

questions.question: The weight of bags of garri is normally distributed with mean 50 kg and standard deviation 4 kg. Given P(0 < Z < 1.25) = 0.3944, the probability that a bag weighs more than 55 kg is
questions.explanation: z = (55 - 50)/4 = 1.25, and P(Z > 1.25) = 0.5 - 0.3944 = 0.1056. Option C is the area between the mean and z = 1.25, option B is P(Z < 1.25), and option D wrongly subtracts the table value from 1 instead of 0.5.

questions.question: Monthly phone bills of students are normally distributed with mean N5,000 and standard deviation N1,000. Given P(0 < Z < 0.8) = 0.2881, the probability that a bill is less than N5,800 is
questions.explanation: z = (5,800 - 5,000)/1,000 = 0.8, so P(Z < 0.8) = 0.5 + 0.2881 = 0.7881. Option B is only the area between the mean and z = 0.8, option A is P(Z > 0.8), and option D is the area between -0.8 and 0.8.

questions.question: Daily output at a factory is normally distributed with mean 70 units and standard deviation 10 units. Given P(0 < Z < 1) = 0.3413 and P(0 < Z < 2) = 0.4772, the probability that output is between 60 and 90 units is
questions.explanation: z for 60 is -1 and z for 90 is 2. The two values are on opposite sides of the mean, so add the areas: 0.3413 + 0.4772 = 0.8185. Option C subtracts the areas, which is only right when both values are on the same side. Option B is the area within one SD, and option A is the area outside the interval.

questions.question: Monthly electricity use by households in an estate is normally distributed with mean 500 kWh and standard deviation 50 kWh. Given P(0 < Z < 1.5) = 0.4332, the probability that a household uses less than 425 kWh is
questions.explanation: z = (425 - 500)/50 = -1.5. By symmetry P(Z < -1.5) = P(Z > 1.5) = 0.5 - 0.4332 = 0.0668. Option A is the area between z = -1.5 and the mean, option B is P(Z > -1.5), and option D subtracts the table value from 1 instead of 0.5.

questions.question: Delivery times are normally distributed with mean 80 minutes and standard deviation 5 minutes. Given P(0 < Z < 1) = 0.3413 and P(0 < Z < 2) = 0.4772, the probability that a delivery takes between 85 and 90 minutes is
questions.explanation: z for 85 is 1 and z for 90 is 2, both above the mean, so subtract: 0.4772 - 0.3413 = 0.1359. Option D adds the areas, which applies only when the values lie on opposite sides of the mean. Options C and A are single table areas measured from the mean.

questions.question: Scores in an aptitude test are normally distributed with mean 200 and standard deviation 20. Given that P(Z > 1.645) = 0.05, the minimum score needed to be in the top 5% is
questions.explanation: x = mean + z x SD = 200 + 1.645 x 20 = 232.9. Option C uses z = -1.645, which marks the bottom 5%. Option A is just one SD above the mean, and option D uses z = 1.96, which marks the top 2.5%.

questions.question: The lifetime of a battery is normally distributed with mean 50 hours and standard deviation 5 hours. Given that P(Z < -1.28) is approximately 0.10, the lifetime below which the shortest-lasting 10% of batteries fall is about
questions.explanation: x = mean + z x SD = 50 + (-1.28)(5) = 50 - 6.4 = 43.6 hours. Option D uses +1.28, which marks the top 10%. Option B subtracts 1.28 without multiplying by the SD, and option A is simply one SD below the mean.

questions.question: IQ scores are normally distributed with mean 100 and standard deviation 15. By the empirical rule, the approximate percentage of scores between 70 and 130 is
questions.explanation: 70 and 130 are 2 standard deviations below and above the mean (100 - 30 and 100 + 30), and the empirical rule says about 95% of values lie within 2 SD. Option C is for 1 SD, option D is for 3 SD, and option A is the area on only one side of the mean.

questions.question: For a normal distribution, the empirical rule says about 68% of values lie within one standard deviation of the mean. The approximate percentage of values above (mean + 1 SD) is
questions.explanation: Outside one SD there is 100% - 68% = 32%, split equally between the two tails by symmetry, so about 16% lie above mean + 1 SD. Option B is the area between the mean and mean + 1 SD, option C is both tails together, and option A is the central area.

questions.question: The lifetimes of 1,000 bulbs are normally distributed with mean 800 hours and standard deviation 40 hours. Given P(0 < Z < 1.5) = 0.4332, the expected number of bulbs lasting more than 860 hours is about
questions.explanation: z = (860 - 800)/40 = 1.5, so P(X > 860) = 0.5 - 0.4332 = 0.0668, and 1,000 x 0.0668 is about 67 bulbs. Option A uses the area between the mean and z = 1.5, option C uses P(Z < 1.5), and option B subtracts the table value from 1 instead of 0.5.

questions.question: Customers arrive at a bank counter at an average rate of 4 per hour, and the time between arrivals follows an exponential distribution. The mean time between arrivals is
questions.explanation: The mean of an exponential distribution is 1/lambda = 1/4 hour = 15 minutes. Option D takes the rate itself as the mean time, option C multiplies 4 by 60 instead of dividing, and option B is the length of the whole hour.
